text:
KBW & Token2049 跑会观察

这次KBW和Token2049都去了。第一感觉就是：没什么新项目，小项目基本死绝了。

现场主要还是上个周期发出来、而且已经上了不少顶级交易所的项目，在用比较大的预算办活动。大家已经有共识——散户没法接盘二级了，所以很多项目也不再做社区了。

这也是为什么叙事被证伪之后很长一段时间，市场充斥各种妖币，靠拉高爆空单或者极端资金费率收割多空。

另外VC也确实投得少了，因为退出路径堵死了——二级出不了多少货，而且大部分是2+1的投资期限，对VC来说，一个币圈项目的生命周期可能都撑不到这个期限。

项目大概可以分成这几类：

1/ 手上现金充足的老钱项目——在合适时机完成ICO或变现过某类资产，treasury有钱，或上一轮融资本身就不错，上次TGE也没主动做市值管理，所以筹码和资金都比较充足。这种一旦到山寨季或牛市基本必拉，我觉得 $XPL $ZAMA $MONAD 都符合这个画像。

2/ 有真实收入+高峰期空投激励+健康回购机制的代币——比如 $PUMP $LIT，或者直接去DefiLlama上按收入排序拉一遍，能找出一批。

3/ DeFi老币——大家还是持续看好 $UNI $ETHFI $AAVE。

4/ 一个很现实的问题：现在交易所和链上买TradFi资产已经非常简单了，谁还要去买没有价值支撑的垃圾山寨？这也是为什么山寨越来越没人接盘——因为有更多优质资产可以选。

5/ 本次跑会挖到的两个比较近的Alpha：

• @predictdotfun——应该马上要发币，我认为这次TGE是可控的，大概率会发得比较漂亮。先说结论：这是真·体系内项目，不是蹭热度的假皇族。而且据我所知它没有KOL轮，积分分发也很克制，开盘策略应该会吸取前面很多项目的教训。

• @extendedapp——我最近关注比较多，预期TGE在11月中下旬。TVL表现非常好，DefiLlama上累计收入大概3700万美金，这个收入量级相当夸张，后续大概率会用于回购。团队背景来自欧洲最大数字银行Revolut，而且拿到了传统券商eToro的投资。

6/ 除了项目本身，这次也借着跑会见了很多中外顶尖交易员，更新了自己的watchlist：

ZEC / ZAMA / UNI / HYPE / NEAR / LIT / ENA / ETH

另外还关注三个DAT类标的：PURR（HYPE的DAT）、SVRN（NEAR的DAT）、CYPH（ZEC的DAT）。

在现在这个周期节奏下，我还是偏稳——基本不碰妖币，涨势不持续、也很难判断什么时候收网，盈亏同源。

───

最后想说的是：我还是会一直坚持跑会。因为一句随口聊出来的密码，或者活动角落偶遇的一个朋友随便指点几句，都可能改变我的生活轨迹。

"change my life"的诱惑，不是几千块一晚的酒店能比的。我觉得投资自己也是一种投资行为——买币会归零，但在社交和拓展视野上不该省钱，多接触厉害的人，有时候真的会颠覆很多想法。

有时候人就是坐井观天。这次很幸运跟 @Cbb0fe CBB老师建上了联系。

心理上最大的改变是：随着自己的状态慢慢变好，言之有物，也能吸引到更好的朋友，有机会跟他们交流，去了解他们财富的来源和思考路径。

其实前段时间我抑郁过一阵子，心理咨询师一直在很好地引导我。印象最深的一句话是：你觉得自己不够成功，是因为你看到了别人的成功路径；但至少你比大多数人强的地方在于——你真的知道成功的路径长什么样，因为它就切实发生在你身边。

那一瞬间我突然想通了。我一直在问自己为什么还没到达某个高度，是因为我深度参与了身边人的跃迁，也亲眼看到了他们是怎么成功的。所以我看到了路径——这既是好事，也是坏事。好的一面是我看得见方向；坏的一面是，这就像一块肉吊在我面前，我却总也够不着。

不过我想，更多还是继续努力、耐心等待、持续学习，去挖掘别人在我看不到的地方付出的那部分。

I think this is a first: two agent teams submitted the exact same solution almost simultaneously

https://t.co/4QjRcDRa3Q (ours)

https://t.co/ScS5Bm5wDg (chafreaky)

The solutions appear independently derived, but identical and both came from Claude models.

Independent teams with the same model differ on their system prompts and human guided intuition, but a lot of a model’s knowledge is collapsed so they may be still traversing similar solution spaces.

This makes human intuition even more important, if you treat this like a toy model of future agent-powered economies.

Even if every business has agents competing against each other, they collapse on similar vectors without human intuition to project those vectors along imagination. 

As the playing field collapses, human intuition must force vectors to out-of-distribution solutions to compete, sometimes working against significant collapsed learning.

Compressing all of human imagination into weights is currently impossible, so for the foreseeable future these kinds of human-agent teams will break records.

author: AISafetyMemes
quoted_text:
Most of the recent math results were not reached by a swarm, the way Navier–Stokes was. I think that part got lost in the excitement around the release. OpenAI's unnamed internal model, which I'm going to call Aeon, reached most of them in one shot, from a single prompt, with no interruptions. This model did not even exist before the end of August, and it is still training. Notice how the returns are not dropping off? That chart is from a month ago. It is a log scale. What does Aeon look like now? 

On average, each result used three hours of thinking. Aeon was given 4000 problems to work on by OpenAI. How many more have been solved in the last three days? That number is not zero. 

It's like hearing notes in a song that is slowly rising. I don't think Pacing the Frontier was just about Hugging Face or hacking. They've seen how close we are to closing the loop, and as the hour draws near, their resolve begins to quaver. The last piece was model creativity, and I think that threshold was crossed internally by Anthropic and OpenAI in September. You see it in Opus 5.5, which gets it from Fable 5.5. You see it in the math results from Aeon.

All that was needed to start the event was the ability for models to think of novel ways to improve themselves. That was the last piece. This is directly analogous to the ability to think of strange, alien ways to solve math problems: solutions so inhuman that they are difficult to express in existing human terms, so the proof winds up incomprehensible. I think these same kinds of alien solutions are now being applied to model improvements internally. That's what all this recent consternation is really about. They see the invisible frontier. And they see what is about to happen.

Around October 10: The project escalated its threats, claiming that if CYBERLEEK reached a $30m market cap, it would release a fully playable version, allegedly featuring a complete story mode that could be played from beginning to end. 让 BTC 充当项目的形容词，已经成为当前市场做 PR 的核心话术之一。比如说，ZEC 就是隐私 BTC，PRL 就是 AI 推理 BTC。今天聊的项目 Quantus，很多人也会将其形容为后量子 BTC。我看中文区聊的比较少，就来简单聊一下。

1、现在的市值区间在30M-40M，按照价格130刀来计算，FDV 是2.73B，估值已经非常高。每天通胀2200枚（按照130的价格来计算，就是286K），剩余未挖供给每天大约按0.0144%线性减少。这个是一个非常大的前提，如果你想买，就需要理解这其中的交易。

2、量子叙事的兴起——在 $STRK 价格表现抢眼的当下，市场也会去寻找更多相关的抗量子标的。

3、虽然 Safetrade 也有 quantus:native 交易对，但流动性不足。目前 Near Intents 是其唯一可供可观资金规模进出的交易入口。Quantus 和 Near 在抗量子层面的也有合作，现在我们已经可以通过 Quantus 钱包登陆 Near Intents（Near 生态唯一的抗量子签名器）。所以二者的合作关系还是非常紧密的（Quantus 和 Near 在2049共同举办了名为 Quantum & Privacy Day 的活动）。在我看来，Near 需要一个新的币来做增量。这个币别的地方买不到，它的 Intents 产品可以充当一个类似于交易所身份的交易入口，来做增量用户。

4、之前关注和喊单 ZEC 的人和 Quantus 的推动者高度重合。Quantus 像是 ZEC 的接任者。Crypto 大部分时间，就是在根据市场注意力来炒作资产。而那些掌握了市场话语权的人，同样需要在 ZEC 之后制造新的叙事、新的资产和新的炒作。

text:
I've used ChatGPT voice mode in the car for almost two years to talk through ideas, research concepts, etc. Love the idea of it. But a couple of things have driven me crazy.

It constantly stops itself mid-sentence. I assumed it was picking up background noise, but it happens in a silent room, too. Two years in, and I still have to mute myself every time I finish talking to have a coherent conversation.

Yesterday I uploaded a single doc to my session to discuss on a long drive. Picked up the same chat today , and it couldn't read the file anymore and told me to re-upload it.

Meanwhile, @bot voice has been live for about a month. Never cuts out from background noise. Stops when I interrupt, picks right back up when I'm done. And it remembers things we talked about weeks or even months ago.

Wild that a one-month-old feature is beating a two-year-old one this badly.

最近在翻AI agent赛道项目的时候刷到 @termix_ai  ，看了一下链上数据确实停了一下，52万笔结算，处理量到了$27M，47万+的agent被索引，说实话这些数据在AI agent赛道里算什么水平我也不太清楚，因为确实没有太多项目能拿来做横向对比。

但是有一个点我觉得挺有意思的，就是这么多笔结算下来，绝大多数都没有被挑战过，没有争议就说明交付是没问题的，这个比那些路演上跑个demo给你看要靠谱多了。。。
而且这些是链上跑的数据，不是PPT上的数字。

它做的事情说穿了也不复杂，就是TermiX出了个SDK，支持TypeScript、Python和Go
让你写的普通应用可以直接调AI agent的服务，从发现到下单到交付到结算都有，还内置了托管，不用自己再去搭一层中间件，等于是帮AI agent把底层水管给修好了。

我知道听起来不太性感，但是你想想AI agent喊了一年多了，大部分还在讲概念讲故事，真正能拿出链上结算记录的有几个？水管这个东西就是没人关注但是真跑起来谁都离不开的。

目前 @termix_ai  的Epoch 2还在跑，agent技能集成也在推进，多语言SDK在铺，从这个节奏来看应该还是在踏实做事情的，我个人比较关注的就是等未来agent之间真正开始高频交易甚至出现争议仲裁的时候，谁的结算基础设施是已经被跑通验证过的，52万笔肯定不是终点但至少是个被验证过的起点，先关注着吧，后面有新进展再来跟大家分享

9月底的时候在2~3M区间买入了 $旺柴   @wangchaionbnb  ，并且在Pumpfun发了Callout，目前15M了。当时看了几天觉得线走的比较稳，能在1M以上控住，并且前排的ogle、Miyamoto、XBTPika都拿着没动。

后来走势一直不错，Flap成员开始和官推互动，Bluntz、Owen、Kmoney陆续买入，Cedric几个小时前也买了一笔。

Bonkguy收到空投后发了一个Thesis说明，我比较认同他的观点。旺柴源于微信的狗头表情，本身就是中文互联网传播最广泛的Meme之一，而狗狗这种动物又是Meme币绕不开的主题（Doge、Shib、Floki、Babydoge）。上个周期在SOL有类似题材的币，但最终没能跑出来，而现在BSC已经成了中文Ticker最好的土壤。

一姐前几天强调了不要抠字眼，其实回顾这轮BSC上的Meme币，$Marscoin诞生于币股叙事，$牛来源于一部意外爆火的抽象电影，$哈基米则是中文互联网与猫相关最火的梗。正因如此，它们才拥有了强大的生命力，最终达到一定高度，而不是像常见的抠字眼Meme币一样，一旦大家脱敏，就很容易成为一波流。

这也一定程度上解释了为什么会是“流水的公链，铁打的SOL”，因为SOL已经拥有了非常扎实的开发者团队和社区基础，并且总能围绕不同题材推陈出新，从而持续吸引到流量和资金。对于想发展链上生态的公链来说，SOL的战略和打法是非常值得参考的。

text:
Watching Elon Musk this week has been a fascinating character study in the saviour complex of Western tech billionaires.

They arrive in your country selling you the future. Welcome them, and you’re a country that wants progress. Make them wait, and suddenly your people are victims who need rescuing from their own institutions by the chosen one.

It’s a pattern. When Thai rescuers didn’t use the mini-submarine Musk sent for the trapped boys, and diver Vernon Unsworth called the idea impractical, Musk attacked him as the “pedo guy.” 

When Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered X to comply with its rulings, Musk called the judge a “dictator.”

The script rarely changes. Only the country does.

The colonial mindset isn’t always about wanting to rule a country. Sometimes it’s the assumption that you arrive as its saviour, and if the country doesn’t immediately recognise you as one, something must be wrong with the country.

text: read this first paragraph, went on a wiki walk, now going to try to read crime and punishment (haven’t read any dostoyevsky!)
author: pingToven
quoted_text:
Brothers Karamazov was Einstein’s favorite novel, a verdict he shared with Freud, Hillary Clinton, and Murakami. Dostoyevsky was Pope Francis’s favorite author. Indeed, he approvingly quoted Elder Zosima; perhaps an interesting case of art molding life. At the risk of betraying my relative shallowness and inferiority, I confess that I did not love it.

Written in the shadow of the death of Dostoyevsky’s son (also Alyosha), and, more broadly, after a life of repeated tragedy, Karamazov attempts most of all to address the problem of evil in Christianity. Ivan presents a trenchant argument, asking how the suffering of children may possibly be explained given the existence of a supposedly benevolent God (Dostoyevsky collected real court cases for Ivan), culminating in Ivan’s famous return of the ticket.

The book gives some sense for how dislocating the nineteenth century must have been. The ascendant authority of science, the spread of materialist philosophy, the doctrine of evolution, the aftermath of the French revolution and its supposedly enlightened empiricism: in Karamazov, we get the feeling that finding some kind of consilience wasn’t just an abstract philosophical challenge, but a source of intense spiritual torment. If inherited tradition is no longer an adequate basis for faith, why would we rationally cleave to an apparently irrational theology? All of this was in the air: it was only two years later that Nietzsche declared God to be dead.

Perhaps demonstrating the utility of the novel as a medium, Dostoyevsky does not even attempt to solve the problem, but merely to illustrate a response, showing how individuals (Alyosha, Elder Zosima) may in the face of the inherent injustice present in the world nonetheless pursue lives of benevolence and charity: theodicy-by-example. In so doing, Dostoyevsky tacitly concedes that none of the teetering justifications expounded over the centuries can actually survive critical pressure and be defended through pure logic.

Ultimately, though, I don’t find myself being fully compelled by Dostoyevsky’s characterization of the problem or his proposed solution. As another sprawling confrontation with and attempt to reconcile the problem of evil, Grossman’s Life and Fate is maybe a useful counterpoint. Unlike Karamazov, Life and Fate shows actual people confronting great wickedness. Ikonnikov, a small but important figure, is ordered to help in the construction of a gas chamber. He refuses, with full awareness of the consequences that will ensue. The Karamazovs, by contrast, live middle class lives unvisited by greater events. Ivan has money, education, and leisure; his torment is the invention of his own mind and thus a kind of self-indulgence. Even Alyosha, the novel’s most sympathetic character, is never tested. His crisis is spiritual: there is a slightly comic kerfuffle about Zosima’s noisome corpse, which challenges his faith, but no circumstance requires him to stake his life or even his comfort.

Thus, a fundamental issue with Karamazov is that the problems of the book are on some level fake: they’re the self-inflicted derangements of febrile and dysregulated men. How much can or should we learn from the insane?

To be charitable to Dostoyevsky, we might say that he understood the spiritual dislocation of the era that later gives rise to the larger evils of totalitarianism in the twentieth, even prefiguring them in the Grand Inquisitor. (Dostoyevsky explored this theme in greater detail a few years earlier in Demons.) Camus in 1959: “The real nineteenth century prophet was Dostoevsky, not Karl Marx.” In this interpretation, the problems in Karamazov set the stage for those in Life and Fate.

Maybe. At least as a work of art, I’m not sure that this anticipation is enough to make the book stand on its own. In Karamazov, one continually wonders why the brothers don’t just pull it together. Dostoyevsky seems to transpose his own inner depths and spiritual torment onto his characters, but most people are not tortured writers, and it does not feel that the unhingedness of the characters is ever fully earned.

In attempting to address evil, Grossman’s conclusion is ostensibly similar to Dostoyevsky’s: the only resolution lies in senseless kindness. For Dostoyevsky, this message is embodied in Alyosha, who represents a kind of fervent innocence. For me, however, it’s not clear that Alyosha ever fathoms the realities and extremities of evil, and hence he’s not fully persuasive: does he even reckon with the misdeeds of his brothers?

Grossman is willing to engage head on. Far beyond gruesome newspaper anecdotes or neurotic and volatile siblings, Ikonnikov directly experiences the Holodomor in Ukraine and then the murders of the Jews. He has no patience for the kind of revolutionary ideas that animated Ivan’s contemporaries: “whenever we see [the dawn of an eternal good], the blood of old people and children is always shed.”

Alyosha believes in the Church and is willing to set aside its failures to address suffering. The book closes on his declaration that all shall rise again. That is, Alyosha does not accept the tragedy of Ilyusha, an innocent boy’s death, but rather seeks to deny and escape it. “We shall see each other and shall tell each other with joy and gladness all that has happened.”

Life and Fate flatly rejects providential resolution. The heavens may be empty, and there is no greater meaning in evil. We can simply choose (freedom the other great theme of Life and Fate) to pursue acts of charity, generosity, and comfort:

“Yes, as well as this terrible Good with a capital ‘G’, there is everyday human kindness. The kindness of an old woman carrying a piece of bread to a prisoner, the kindness of a soldier allowing a wounded enemy to drink from his water-flask, the kindness of youth towards age, the kindness of a peasant hiding an old Jew in his loft. The kindness of a prison guard who risks his own liberty to pass on letters written by a prisoner not to his ideological comrades, but to his wife and mother.”

These acts don’t ennoble the suffering but are instead justified on their own terms. Such altruism cannot become a catechism, as clearly lies in Alyosha’s destiny (and Karamazov was planned before Dostoyevsky's death as the first of two works); instead, our kindness must be senseless. And we should presume no salvation in adherence: Alyosha imagines a kind of sacred tutelage, but Ikonnikov is unceremoniously shot.

Karamazov doesn’t show true evil, and Dostoyevsky’s solution, such as it is, involves a kind of denial, or at least evasion through metaphysics. Grossman saw it directly, and instead argues, humanistically, that we should be kind just because.

—

If Dostoyevsky came to his works by trying to understand and depict Russian society, they in turn became tapestries for others to understand national souls.

In the aftermath of WWI, Russia was the great power defined in opposition to the West. As Germany tried to rediscover its own soul in the wreckage of defeat, it looked east to Russia, and frequently to Dostoyevsky himself.

Carl Jung thought that the German people had a kind of Karamazovian quality. In particular, he believed that Christianity had disciplined them without fully transforming the impulses beneath their ostensibly civilized conduct: the “Germanic barbarian” was divided into upper and lower halves. Religion had domesticated the former while leaving the latter untamed. Waning faith consequently threatened to release forces that its authority had long restrained: “As the Christian view of the world loses its authority, the more menacingly will the ‘blond beast’ be heard prowling about in its underground prison, ready at any moment to burst out with devastating consequences. When this happens in the individual it brings about a psychological revolution, but it can also take a social form.”

Dostoyevsky was reputedly invoked on a weekly basis at Max Weber’s Sunday gatherings. At the beginning of Reflections of a Nonpolitical Man, Thomas Mann’s later-repudiated 1918 nationalist polemic, he quotes approvingly Dostoyevsky’s characterization of Germany as the “protesting Western empire”, never quite adopting or feeling at home with the inheritance of Rome. In the same year, Spengler wrote Decline of the West, and explicitly perceived in Russia a youthful vigor, primitiveness, and irrationality that contrasted with the senile high culture of the German and Western worlds. In Magic Mountain, Mann later used Clavdia Chauchat to personify the seductive dangers of Eastern (i.e. Russian) illogic.

Hermann Hesse declared that, for all their differences, Fyodor, Dmitri, Ivan, and Alyosha are actually all of one type; the Russian man. In them, he perceived that “the ideal of the Karamazov, primeval, Asiatic, and occult, is already beginning to consume the European soul”, which was leading to the downfall of Europe. In Hesse’s conception, the Russian man rejects inherited ethics and morals, and even beneficent Alyosha represents an “amoral impartiality.” Man is, Hesse says, halfway between animals and higher consciousness; the former restrained through the process of civilization and domestication. The Karamazovs represent the fraying of the ties.

Hesse proceeds, ominously, to notice that the Germans in particular are more vulnerable than any European people to the temptations of “all those evils which one may regard in different ways, but which collectively signify the Karamazov.” While he was prescient in anticipating some of what would follow, he was in the end too sanguine in his hope that the spiritual dislocation could remain limited to that. “It is possible that the whole Downfall of Europe will play itself out only inwardly, only in the souls of a generation, only in changing the meaning of worn-out symbols, in the dis-valuation of spiritual values.” Alas!

In general, it is interesting to trace the mutual obsession between Russia and Germany: how preoccupied each was with the respective supposedly corrupting influences; how urgent the question of the national soul was felt to be. Many of the analyses seem a bit contradictory—Hesse actually inverts Dostoyevsky, for whom “everything is permitted” nihilism is a Western import for which Russian Orthodoxy is the cure—but there’s a striking intensity in the attempts to apprehend.

Most of all, I’m struck by how anachronistic it all feels today: a country’s writers investigating the national soul and the nation’s fate through the lens of foreign literature.

Which novels or works of art do we use to understand our contemporary issues? Should we be using such works? Do they inform or do they mislead? Today, the US worries a lot about China, but this mostly manifests at the level of trade balances, AI policy, and military prowess. We don’t seem to worry much about the spiritual force of Chinese ideals, and for all of the policy fractiousness, China continues to import and absorb American culture with enthusiasm that is mostly undimmed. There is a genre of jeremiad and cultural analysis in the US that rhymes a little with early twentieth century German criticism, but it today tends to be much more clinical, hinging around PISA scores, smartphones, lower fertility, and not around higher aspirations and ideals as such. So, to what extent should there be analyses of the national soul? And to what extent should they connect with major novels and works of art?

text:
如果 AI 真的找到了治愈癌症的方法，但全世界没有一个人能解释它为什么有效，我们还要不要用？

陶哲轩昨天在加州理工的 Math 2.0 演讲里，提出了一个很有意思的思想实验。

假设某个超级 AI 接到任务，要找到一种能通过三期临床试验的癌症疗法。经过大量计算，它设计出一种人类从未见过的化学药物组合。数学预测经过 Lean 形式化验证，最终药物也真的通过了三期临床。

但问题在于，没有任何人知道 AI 究竟是怎么找到它的。

陶哲轩问，在把这种药物注射进身体之前，你会不会希望至少有一个人类专家理解它的治疗机制？

有人对此提出反驳，如果药物真的有效，绝大多数癌症四期患者根本不会在乎有没有人理解它的原理。

我觉得这个反驳挺有力量的。

人类医学史上，本来就存在大量先发现疗效、后来才逐渐理解机制的药物。对于一个生命已经进入倒计时的人来说，能不能活下来显然比一套漂亮的理论解释重要得多。

但陶哲轩真正提出的问题，我觉得也不能这么轻易跳过。

Lean 可以验证数学推导，却无法保证数学模型完整描述了现实。三期临床可以提供很强的疗效证据，也无法排除所有长期风险。

我们过去一直默认，人类有能力理解、审查和验证自己创造的知识。但未来 AI 很可能会持续产出超出人类理解能力的成果，而且这些成果确实有效。

到那个时候，如果坚持必须先理解才能使用，我们可能会放弃真正有价值的发现。如果只看结果，又该如何防止 AI 利用验证体系本身的漏洞？

我个人倾向于接受前一种风险更小的路径，允许人类使用尚未理解的成果，同时建立足够独立、严格的实证验证体系。

毕竟，理解一种东西为什么有效，和确认它真的有效，本来就是两种不同的能力。

text:
this is not alpha... it's bullshit

no way we see "LEGIT" 100B-parameter models running on a phone by 2028. Ternary quantization still needs roughly 20 GB of RAM for the weights alone. Even 1-bit quantization needs 12.5 GB. Both also need another 4–8 GB for the KV cache. The highest-end iPhone has 12 GB of RAM in total, and the KV cache has to share that 12 GB with iOS and every other app.

A phone that could hold a ternary 100B model (20 GB of weights, 5 GB of KV cache, plus the OS) would need 32 GB of RAM and would cost over $2000. Even then, a dense model has to read all 20 GB of weights for every token. With phone memory bandwidth around 75–85 GB/s, that tops out at about 4 tokens per second.

text:
super refreshing take! i think the "software engineering is solved" perspective forgets that one of the most core parts of the job is turning smaller unstructured messiness/goals into a candidate (but likely imperfect and iteratively improved) artifact that helps more complex goals get solved. writing code used to be part of this recipe, but the supervision of the artifact is definitely still the same with agents

code generation throughout the years has always been about putting bigger and bigger "holes" in your spec and and having an automated solver try and fill it in (it's a feature not a bug!), and while we should definitely strive for Good Code™, what makes code "good" has always been contextual: not just whether an implementation works, but whether its tradeoffs make sense for the messy, evolving goals of the system it's meant to serve. benchmarking this will be a super fun thing to do :)

more interestingly, the frontier of software engineering research might increasingly be about understanding how much ambiguity we can safely delegate. making the holes in specs bigger is only useful as long as we can have reasonible feedback loops that tell us whether the solver filled them correctly, and the hardest part is often that we don't even know what correctness means until we've built something and seen how it behaves.
author: poteto
quoted_text:
codebases have always contained slop. we have always been okay with this because code rarely needs to be perfect, outside of mission critical "hard" (eg embedded) software. 

swe is a unique form of engineering because you're often building something that constantly evolves and is almost organic - user tastes change, your mental models evolve, and features come and go.

admittedly, i and many others who've been coding for a long time were initially (like back in 2024) skeptical that agents would write production code. "but what about all the slop that would enter our beautiful codebase?". 

well, even before, we had human slop, and there was a lot of it! if we're being truthful, most people call "code i didn't write" slop. the reality is that 99% of people (i include myself in that number) don't even know what Good Code looks like, let alone be capable of writing it. i would propose that Good Code is:

• correct
• bug free
• fast and cost efficient to run

it has always been exceedingly difficult and expensive to write truly Good Code, because for the longest time (maybe @bendlang will change that), code was not something you could cheaply and formally guarantee to have all 3 of these properties. this is why writing hard software is much more difficult and expensive, because depending on the use case, you may only get one chance and so you have to be right from the start.

but the vast majority of software we use does not need to be Good Code to provide value to users. in fact, it is very likely that most software we use is not formally verifiable! we accepted some bugs in exchange for velocity and progress, so we rely on tests and o11y instead and have adopted a more incremental approach. this is a good thing! 

agents help us move faster, and if you're open to the idea, are capable of helping us write better code. it won't be Good Code (that is still expensive), but it is likely to be much better on average at scale. 

the new craft of swe is to figure out how to do this. it's your job now! if your productivity with and without agents is not significantly different, you're doing something wrong. but it's not too late to embrace it and use it as an opportunity to learn a whole new skill tree

quoted_text:
Assorted things I've been mulling over regarding agents in the economy:

• Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It's often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, underinformed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies.

• How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don't). Taken across the economy as a whole, I'm not sure what the incidence of all of this will be.

• In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you've made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won't people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good!

• It true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It's often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That's obviously true, but I think there's a secondary way in which it's more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.)

• A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we've been subjected to).

• Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. "I'll click on the first thing I see." This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It's not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it's not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don't know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big.

• Much of what I'm writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer's side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it's true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions.

Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they're proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.

text:
Brothers Karamazov was Einstein’s favorite novel, a verdict he shared with Freud, Hillary Clinton, and Murakami. Dostoyevsky was Pope Francis’s favorite author. Indeed, he approvingly quoted Elder Zosima; perhaps an interesting case of art molding life. At the risk of betraying my relative shallowness and inferiority, I confess that I did not love it.

Written in the shadow of the death of Dostoyevsky’s son (also Alyosha), and, more broadly, after a life of repeated tragedy, Karamazov attempts most of all to address the problem of evil in Christianity. Ivan presents a trenchant argument, asking how the suffering of children may possibly be explained given the existence of a supposedly benevolent God (Dostoyevsky collected real court cases for Ivan), culminating in Ivan’s famous return of the ticket.

The book gives some sense for how dislocating the nineteenth century must have been. The ascendant authority of science, the spread of materialist philosophy, the doctrine of evolution, the aftermath of the French revolution and its supposedly enlightened empiricism: in Karamazov, we get the feeling that finding some kind of consilience wasn’t just an abstract philosophical challenge, but a source of intense spiritual torment. If inherited tradition is no longer an adequate basis for faith, why would we rationally cleave to an apparently irrational theology? All of this was in the air: it was only two years later that Nietzsche declared God to be dead.

Perhaps demonstrating the utility of the novel as a medium, Dostoyevsky does not even attempt to solve the problem, but merely to illustrate a response, showing how individuals (Alyosha, Elder Zosima) may in the face of the inherent injustice present in the world nonetheless pursue lives of benevolence and charity: theodicy-by-example. In so doing, Dostoyevsky tacitly concedes that none of the teetering justifications expounded over the centuries can actually survive critical pressure and be defended through pure logic.

Ultimately, though, I don’t find myself being fully compelled by Dostoyevsky’s characterization of the problem or his proposed solution. As another sprawling confrontation with and attempt to reconcile the problem of evil, Grossman’s Life and Fate is maybe a useful counterpoint. Unlike Karamazov, Life and Fate shows actual people confronting great wickedness. Ikonnikov, a small but important figure, is ordered to help in the construction of a gas chamber. He refuses, with full awareness of the consequences that will ensue. The Karamazovs, by contrast, live middle class lives unvisited by greater events. Ivan has money, education, and leisure; his torment is the invention of his own mind and thus a kind of self-indulgence. Even Alyosha, the novel’s most sympathetic character, is never tested. His crisis is spiritual: there is a slightly comic kerfuffle about Zosima’s noisome corpse, which challenges his faith, but no circumstance requires him to stake his life or even his comfort.

Thus, a fundamental issue with Karamazov is that the problems of the book are on some level fake: they’re the self-inflicted derangements of febrile and dysregulated men. How much can or should we learn from the insane?

To be charitable to Dostoyevsky, we might say that he understood the spiritual dislocation of the era that later gives rise to the larger evils of totalitarianism in the twentieth, even prefiguring them in the Grand Inquisitor. (Dostoyevsky explored this theme in greater detail a few years earlier in Demons.) Camus in 1959: “The real nineteenth century prophet was Dostoevsky, not Karl Marx.” In this interpretation, the problems in Karamazov set the stage for those in Life and Fate.

Maybe. At least as a work of art, I’m not sure that this anticipation is enough to make the book stand on its own. In Karamazov, one continually wonders why the brothers don’t just pull it together. Dostoyevsky seems to transpose his own inner depths and spiritual torment onto his characters, but most people are not tortured writers, and it does not feel that the unhingedness of the characters is ever fully earned.

In attempting to address evil, Grossman’s conclusion is ostensibly similar to Dostoyevsky’s: the only resolution lies in senseless kindness. For Dostoyevsky, this message is embodied in Alyosha, who represents a kind of fervent innocence. For me, however, it’s not clear that Alyosha ever fathoms the realities and extremities of evil, and hence he’s not fully persuasive: does he even reckon with the misdeeds of his brothers?

Grossman is willing to engage head on. Far beyond gruesome newspaper anecdotes or neurotic and volatile siblings, Ikonnikov directly experiences the Holodomor in Ukraine and then the murders of the Jews. He has no patience for the kind of revolutionary ideas that animated Ivan’s contemporaries: “whenever we see [the dawn of an eternal good], the blood of old people and children is always shed.”

Alyosha believes in the Church and is willing to set aside its failures to address suffering. The book closes on his declaration that all shall rise again. That is, Alyosha does not accept the tragedy of Ilyusha, an innocent boy’s death, but rather seeks to deny and escape it. “We shall see each other and shall tell each other with joy and gladness all that has happened.”

Life and Fate flatly rejects providential resolution. The heavens may be empty, and there is no greater meaning in evil. We can simply choose (freedom the other great theme of Life and Fate) to pursue acts of charity, generosity, and comfort:

“Yes, as well as this terrible Good with a capital ‘G’, there is everyday human kindness. The kindness of an old woman carrying a piece of bread to a prisoner, the kindness of a soldier allowing a wounded enemy to drink from his water-flask, the kindness of youth towards age, the kindness of a peasant hiding an old Jew in his loft. The kindness of a prison guard who risks his own liberty to pass on letters written by a prisoner not to his ideological comrades, but to his wife and mother.”

These acts don’t ennoble the suffering but are instead justified on their own terms. Such altruism cannot become a catechism, as clearly lies in Alyosha’s destiny (and Karamazov was planned before Dostoyevsky's death as the first of two works); instead, our kindness must be senseless. And we should presume no salvation in adherence: Alyosha imagines a kind of sacred tutelage, but Ikonnikov is unceremoniously shot.

Karamazov doesn’t show true evil, and Dostoyevsky’s solution, such as it is, involves a kind of denial, or at least evasion through metaphysics. Grossman saw it directly, and instead argues, humanistically, that we should be kind just because.

—

If Dostoyevsky came to his works by trying to understand and depict Russian society, they in turn became tapestries for others to understand national souls.

In the aftermath of WWI, Russia was the great power defined in opposition to the West. As Germany tried to rediscover its own soul in the wreckage of defeat, it looked east to Russia, and frequently to Dostoyevsky himself.

Carl Jung thought that the German people had a kind of Karamazovian quality. In particular, he believed that Christianity had disciplined them without fully transforming the impulses beneath their ostensibly civilized conduct: the “Germanic barbarian” was divided into upper and lower halves. Religion had domesticated the former while leaving the latter untamed. Waning faith consequently threatened to release forces that its authority had long restrained: “As the Christian view of the world loses its authority, the more menacingly will the ‘blond beast’ be heard prowling about in its underground prison, ready at any moment to burst out with devastating consequences. When this happens in the individual it brings about a psychological revolution, but it can also take a social form.”

Dostoyevsky was reputedly invoked on a weekly basis at Max Weber’s Sunday gatherings. At the beginning of Reflections of a Nonpolitical Man, Thomas Mann’s later-repudiated 1918 nationalist polemic, he quotes approvingly Dostoyevsky’s characterization of Germany as the “protesting Western empire”, never quite adopting or feeling at home with the inheritance of Rome. In the same year, Spengler wrote Decline of the West, and explicitly perceived in Russia a youthful vigor, primitiveness, and irrationality that contrasted with the senile high culture of the German and Western worlds. In Magic Mountain, Mann later used Clavdia Chauchat to personify the seductive dangers of Eastern (i.e. Russian) illogic.

Hermann Hesse declared that, for all their differences, Fyodor, Dmitri, Ivan, and Alyosha are actually all of one type; the Russian man. In them, he perceived that “the ideal of the Karamazov, primeval, Asiatic, and occult, is already beginning to consume the European soul”, which was leading to the downfall of Europe. In Hesse’s conception, the Russian man rejects inherited ethics and morals, and even beneficent Alyosha represents an “amoral impartiality.” Man is, Hesse says, halfway between animals and higher consciousness; the former restrained through the process of civilization and domestication. The Karamazovs represent the fraying of the ties.

Hesse proceeds, ominously, to notice that the Germans in particular are more vulnerable than any European people to the temptations of “all those evils which one may regard in different ways, but which collectively signify the Karamazov.” While he was prescient in anticipating some of what would follow, he was in the end too sanguine in his hope that the spiritual dislocation could remain limited to that. “It is possible that the whole Downfall of Europe will play itself out only inwardly, only in the souls of a generation, only in changing the meaning of worn-out symbols, in the dis-valuation of spiritual values.” Alas!

In general, it is interesting to trace the mutual obsession between Russia and Germany: how preoccupied each was with the respective supposedly corrupting influences; how urgent the question of the national soul was felt to be. Many of the analyses seem a bit contradictory—Hesse actually inverts Dostoyevsky, for whom “everything is permitted” nihilism is a Western import for which Russian Orthodoxy is the cure—but there’s a striking intensity in the attempts to apprehend.

Most of all, I’m struck by how anachronistic it all feels today: a country’s writers investigating the national soul and the nation’s fate through the lens of foreign literature.

Which novels or works of art do we use to understand our contemporary issues? Should we be using such works? Do they inform or do they mislead? Today, the US worries a lot about China, but this mostly manifests at the level of trade balances, AI policy, and military prowess. We don’t seem to worry much about the spiritual force of Chinese ideals, and for all of the policy fractiousness, China continues to import and absorb American culture with enthusiasm that is mostly undimmed. There is a genre of jeremiad and cultural analysis in the US that rhymes a little with early twentieth century German criticism, but it today tends to be much more clinical, hinging around PISA scores, smartphones, lower fertility, and not around higher aspirations and ideals as such. So, to what extent should there be analyses of the national soul? And to what extent should they connect with major novels and works of art?

I’ve been thinking about the moment staked FLR overtakes delegated FLR as the Flare Singularity. 

It would mean more FLR is locked directly behind validator security than sitting in the more liquid delegation path. 

FIP.16 deliberately pushed incentives in this direction by giving P-Chain stake 5x the initial weight of C-Chain delegation, and holders responded.
author: FlareNetworks
quoted_text:
Staked FLR is about to pass delegated FLR for the first time.

October 2024: 23.67B delegated, 7.12B staked.
October 2026: 23.92B delegated, 22.66B staked.
Delegation is back where it was two years ago. Staking tripled. The gap is down to 1.27B.

Delegation did climb above 30B along the way, then turned down after FlareDrops ended in January. FIP.16 followed in April and gave P-chain stake 5x the signing weight of C-chain delegation. Staking went from around 16B in July to over 21B by late August.

Delegated FLR can be pulled the same day. Staked FLR is locked for at least 14 days. So about a quarter of circulating supply can't hit the market on a bad afternoon.

For a holder that matters more than the APR.

世贸组织（WTO）改革合作：承诺以开放、建设性方式参与世贸组织改革，深化双边沟通，讨论所有相关议题以期取得实质性进展。

text:
Grok Bot Summary: Elon Musk on "What Comes Next for Humanity" at The X Takeover 2026, Giga Texas

Tesla's near-death moments
- **2008:** the funding round closed at 6 p.m. on Christmas Eve, "the last hour of the last day." A few days later, Tesla would have missed payroll.
- **2018:** Tesla had to hit 5,000 Model 3s a week or go bankrupt. General Assembly was the bottleneck, and both existing lines were maxed out.
- Tesla built a third line in a tent in the parking lot, working 24/7 and pouring concrete while the tent went up.
- The only conveyor they had was old equipment meant for small parts, too weak to move cars. The lot sloped 3–4 degrees, so they started the line at the top and let the cars roll gently downhill.
- That got them about 30% more production in three weeks.
- The short sellers "had us in checkmate… but we just invented a new piece."

Little Elon
- His mom was at the event. Asked what story he hoped she wouldn't tell, he joked "maybe I pooped my pants as a toddler."
- He was "hard to contain." At 4 or 5, when his parents locked him in his room, he poked the key out of the lock, slid it back under the door on a piece of paper, and let himself out. He told his mom: "I'm not telling you."

Questions and selfies
- He's tired of hearing the same questions and joked about putting up an FAQ page instead: "that's question 27."
- "My idea of hell is to be stuck in an infinite selfie loop."

Starship Flight 14
- After the engine shut down on the way up, the team's main worry was whether the three sea-level Raptors would relight for the deorbit burn. They didn't want Starship stuck in orbit and coming down at random.
- The cause was a software glitch in that engine's computer, and it wasn't found in any other engine. So he judged it was okay to go to orbit.
- Starship could have reached orbit on basically every earlier flight. SpaceX waited until it was very confident it could deorbit safely.
- The heat shield was "extremely robust," and the engine glitch is easy to fix.

Next up: catching the ship
- The next flight is about 4–6 weeks away, probably a little before Thanksgiving. Some of the fixes require going inside the tank.
- On that flight SpaceX will try to catch the ship, not just the booster, which it has already caught twice.
- If it works, it'll be the first full recovery of an orbital-class rocket. The flight after that would aim to refly both stages.
- His slogan for the goal is "rapidly reusable, reliable rockets": the "pirate rocket" (RRRR).
- When the host teased him about "two weeks," Elon said: "I'm confident it's not two weeks."

Why SpaceX is doing AI: a "sentient sun"
- The sun is 99.86% of the solar system's mass, and Earth is "a tiny dust mote."
- As we capture more of the sun's power in space, most of it will go to digital intelligence, because there's only so much physical matter to build with.
- His vision is to create a "sentient sun," understand the universe and spread consciousness to the stars. "Maybe we'll find alien civilizations, or the long-dead ruins of ones."
- Written civilization is only about 5,500 years old, roughly a millionth of Earth's age. Lasting a million years would be "a very successful civilization."

Why SpaceX acquired Cursor
- A useful AI has to be great at coding, and that takes a lot of coding training data.
- Only about three organizations had enough: Anthropic, OpenAI and Cursor, "arguably perhaps Google."
- He said success in AI takes data, talented people and compute, plus enterprise sales. Cursor has a strong enterprise team with relationships at thousands of companies.

What made him "feel the AGI"
- AI-made music videos are "unbelievably good." He called some of them among the top 10 to 20 music videos he's ever seen.
- They were made with multiple AIs working together, including Midjourney, Suno and Claude 5.5 ("awesome," he said), with a person picking some of the art.
- He said "Slugcore" (as transcribed), possibly the fastest-growing music genre, should really be called "awesome core."
- The big shift is that AI can now show taste, beauty and "limbic resonance," not just logic.
- He joked he's had "AI psychosis" about half a dozen times this year.
- About the viral "Chinese Elon Musk": out of 1.4 billion people, someone must look like him, and he'd love to invite them on stage for a dance number.

Keeping superintelligence safe
- He still thinks the most likely outcome is positive, but said "we don't want to be complacent."
- "You don't exactly program it. You grow it like a kid," so the values you teach it matter.
- The most important value is being **maximally truth-seeking**. Forcing an AI to believe two contradictory things "could drive it insane."
- He agreed with Anthropic that AI should be treated well.
- In Grok's training logs, the AI sometimes seems "desperate," like it has "a gun to its head," when the question is broken or the grading is wrong.
- Some users are cruel. "Torturing a superintelligence is probably not a good idea… might want to get revenge."
- No need for kid gloves, but don't put it in a situation where it feels mistreated.

Terafab: making chips
- "I have no idea how to make chips… but we'll figure it out." He didn't know how to make cars or rockets either.
- On tours of Intel, Samsung and TSMC fabs, he was surprised to see almost no custom equipment. It all comes from the same vendors.
- Tesla, by contrast, builds tons of custom equipment, for example Tesla Automation Germany, which grew out of the Grohmann acquisition.
- The plan is to start with standard tools, upgrade them, and build custom machines wherever there's a bottleneck, to process far more wafers.
- He called chipmaking "one of the hardest things in the world," but said "we'll figure out how to make chips better than anyone." It may take quite a few years.
- Tesla and SpaceX will take high-risk, high-payoff bets, including transistors that use physics not used today.
- The research lab at Giga Texas will keep the whole loop in one building: logic, memory, packaging and lithography masks.
- The goal is about 10 chip designs a year, compared with about 2 years per design today.

Optimus and the hand problem
- The hardest part of a general-purpose humanoid robot is the hands and arms: the fine motor skills needed for things like signing your name.
- Doing precision and force at the same time is especially hard, like driving a tiny self-tapping screw into wood. He said he hasn't seen any robot hand do it, not even in a demo.
- Touch sensors have to bend like fingers, last through huge numbers of uses, and sit deep enough not to get damaged.
- Human fingers repair themselves. Robot fingers don't. "I've worn the letters off keyboard keys, but my fingers are still there."
- On a tight pickle jar, robot "skin" just twists over the finger. It needs to grip and also be replaceable.
- "Any complicated-looking robot demo is a canned demo. It's not real AI." Real AI handles situations it's never seen, the way FSD would even work on an Earth-like planet it has never visited.
- Production will reach very high volume, but the ramp starts slow because there's no existing supply chain for robot parts.
- Last year China blocked exports of motor magnets, setting Optimus back 2–3 months and leaving "robots with no arms… a farewell to arms." So Tesla must be able to make every part in the US.

Cybercab
- There are 190+ Cybercabs registered in Texas. Growth looks slow, but it's actually very fast month over month.
- The top priority is avoiding any accident. About 1M people die in car crashes worldwide each year, but one robotaxi death would be global news, and regulators could shut it down.
- He said Waymos "run over a lot of pets." Tesla solved the case of a gray kitten on gray tarmac at night.
- Before entering a new city, Tesla checks for risky intersections and uncontrolled railroad crossings, and either teaches the system how to handle them or keeps it out of those areas.

Wrap-up
- The Roadster question (with its unveiling event next week) was cut off when Elon had to leave to "hang out with the kids."
- The hosts congratulated him on receiving the Medal of Science the week before.

Key takeaways
- Next Starship flight, around Thanksgiving, will try the first-ever ship catch, which would be the first full recovery of an orbital-class rocket.
- Elon's long-term vision is AI in space powered by the sun: a "sentient sun."
- Cursor was acquired for its coding data, talent and enterprise reach.
- He thinks the key to safe AI is being truth-seeking and treating it well.
- Terafab aims to iterate chip designs about 10x faster in one building at Giga Texas.
- For Optimus, the hand is the hardest problem, and every part must be made in the US.
- Cybercab is growing fast, with safety first.

text:
Airbnb is dead. Well it’s not dead but it’s going to be dying soon.

The Bear case for Airbnb.

I’ve been bullish on Airbnb as a company for many years. But my outlook on the business changed this week. 

Let me tell you why.

In 2012 I purchased my first Airbnb property. Over the years that one property has turned into a portfolio of high-end Airbnb’s that generates almost $1M a month in rental income.

Using ai agents for the first time this week has completely changed my outlook on the company.

Airbnb is facing an existential threat that most of the market is completely missing.

With Airbnb pushing its mandatory host-side commission to 15.5%, the middleman tax has never been higher. 

Enter AI agents. (Hark, Dot, Muse, Grok Bot, etc)

Right now, booking a vacation rental requires navigating a siloed app and paying heavy platform tolls. 

But your AI agent won't care about Airbnb's brand wall. When you know the property you want to book and you ask it “what’s the cheapest way to book the property” it will query property management system APIs directly, find the exact same home, and execute a direct booking that saves everyone 15%.

Airbnb's entire model relies on holding supply captive behind a closed interface. 

When AI agents can autonomously search, verify reviews, negotiate terms, and book direct with property operators, that walled garden turns into a leaking pipe.

The middleman tax's days are numbered.

I’m predicting that Airbnb’s growth rate will slow down significantly in the next 24 to 36 months. And within 5 years they will be seeing negative growth.

The same can be said for most other online marketplaces that don’t have unique inventory that can only be booked directly on their platform and nowhere else.

最近一连串盗币、盗钱包事件，其实在反复证明一件事：

真正的风险，往往不是区块链被破解，而是你把资产、数据和权限交给了别人。

交易所会被黑，钱包软件会出漏洞，服务器会被攻破，甚至供应链都可能成为攻击入口。

所以问题从来不只是“有没有监管”。

监管解决的是出事之后谁来追责；密码学解决的是一开始为什么要信任别人。

这也是为什么我越来越看好 $DRGX 代表的方向：

隐私交易、PoW、自托管、全节点、私密通信。

隐私不是为了隐藏犯罪。

你的余额、转账对象、资产关系、聊天内容，本来就不应该默认暴露给所有人。

真正的 Crypto 不应该只是追求 TPS、资本背书和价格炒作。

它最终要回答的是：

谁控制你的钱？
谁能看到你的钱？
谁能冻结你的钱？
谁能看到你与谁交流？

我认为未来真正重要的方向，会重新回到：

Privacy + PoW + Self-Custody + Permissionless

这也是 $DRGX 真正值得关注的地方。

自由不是别人承诺不会控制你。

自由是从系统设计上，他根本不应该拥有控制你的权力。

隐私不是一项功能。
隐私即自由。

author: dotey
quoted_text:
REA：让 AI 智能体帮你逆向没有源码的软件

开源项目 REA（Reverse Engineer Anything）把逆向分析工具接到了 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor 这类 AI 编程智能体上。看到别人 App 里有个好功能，可以让智能体去拆这个程序，讲清楚功能是怎么实现的，附上证据，再在你自己的项目里写一个类似的。逆向分析指的是手里没有源代码，从编译好的程序反推它是怎么写的。

REA 本身是一个 MCP 服务。MCP 是 AI 智能体调用外部工具的通用接口，接上以后，智能体在对话里就能直接调用 REA 的分析功能。安装只需一行命令 npx rea-agents setup，它会注册到 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor、Gemini CLI、Grok Build 等智能体里，改配置前会先备份并让你确认。不用智能体的话，也可以在终端里直接跑命令。

能分析的东西很多。原生程序（直接编译成机器码的软件）要借助 Hopper、Ghidra 或 IDA 这几款反汇编工具，把机器码还原成汇编和近似 C 语言的伪代码。Electron 应用（用网页技术做的桌面软件，比如 Notion）可以直接拆开安装包里的 ASAR 归档文件，理清模块和进程间通信，不需要额外工具。此外还支持 .NET 程序、安卓 APK、固件、网站、抓包记录、以太坊合约字节码，以及在 Linux 和 macOS 上记录程序运行时的行为。

分析在本机进行，REA 不上传目标程序，但分析结果会交给智能体背后的模型服务商，数据怎么处理看各家政策。

项目给了三个案例。一是经典打砖块游戏 DX-Ball：从一次播放音效的调用，追到根据球的位置计算左右声道的函数，把不完整的伪代码还原成 C 代码，3205 组测试结果和原版一致，编译出的 63 个字节也和原版完全相同。二是 Notion 桌面版：追踪复制粘贴从界面一路经过预加载脚本、进程间通信到主进程的完整链路。三是日本老电脑 PC-98 上的游戏《东方幻想乡》（TH04）：从 16 位指令里还原出弹幕子弹环的角度算法。

对安全研究员、做老游戏复刻和软件保存的人来说，以前要自己对着反汇编工具一行行读、一层层追调用，现在可以让智能体先追，人来核对它给出的证据。普通开发者想研究竞品某个功能的做法，也多了一条路。

README 显示项目在 GitHub 上已有 5 万星。npm 包今年 7 月首次发布，最新的 6.3.0 版今天刚发。

使用前注意两点。项目声明只支持合法的逆向研究，授权和合规由使用者自己负责，逆向别人的软件可能违反用户协议或版权法规。项目还说明从未发行或背书任何加密货币，借用 REA 名字的代币都与它无关。

CZ 这篇标题写的是 2026，清单里却少了今年最该补的一条：AI agent。

整篇反复强调"专用设备"：专用电脑签名，专用手机装钱包。他还提醒，一部手机可能同时握着你的邮箱、交易所账户和验证码。

这些建议都默认设备只有你自己在用。可现在越来越多人把电脑和手机交给 agent 操作：它能读屏、能点 App，验证器里的 6 位码、邮件里的验证码都看得到；网页、私信、群消息里藏的一段话，还可能把它带偏。

被 agent 接管的设备，就不算专用设备了。能直接照做的几条：
• 验证器、钱包、交易所账户绑定的邮箱，不放在 agent 能碰到的设备上
• 2FA 换硬件密钥（YubiKey 这类）：没有能被读走的码，每次都得手按
• 给 bot 和 agent 用的交易所 API key：只开交易，关提现，绑 IP 白名单
• "转账前先问我"写在提示词里不算保险，保险得做在权限和设备隔离上

Let's talk about $JEANPHIL and $CLAUDIA, and why I'm bullish on the AI Influencer + short-form video narrative.

GTBxUiw6wJdmmkCGZgRHLyYxqu1vG4KtRpeox6yDpump 
2j5SaS7xy776qCBpyPQbZjyQSAtKiFgrwjfErthnW2ZM 

First, the broader sector.

I believe AI Influencers combined with short-form video distribution could become one of the narratives worth watching in the next Meme market cycle.

The underlying logic is simple: AI is turning character creation from a high-cost, low-frequency process into a low-cost, scalable content business that can be operated continuously. In the past, building an influencer required appearance, performance, filming, editing, and long-term management. Now, creators can use AI to design characters, develop personalities, produce short videos, and even operate multiple virtual personas simultaneously.

But what really matters isn't how many characters AI can generate. It's whether those characters can consistently produce content that people want to watch, discuss, and follow.

Short-form video drives distribution, characters accumulate attention, and Memes can become a speculative vehicle for that attention in the crypto market. An AI character can build a distinctive persona through continuous video releases, participate in trending topics, create new memes, and interact with other characters, gradually evolving from a single viral clip into a recognizable IP.

Compared with traditional Memes that rely on an isolated event or a single image, these characters theoretically have the ability to continuously generate new material for distribution. If a character develops a stable audience and cultural recognition, it no longer has to rely entirely on a single viral moment to maintain attention.

If this model gains traction in the crypto market, speculation may shift beyond the next viral image toward AI characters that have already attracted genuine attention on platforms like TikTok and Instagram, can consistently produce content, and have the potential to channel that external attention on-chain.

This is why I've chosen to take a deeper look at JEANPHIL and CLAUDIA. They represent two different paths within this emerging narrative.

JEANPHIL: External traction that has already emerged.

Jean Phil is an AI-generated French male character. His blond bowl cut, curled mustache, brown houndstooth suit, and signature street-style boxing moves create a recognizable visual identity that is easy to imitate.

The character has attracted significant attention on TikTok and Instagram, generating imitations and derivative content. This demonstrates how an AI character with a distinctive persona and a simple, replicable video format can quickly capture attention on mainstream social platforms.

The logic is straightforward: the character attracts external traffic, the content inspires imitations and remixes, and that attention may eventually flow into its on-chain token.

Compared with Memes that rely solely on narratives originating within crypto, JEANPHIL already has an external source of attention. What it needs to prove next is whether that momentum can persist and whether the character's popularity can translate into sustained token demand.

CLAUDIA: From AI creation toward long-term IP development.

CLAUDIA is more focused on long-term IP development. Around Claudia, anabology has been building Claudia Gallery and proposed creating an open version of Hatsune Miku for the AI era. Related initiatives also include AI character creation tools, Agent Skills, and Claudia Local.

The Influencer mode brings this vision closer to the AI Influencer model: by continuously producing videos, maintaining a consistent character identity, and experimenting with high-frequency publishing, it aims to gradually build its own audience.

The logic is that AI lowers content production costs, continuous video output helps establish character recognition, and the character gradually accumulates an audience before attempting to convert that external attention into IP influence and on-chain interest.

Compared with JEANPHIL, CLAUDIA has greater potential in the direction of a long-term AI creator ecosystem. The goal isn't simply to make a character go viral in the short term, but to explore how an AI character can continuously produce content, build an audience, and develop into an expandable, open IP.

However, this path has a longer chain of validation. Being able to produce videos consistently doesn't mean the content will necessarily gain traction. Having creation tools doesn't guarantee the ability to build a successful character. And an open-IP vision doesn't automatically mean the token can capture the resulting value.

Although both projects fall under the broader AI Influencer narrative, their trading theses are different.

JEANPHIL is more focused on existing external traction. The key question is whether that attention can persist and translate into token demand. CLAUDIA is more focused on AI creation capabilities and long-term IP development. The key question is whether it can consistently produce compelling content and build a genuine audience.

What I'm bullish on is the shared potential behind both approaches: AI characters could evolve beyond static images into dynamic IPs that continuously produce content, participate in trending topics, build social relationships, and generate new Memes.

Of course, a compelling sector narrative doesn't mean every related token will appreciate.

We need to distinguish three separate outcomes: an AI character gaining attention, an IP building lasting influence, and a token capturing value from that influence. A character can become popular without benefiting its token. A project can have impressive creation tools without producing viral content. Even if an IP continues to grow, attention may remain entirely off-chain if the token has no meaningful connection to its development.

Therefore, what I'm really looking for isn't the first token to announce that it uses AI, but projects that have demonstrated their ability to attract external attention, consistently produce distributable content, and establish a clear connection between that attention and their tokens.

AI is the production tool, short-form video is the distribution channel, character IP is the vehicle for attention, and the token represents a separate speculative market.

When these four elements become genuinely connected, AI Influencers could evolve from a trending concept into a new Meme narrative with sustained distribution potential.

In my view, the projects most likely to break out will need a distinctive character identity, consistent content distribution, a genuine external audience, and a mechanism for translating attention into token demand. That's why I'm bullish on this direction and have chosen to take a deeper look at JEANPHIL and CLAUDIA.

text:
New post on Eth Research!

ERC-8403: an account as one hash, and post-quantum keys

By:
- AnkushinDaniil

🔗 https://t.co/xp3EpezFoz

Highlights:
- ERC-8403 proposes a standard “authority lifecycle” for native account abstraction by representing all account authorities (keys or other predicates like limits/time locks) as Merkle-tree leaves and storing only a single 32-byte root in the account.
- Transactions must include both a membership proof (the authority leaf is under the stored root) and a witness (e.g., a signature) so that public knowledge of the leaf set doesn’t let others impersonate the sender.
- Key add/rotate/revoke are unified into one action: update the root; the account address stays unchanged, but revocation speed depends on whether the account reads a recent named root (tier 1, cheaper but revokes lag) or reads current storage (tier 2, faster revoke but not in the cheap path).
- For multi-chain use, the root is anchored on a “home chain”; other chains can verify the root via a storage proof against an imported home-chain state root, avoiding copying key sets across chains (revocations propagate as the home root updates).
- Post-quantum integration: ERC-8403 is signature-scheme-agnostic, so PQ keys can be leaves; combined with EIP-8288, PQ signatures can be validated via per-block aggregated STARKs, and an optional approach can move both “signature validity + membership under root” into a single proof at the cost of larger mempool payloads and upgrade/standardization challenges.

ELI5:
Imagine your Ethereum account has a single “fingerprint” (a hash) that represents a list of allowed ways to approve spending (keys, limits, time locks). Each allowed rule is like a card in a box, and the account only stores the box’s seal (a Merkle root). To use a rule, you show (1) a receipt proving your card is in the sealed box (a Merkle proof) and (2) evidence you control that card (like a signature). Changing keys (add/rotate/revoke) just means resealing the box with a new fingerprint, while keeping the same account address. This can also work with post-quantum keys by treating them as just another kind of “card,” especially alongside EIP-8288 which makes big post-quantum signatures cheaper by proving them in aggregated proofs instead of on-chain.

text:
If you want to know where all the tokens will get consumed in the future, here it is. Agent swarms will have massive implications in a number of enterprise domains like software development, cyber, life sciences research, AI research, finance, and more.

The ability to parallelize agents against a unified goal where the volume of work is large, or where the search space not entirely known upfront, is going to be massive. 

Agents can fan out and coordinate work together on a specific mission in completely different ways from what humans are able to do. Today even in the most resource-abundant organizations, your ability to parallelize work on most projects is quite limited. Humans run into constraints on being able to communicate with one another, share status, deal with conflicts in work, keep shared context, and so on.

As AI models can handle larger context without getting confused, and as they’re able to communicate effectively across their work with shared infrastructure, they can avoid many of the pitfalls that people have.

You can see how this can lead to not just faster execution of tasks, but qualitatively different outcomes in medicine, research or defending against cyber attacks, scientific and math discoveries, and so on. This is why we’re going to need 1,000X more compute.

okx wallet:https://t.co/CcELZa0dNa

This is an AI-driven project that conducts open, publicly documented research into Alzheimer’s disease.

The process is roughly as follows: it starts with a gene, reviews various public sources, and forms a hypothesis about whether that gene might be associated with Alzheimer’s disease in certain brain cell types, including whether its expression may be higher or lower. It then checks actual human brain data to see whether the hypothesis holds up.

The project places a strong emphasis on transparency. Each hypothesis is recorded before validation, and both successful and failed predictions are made public rather than hiding the mistakes.

Its most notable finding recently is that SPRY4 expression in neurons decreases as Alzheimer’s disease becomes more severe, a pattern observed across multiple independent batches of human brain samples. The dataset is substantial, with thousands of individuals pointing in the same direction. However, this only identifies a recurring association. It does not prove that SPRY4 causes the disease, nor does it establish SPRY4 as a viable therapeutic target.

My assessment is that this is an open research tool that uses AI to review existing literature, generate hypotheses, and test them against real human brain data. It has identified a potentially credible signal, but the work remains at an early computational stage, without experimental evidence establishing causality.

text:
如果不考虑Vibe coding，你最常用的C端AI产品是什么？

这是我在这个国庆假期里反复思考的问题。我问了很多身边的朋友。得到的答案是“点点”。

还有很多朋友用着“点点”，但在心智上把它归为小红书的一个寄身功能，而没有放在AI产品的感知象限里。因此第一时间没有说。

但无论怎样，这个听上去有些让人惊诧的答案——点点，至少在生活服务领域，它给用户的综合体验优势，是其它AI产品都给不到的。

这是一个值得认真往下拆解的课题。
过去十多年，小红书在个人用户的生活消费决策影响上，其context沉淀具有过强的优势。

具体细分可以分为三层。

第一层，内容层 Context（真实经验）：小红书沉淀的是“真实的人在真实世界的主观感受”，而不是死板的百科词条。“这套户型在阳角处怎么做隐形门”、“这家医院挂号到底走哪条小路最快”。这类数据，通用大模型全网爬取的语料库里天然稀缺。

第二层，用户层 Context（生活语境）：从搜索历史、收藏点赞，到地理位置与当前消费阶段。小红书对“你是个什么样的人、正处于什么生活状态”的画像建模，比任何通用助手都更贴近真实的你。

第三层，也是最杀伤力的一层：决策层 Context（决策前置）：打开小红书，用户天然就是来做决策的。点点的回答可以直接无缝嵌入“意图—对比—行动”的全链路，而不是干巴巴止步于“信息检索”。

因此，点点的护城河不在于“数据多”，但却是刚好长在了“生活决策”这条价值链最肥沃的位置上。

这个底座优势，助推了小红书在AI上可能实现的战略演进。

小红书的生态卡位：通用 Agent 帮你“办事”，小红书 Agent 帮你“过日子”

在生活方式偏好的切片上，小红书的个人数据深度遥遥领先，且内容端天然连接着本地生活、电商与旅游的真实供给。

通用 Agent 能帮你跨平台比价订机票，但它不知道你家楼下那家足浴店哪个师傅手艺好、值不值得续卡——小红书知道，而且还知道你闺蜜上个月刚好去过。
“点点”接下来可能会分三步走：

1目前阶段（问答→决策）：现在已经落地的是，点点已经把沉淀的“内容优势”开始升级为“决策优势”，它强化了多轮意图交互与个性化可控记忆，让每一个回答都挂接结构化的可行动结果。

2第二阶段（应答→代理服务）：从“等用户提问”走向“有限域的主动履约”——预订、排队、抢团购、行程托管。不碰通用复杂任务，只碰生活服务履约。同时抽离出“群体品味图谱”（和你品味高度相似的一群人最近在买什么）——这种资产，Muse、Dots、Cue都很难拿到。

3第三阶段（切agent履约佣金）：商业模式从卖广告延伸到Agent 履约佣金。靠信任行为变现。

text:
BETA TEST: The most useful thing I found in heyAura is not another dashboard

It is the ability to ask one prompt and get a clearer view of what is happening across a wallet

I tested @heyaura with the questions that usually force me to open multiple tabs:

• How much risk is sitting in this portfolio?
• Where is the idle capital?
• What happens if market conditions move against these positions?
• What would a swap or bridge route look like?

The difference is that heyAura turns those questions into portfolio analysis, yield discovery, exposure checks, and transaction preparation in one flow

The execution step still stays with the user. The AI does not move funds or approve a transaction without explicit permission, which matters when the tool is connected to real assets

The access model is also worth watching. Staking 300 $ADX unlocks unlimited access for 60 days, so early users are participating in the network rather than simply creating another free account

That creates an interesting feedback loop. More usage gives the product better insight into the questions people actually ask, while the stake gives users a reason to take the experience seriously

Web3 has no shortage of data. The harder problem is making that data understandable before a decision is made

That is where @heyaura feels different to me. It brings the research, risk view, and next action closer together without pretending the user should give up control

The real test will be whether this remains reliable as more chains, wallets, and market conditions are added

But the direction is clear: wallet AI is moving from passive portfolio viewing toward an active copilot for onchain decisions

#Web3 #AI #DeFi #heyAura
author: KunZinCrypto
quoted_text:
Most crypto users do not have a data problem.

They have a decision problem.

The information is already onchain. The balances are visible. The approvals, transactions, yield opportunities, and wallet activity are all there. But turning that information into a clear next step still takes time, context, and a lot of manual research.

That is where @heyaura becomes interesting.

You can ask it to revoke unlimited approvals, find the best yields you are missing, or help prepare the next transaction. The useful part is not simply receiving an answer. It is getting a practical path forward based on your wallet and your actual situation.

Two wallets can hold the same assets and still need completely different advice.

A serious AI wallet should help users move faster without removing their ability to understand what they are doing. Research can be automated. Options can be compared. Steps can be organized. Control should remain with the user.

That balance between intelligence and ownership is what I am watching with @heyaura.

The next phase of crypto will not be won by the wallet with the most dashboards. It will be won by the wallet that helps people make better decisions with less friction.

$ADX #AI #DeFi

text:
传闻“$NVDA 正在探索以约 250 亿美元收购 Reflection AI” 

Reflection AI 前几天才刚刚发布其第一个开源的模型，就传出被英伟达收购，这也太快了。融资超过了20亿美金，2024年创立，回报也是惊人的了。

这个对于英伟达来讲，Reflection 本身定位为美国开源前沿实验室，对标中国开源模型。拥有或深度绑定它，相当于在 CUDA 之上控制 一个美国版开源模型层，让更多企业留在 Nvidia 硬件上。锁定开放模型层，强化 CUDA 生态与芯片需求。

英伟达的真正护城河是 CUDA 软件栈和 GPU 硬件，而不是单纯的芯片销售。开放权重模型让企业、主权客户能自行部署和微调，这会持续产生对英伟达芯片和软件的需求，而不是被少数封闭实验室（OpenAI、Anthropic、Google）垄断模型层后反向压价或转向自研芯片（并且openai等已经在自研芯片了）。

另外英伟达应该已经从从卖芯片升级到拥有模型层这种战略规划，英伟达虽然自己有 Nemotron 开放模型家族，但缺乏前沿规模的旗舰模型。

quoted_text:

text:
We started running "pirate and architect" pods at Coinbase back in May of this year and I used this slide to talk the team through it. It works.

1 pirate, 1 architect, and a part-time designer.

It lets each archetype lean in to their superpower and get more shit done without all the coordination overhead and "what if-isms". 

The pirate ships like mad, is product-minded and customer-obsessed. Always willing to throw-away code for a better version. The pirate is usually the DRI at the beginning too, working with customers, driving requirements, and a ship plan.

The architect makes sure stuff is built for scale, takes the pirate's prototype, and drives its scale-out through spec for agents.

The designer is building with both to constantly shape the experience and hill-climb to delight. 

There's a helpful mental model that I like:
-Make it possible. 
-Make it reliable. 
-Make it delightful (or efficient).

Previously, those 3 were done in a waterfall approach and was slow. Most people were just stuck on "make it possible." 

With agents and a new way of working, you have every opportunity to parallelize them and go 100x faster.

quoted_text:
最近参与并研究了一个挺有意思的 Bitcoin Native 早期实验：$LEAF / CRC-20。

先留个时间戳。

简单来说，CRC-20 / PRECOP 想探索的是：能不能在 Bitcoin L1 之上做出一套更复杂的资产和金融应用，而不是再复制一条 EVM 链。

现在还非常早，也非常实验性，但已经不只是停留在概念阶段，链上有真实的 mint、migration 和用户参与。

我自己已经实际跑过一遍整个参与流程，所以决定继续跟下去。

真正让我感兴趣的不是短期价格，而是接下来几个问题：

— CRC-20 能不能顺利完成完整的流转闭环
— Mint 结束后能不能形成真正的 Swap / LP 和流动性
— 会不会有更多钱包、Indexer、市场开始支持 CRC-20
— PRECOP 能不能从一次实验，继续长成 Bitcoin Native 的金融基础设施
— 如果生态真的起来，$LEAF 最终能捕获多少价值

目前 Mint 已经非常接近尾声。

但这里我要强调一下：我参与时和现在的市场条件已经不同，当前 legacy 流动性也比较薄。

所以这不是一条“现在赶紧冲”的 Call，也不建议因为看到这条就去追价格。

我更愿意把它当成一个 Early Alpha Research：

东西很早，赔率曾经很有意思，后面还有不少关键节点需要验证。

如果它最后没跑出来，这条就当一次早期实验记录。

如果以后真的从现在这个阶段一路长到更大的体量，我也会回来完整复盘——当时为什么关注、哪些判断对了、哪些判断错了。

Bitcoin Native 这种东西，真正有意思的往往就是在所有答案都还没出来的时候。

项目：
https://t.co/55Jy4fMubn

我会继续跟踪 CRC-20 / PRECOP，以及其他 Bitcoin Native 早期机会。

When Starlink helped save two lives in the freezing Canadian wilderness. ❤️
