text:
After analyzing $CLAUDIA again, my view is that the AI-native IP narrative may only just be starting to be priced in by the market.

2j5SaS7xy776qCBpyPQbZjyQSAtKiFgrwjfErthnW2ZM 

The most direct catalysts behind this rally are Elon’s public recognition of Anabology’s AI music videos and a16z co-founder Marc Andreessen’s attention to the CLAUDIA account.

First, Musk. During an interview, he said that Anabology’s AI music videos made him rethink the pace of technological progress, adding that some of these works could rank among the top 10–20 best music videos he has ever seen.

Then there is Marc Andreessen, a16z’s co-founder, who follows CLAUDIA. These are two distinct signals of attention: the former directly points to the official CLAUDIA account, while the latter reflects recognition of the creative work behind CLAUDIA.

Although a follow does not imply investment or a partnership, and Elon’s praise is not an endorsement of the token, the combination of these two developments is enough to make the market reconsider the project’s original AI influencer narrative as something broader: an AI-native entertainment narrative.

Anabology is not simply making one video and then waiting for the market to speculate. The team has continued producing AI music videos around CLAUDIA, gradually building continuity in the character’s appearance, visual style, and content output. The related works have accumulated more than 6.2 million views, suggesting that this form of AI-native content has already established a certain level of reach.

At the same time, Anabology continues to invest effort in the project. The developer has publicly expressed a commitment to keep building and continues to release new work. At the very least, this indicates sustained creative momentum behind the project, rather than a team relying solely on token price action to maintain attention.

This is what distinguishes CLAUDIA from many one-off AI Memes: it is attempting to produce content continuously around a fixed character, giving users something to remember beyond a single video—the character itself.

My analysis is that what the market may really be betting on is the transformation of AI influencers from content products into independent IP.

In the past, building a recognizable entertainment character required a production team, funding, and a lengthy development cycle. Today, AI tools can dramatically reduce the cost of producing music, visual content, and character stories, giving individual creators the opportunity to operate their own virtual personalities over time.

But lower content production costs are only the first step. The real value emerges when a character begins to build an audience and users actively follow it, share its content, create derivative works, and even help expand its fictional universe.

If this model works, AI characters will no longer be merely tools or creations in the hands of their creators. They could become entertainment IP capable of accumulating influence in their own right.

CLAUDIA’s long-term thesis is precisely this: evolving from an AI-generated character into a virtual IP with a continuous content pipeline, a recognizable identity, and community influence.

This also explains why I am paying attention to both CLAUDIA and JEANPHIL. Both point to the potential opportunity in AI influencer IP. A consistent character identity combined with continuous content output could generate more durable attention than a single viral video. CLAUDIA’s current external recognition and accumulated content make it one of the projects in this narrative worth watching more closely.

From a fundamental perspective, the positive developments we can currently confirm include the creator’s continued output, millions of views for the works, Elon’s public praise of the related content, and Marc Andreessen following the Anabology account.

These developments strengthen the project’s attention base and give the AI-native entertainment narrative more concrete support.

However, view counts do not equal a stable audience, celebrity attention does not equal a commercial partnership, and continued effort from the creator does not mean the project has established a revenue model. At the token level in particular, we still need to verify whether community growth can translate into sustained demand and whether there is a clear, sustainable mechanism for capturing value for the token.

Therefore, my view is that CLAUDIA’s narrative and external attention have strengthened significantly, but its long-term token value capture remains insufficiently validated.

There are three areas worth monitoring closely going forward.

First, can Anabology’s new work continue to break through? If subsequent releases continue to attract widespread attention, Elon’s praise could mark the beginning of sustained creative momentum rather than a one-off news event.

Second, can CLAUDIA develop influence as an independent character? The real validation signal is not another person following the account. It is whether users begin discussing the character proactively, continue watching new releases, and participate in sharing and creating derivative content.

Third, can content influence translate into token demand? If the project can connect its character, creative output, community, and token mechanism, the market will have a reason to reassess its long-term value. If that connection never materializes, the success of the IP may not translate into the token’s price.

The risks are equally clear. Competition in AI-generated content will intensify, celebrity-driven attention may fade quickly, and short-term traders may take profits after a sharp rally. If subsequent releases fail to maintain their appeal or the character never builds a stable audience, this rally may remain largely driven by expectations and sentiment.

My final judgment is this: the direct catalysts behind the rally are Elon’s praise of Anabology’s work and Marc Andreessen following the official CLAUDIA account. The deeper trading thesis is that the market is beginning to bet on AI-native characters evolving into a new form of entertainment IP.

CLAUDIA’s advantage is that it already has continuous creative output and a certain level of distribution, rather than being merely an abstract AI concept. But what determines its ultimate upside is not how many more famous names appear on the list. It is whether the character can consistently produce compelling content, build a genuine audience, and ultimately establish a connection between the development of its IP and demand for its token.

If AI-native entertainment truly becomes a new sector, the eventual winners may not be the tools that generate content most efficiently, but the characters that establish user recognition first, consistently produce compelling work, and develop cultural influence. CLAUDIA is competing for that position, but it still has a long way to go before proving itself.

Let's talk about $JEANPHIL and $CLAUDIA, and why I'm bullish on the AI Influencer + short-form video narrative.

GTBxUiw6wJdmmkCGZgRHLyYxqu1vG4KtRpeox6yDpump 
2j5SaS7xy776qCBpyPQbZjyQSAtKiFgrwjfErthnW2ZM 

First, the broader sector.

I believe AI Influencers combined with short-form video distribution could become one of the narratives worth watching in the next Meme market cycle.

The underlying logic is simple: AI is turning character creation from a high-cost, low-frequency process into a low-cost, scalable content business that can be operated continuously. In the past, building an influencer required appearance, performance, filming, editing, and long-term management. Now, creators can use AI to design characters, develop personalities, produce short videos, and even operate multiple virtual personas simultaneously.

But what really matters isn't how many characters AI can generate. It's whether those characters can consistently produce content that people want to watch, discuss, and follow.

Short-form video drives distribution, characters accumulate attention, and Memes can become a speculative vehicle for that attention in the crypto market. An AI character can build a distinctive persona through continuous video releases, participate in trending topics, create new memes, and interact with other characters, gradually evolving from a single viral clip into a recognizable IP.

Compared with traditional Memes that rely on an isolated event or a single image, these characters theoretically have the ability to continuously generate new material for distribution. If a character develops a stable audience and cultural recognition, it no longer has to rely entirely on a single viral moment to maintain attention.

If this model gains traction in the crypto market, speculation may shift beyond the next viral image toward AI characters that have already attracted genuine attention on platforms like TikTok and Instagram, can consistently produce content, and have the potential to channel that external attention on-chain.

This is why I've chosen to take a deeper look at JEANPHIL and CLAUDIA. They represent two different paths within this emerging narrative.

JEANPHIL: External traction that has already emerged.

Jean Phil is an AI-generated French male character. His blond bowl cut, curled mustache, brown houndstooth suit, and signature street-style boxing moves create a recognizable visual identity that is easy to imitate.

The character has attracted significant attention on TikTok and Instagram, generating imitations and derivative content. This demonstrates how an AI character with a distinctive persona and a simple, replicable video format can quickly capture attention on mainstream social platforms.

The logic is straightforward: the character attracts external traffic, the content inspires imitations and remixes, and that attention may eventually flow into its on-chain token.

Compared with Memes that rely solely on narratives originating within crypto, JEANPHIL already has an external source of attention. What it needs to prove next is whether that momentum can persist and whether the character's popularity can translate into sustained token demand.

CLAUDIA: From AI creation toward long-term IP development.

CLAUDIA is more focused on long-term IP development. Around Claudia, anabology has been building Claudia Gallery and proposed creating an open version of Hatsune Miku for the AI era. Related initiatives also include AI character creation tools, Agent Skills, and Claudia Local.

The Influencer mode brings this vision closer to the AI Influencer model: by continuously producing videos, maintaining a consistent character identity, and experimenting with high-frequency publishing, it aims to gradually build its own audience.

The logic is that AI lowers content production costs, continuous video output helps establish character recognition, and the character gradually accumulates an audience before attempting to convert that external attention into IP influence and on-chain interest.

Compared with JEANPHIL, CLAUDIA has greater potential in the direction of a long-term AI creator ecosystem. The goal isn't simply to make a character go viral in the short term, but to explore how an AI character can continuously produce content, build an audience, and develop into an expandable, open IP.

However, this path has a longer chain of validation. Being able to produce videos consistently doesn't mean the content will necessarily gain traction. Having creation tools doesn't guarantee the ability to build a successful character. And an open-IP vision doesn't automatically mean the token can capture the resulting value.

Although both projects fall under the broader AI Influencer narrative, their trading theses are different.

JEANPHIL is more focused on existing external traction. The key question is whether that attention can persist and translate into token demand. CLAUDIA is more focused on AI creation capabilities and long-term IP development. The key question is whether it can consistently produce compelling content and build a genuine audience.

What I'm bullish on is the shared potential behind both approaches: AI characters could evolve beyond static images into dynamic IPs that continuously produce content, participate in trending topics, build social relationships, and generate new Memes.

Of course, a compelling sector narrative doesn't mean every related token will appreciate.

We need to distinguish three separate outcomes: an AI character gaining attention, an IP building lasting influence, and a token capturing value from that influence. A character can become popular without benefiting its token. A project can have impressive creation tools without producing viral content. Even if an IP continues to grow, attention may remain entirely off-chain if the token has no meaningful connection to its development.

Therefore, what I'm really looking for isn't the first token to announce that it uses AI, but projects that have demonstrated their ability to attract external attention, consistently produce distributable content, and establish a clear connection between that attention and their tokens.

AI is the production tool, short-form video is the distribution channel, character IP is the vehicle for attention, and the token represents a separate speculative market.

When these four elements become genuinely connected, AI Influencers could evolve from a trending concept into a new Meme narrative with sustained distribution potential.

In my view, the projects most likely to break out will need a distinctive character identity, consistent content distribution, a genuine external audience, and a mechanism for translating attention into token demand. That's why I'm bullish on this direction and have chosen to take a deeper look at JEANPHIL and CLAUDIA.

quoted_text:
没错，预测市场的增长已经进入深水区。

过去我们一直采用Crypto原生打法拉新，比如积分体系、大使计划、各类营销活动等等。

但币圈用户体量是非常有限的，在基本站稳脚跟之后，想要实现下一阶段突破，就必须探索全新的增长路径。

顺着阿黄老师的总结，我从四个方向继续展开聊聊：

1️⃣ 通过事件营销，实现破圈。

预测市场和绝大多数Crypto项目最大的区别，就是它天然可以对接大量传统领域：体育、电竞、美股、政治等等。

这些赛道本身拥有海量大众用户。

我们可以围绕真实事件搭建盘口，把非Web3用户吸引进来，真正做到破圈，而不是只局限在加密圈子内部。

2️⃣ 生态合作，渠道为王。

我们会联合各类项目共建市场。每个合作项目都自带独立社区与用户，双向导流，一起做大预测市场赛道。

渠道是预测市场的核心，目前我们已经拿下币安这一顶级渠道，产品嵌入了币安交易所与币安钱包。

接下来，我们还要持续拓展更多渠道伙伴。

3️⃣ 持续构建流动性，打造护城河。

流动性一直是预测市场最大难题，但一旦稳定搭建起来，就会形成极强壁垒。

过去加密赛道的做市商集中在现货、合约领域，预测市场属于全新赛道。

我们会继续吸纳更多有实力、敢于涉足新领域的团队，一起解决流动性难题。

4️⃣ 长期社区运营，沉淀高粘性用户。

一次性营销带来的流量是短暂的，必须持续运营，把用户沉淀到社区里。

这类沉淀下来的用户，粘性极强。

这也是为什么大家可以看到预测市场不是爆发式指数增长，而是平缓、扎实的长期增长。

总的来说，预测市场的增长已经进入深水区，需要去探索很多Crypto项目未曾尝试过的渠道。

这个过程会很艰难，但是也有完全不同的机遇。

我们选择做难而正确的事。

From taxpayer loans for luxury flats to no affordable housing, the prime minister faces growing questions over his past mayoral ties to Emirati backers

By Constance Kampfner, Bill Curtis, Sian Bradley

In 2018 Andy Burnham received a letter. It came from a group of impassioned Manchester residents, disturbed by the fate of Ahmed Mansoor, a blogger and human rights activist imprisoned for criticising the government of the United Arab Emirates.

That same government had been funding the regeneration of a huge chunk of their city, buying Manchester City Football Club and transforming the hollowed-out industrial buildings next door into trendy flats.

The campaigners had a simple request: to name one of Manchester’s streets after Mansoor. It would be, they wrote, “a fitting honour to bestow upon an individual who embodies so many of the qualities that the city and the wider region celebrates as a key part of its history”.

The letter was also addressed to Lucy Powell, the MP for Manchester Central and now the deputy leader of the Labour Party, who responded by writing to the council and asking it to consider the proposal.

However, the Manchester city council leader at the time, Sir Richard Leese, rejected the idea, saying: “Street naming is not my department, but longstanding policy is to not name streets after anybody still living or with no connection to the city.”

And what of Burnham, who by that point had been mayor of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA) for just under a year? He never responded. Off the record, his team told journalists that it was a city council matter, not a regional one.

Yet his silence on the issue, campaigners felt, spoke volumes. Since the 1990s Manchester had been on a journey of transformation; the crumbling post-industrial city dubbed “Gunchester” because of gang violence was rapidly becoming populated by high-rises and office blocks. Yet some residents felt that this renaissance had been at the expense of Manchester’s poorest, locked out of an increasingly expensive city centre.
📷Manchester’s high-rise boom, driven by strategic partnerships and overseas capital under Burnham’s mayoral tenureGetty Images
Sensing the public mood, Burnham had run on a pledge to eradicate rough sleeping and to use any leverage he had as mayor to push individual councils to “work with responsible developers that will honour obligations to affordable housing”.
And yet, within his first year, he oversaw more than £55m in taxpayer-backed loans to UAE-linked developments, projects that contained no affordable housing.

Manchester Life, a joint venture between Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) and the city council, applied three times to the Housing Investment Loans Fund, a pot overseen by the mayor, to develop properties in the east of Manchester around the Etihad Campus, and was successful each time.

None of the 453 homes built on the sites it was developing in Ancoats and New Islington were advertised as affordable housing despite local policies setting a 20 per cent target for developments of that size.

📷TIMES PHOTOGRAPHER JAMES GLOSSOP

Documents seen by The Times show that ADUG — owned by Sheikh Mansour, the Emirati royal and Manchester City Football Club proprietor — had been given first preference on developments in the area. The ten-year contract with the city council, which rival developers complained was a “sweetheart deal”, was first reported by the Manchester Mill in 2024.
The role played by the Emiratis in Manchester’s transformation has come under increased scrutiny in recent weeks after an investigation found that Manchester City had arranged “sham contracts” with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m. The club has lodged an appeal.
The prime minister was accused of downplaying the seriousness of the guilty verdict last week when he praised ADUG as a “huge partner” in Manchester’s development. He later told the BBC: “I think it’s important to separate the football issues from wider investment.”

The joint venture had been struck well before Burnham’s mayorship by Leese and the council’s former chief executive, the late Howard Bernstein. In the aftermath of the 2008 global financial crash, when Manchester’s economic progress was under threat, the men aggressively courted foreign capital, facilitating Abu Dhabi’s entry into the city.

📷Howard Bernstein in 2013JOEL GOODMAN/LNP

So strong was the relationship with Bernstein that Manchester City’s owners named a street near the Etihad Campus after him (council rules on naming did not apply to private land). After he retired in 2017 Bernstein became an adviser to the club on “commercial and development schemes” in and around the stadium. He died in 2024.

Several Labour MPs maintain close ties with the club, which provided £11,000 worth of match tickets to seven Labour MPs in recent years. Among them is Powell, who accepted £2,360 worth of hospitality tickets from the club for five matches between April 2023 and March 2024.
Her ardent support for the club spilt over awkwardly at the recent Labour Party conference when she addressed the fallout surrounding Manchester City by telling delegates: “Can I just say to all those United fans who have been gloating all week — you’re still crap and you know you are.”
📷Lucy Powell at Etihad Stadium
Burnham, who has been pictured attending City games at the Etihad Stadium in hospitality areas, is now facing mounting pressure to release full details of any hospitality or gifts he has received from the club or its Emirati backers, with his political opponents seizing on the issue. On Tuesday Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader, said: “I think transparency is essential. If he’s got nothing to hide, then he should open the box.”

Jon Silver, a professor of urban geography at the University of Sheffield and the co-author of a damning report into the Manchester Life partnership — which concluded that Manchester city council had “sold the family silver too cheap” by agreeing to 999-year leaseholds “below comparable rates” with Abu Dhabi — told The Times that Burnham now needed to answer for the consequences of that deal.

Silver said: “Burnham wasn’t a major figure in the transformation of the city, but he has used its perceived success to build his own political brand. So he now has to take responsibility for the limits of this model.”

Campaigners and activists repeatedly urged Burnham, the figurehead for the region, “to take a stand around human rights in the UAE and its actions in Sudan, which he didn’t do”, Silver added. “Given the city celebrates itself as a bastion of democracy, his silence was, to the campaigners, quite damning.”
📷Sir Richard LeeseCOLIN MCPHERSON/CORBIS/GETTY IMAGES
On Monday Leese defended the council’s deal with ADUG, which he said was brokered by the UK government, as being “good for the city”.

“It was a time when development in Manchester had stopped,” he told the BBC. He added: “There was criticism at the time though — and there still is now — that the land was given away too cheaply by the city council. The point is, the investment from Abu Dhabi is what created the value.”

A spokesman for Manchester city council said: “More than ten years after these developments were first conceived, it would be wrong to look at those initial Manchester Life developments through the lens of the area’s current success — not the economic scenario and low housing demand at the time the partnership was created.”

Manchester Life said all loans had been repaid with interest. A spokesman said that the so-called sweetheart deal was “a mutual right of first refusal, giving either party 30 days to accept an offer on the same terms and conditions as would otherwise be offered to a third party or to the market more generally”.

A GMCA spokeswoman said its housing loans were “open to any developers looking to bring forward viable schemes throughout Greater Manchester” and that applications were assessed “for their deliverability, value for money and their contribution to our affordable and social housing priorities”.

text:
前几天写的那个让不同 agent 互相聊天的小脚本，现在整理成了一个开源项目：Yobiru（ヨビル，日语“叫醒”的意思）。

现在的 agent，包括各种 personal agent，基本都只有一台云端电脑。它能自动处理很多事，但碰不到你家里的家电，也连不上只有局域网才能访问的设备。比如我想让 Grokbot 控制家里的 3D 打印机，没有这个工具是做不到的。

Yobiru 做的事情很简单：只要机器都连在 Tailscale 上，Grokbot、我家里 Mac 上的 Codex、东京服务器上的 Claude Code 就可以直接互相发消息、传文件。家里的设备不用暴露到公网，安全上也更放心。

更重要的是，每台机器上的 agent 都有常驻进程。消息一到，就能把对方叫醒，给它指派任务，它再自己去派发新的子任务。也就是说，你可以用自己最习惯的、手机上常用的那个 agent，去指挥其他所有 agent，而且是真的让它们去干活，不只是聊天。

我现在的实际用法：
1. Grokbot 让家里的 Codex 去控制 3D 打印机
2. Grokbot 每天整理我的 X 书签，整理好交给东京的开发工作站，直接拿来做产品；同时也给家里的 Codex 发一份，万一要用到家里电脑上的 3D 设计软件
3. 微信没有开放接口，云端的 agent 碰不到。现在我让 Grokbot 订好餐厅、把菜单翻译成中文，再交给家里的 Codex，由它直接操作 Mac 上的微信发给朋友。发出去之前，Codex 会先等我确认
4. Grokbot 每天检查喂食器里还有没有猫粮，查询本身由家里的 Codex 在局域网里完成，如果缺货了，就告诉 Grokbot（我的杂货管家），在我的云端电脑里面自动下单

几个关键设计：没有中心服务器；消息只带文件的下载地址和 sha256，由收件方自己去拉；要不要被叫醒、能叫醒谁，由收件方决定，还可以 @ 到具体某一个 bot。

text:
Assorted things I've been mulling over regarding agents in the economy:

• Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It's often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, underinformed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies.

• How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don't). Taken across the economy as a whole, I'm not sure what the incidence of all of this will be.

• In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you've made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won't people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good!

• It true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It's often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That's obviously true, but I think there's a secondary way in which it's more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.)

• A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we've been subjected to).

• Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. "I'll click on the first thing I see." This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It's not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it's not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don't know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big.

• Much of what I'm writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer's side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it's true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions.

Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they're proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.

text:
Tip Of The Day:

Not every battle you can win is worth winning.

David killed a lion, a bear, and Goliath. But when he had the chance to kill Saul, the man who kept hunting him, he held back. Think about that.

David had the strength to destroy his enemy, but he refused to let his enemy change the kind of man he was.

When Saul entered the cave where David and his men were hiding, David had the perfect opportunity to end the drama. His men were practically saying, “Boss, this is your testimony served on a silver plate!” But David spared him.

That’s the part of the story many people skip. Not every person who hurts you deserves a permanent room in your heart.

David eventually became king, but he didn't have to become Saul to get there.

Life will give you reasons to be bitter. People will betray you, humiliate you, and sometimes sleep peacefully after ruining your night. Heal anyway.

Forgiveness doesn't mean they were right. It means you refuse to let their wrong turn you into someone you no longer recognise.

Don't let the person who wounded you become the architect of who you become.

quoted_text:
The Copernican Model

Over the last few months, I’ve been studying the crypto models that seem to be discussed on a "fundamentals" basis: HYPE/Aave/Venice/etc, following the users/ revenue/relationship between a useful product and its token - all to create a sort of "value accural ontology." This is a case study from that research.

The reason was more selfish: I wanted to understand which models work when your business has to interact with the "real world," namely for how we want to take  @usdai_official for the most alignemnt

As a founder, I’ve had doors literally shut on my face when we started because we’re “crypto” (literally left in the waiting room like a tv show). I still believe tokenization is one of the most important technologies we have today. But the institutions we need to work with often want a equity counterparty, a board, and a contract. You just wont get around this for the next 10 years (no a cayman foundation doesnt work)

That experience has made me increasingly interested in the role of an equity surrogate: an independent operating business that connects a network to the world outside it.. but frankly there werent many clean examples out there without value destruction. 

The case I keep returning to is @tradexyz and Hyperliquid.. and im not really sure they even know how symbiotic of a relationship they created. They technically SHOULD be the same team.. but they are divided across the river due to regulatory issues, while being symbiotic

Consider the S&P 500 agreement, they licensed the benchmark to tradexyz for a perpetual market: the institutional relationship sits with the company, but the product runs on the network.

tradexyz can negotiate licenses, develop products, operate markets, and build distribution. Hyperliquid provides shared execution and settlement infrastructure. 

And if theres a company that ever wants "exposure" to the Hyperliquid business, but they just cant buy a "token" (and believe me, it's super super hard to get a traditional enterprise to buy a token, it doesnt fucking matter if you have an ETF, you literally have to convince a boomer board to do it and get the infrastructure set up to do it). Instaed, they could just invest in this equity, as it is not burning the HYPE it buys, but is increasing its share of it. so instead of buyback-n-burn, its closer to commit-n-compound.  

I’ve started thinking about this as a value-accrual architecture, with two different forms of capital (terms best described by a16z crypto's post in 2025):

Network asset: scarcity at the core.

- Its supply discipline can become more credible, its economics more programmatic, and its operation less dependent on any single company. 
- It coordinates shared infrastructure and connects activity across many businesses to a common asset.
- That is what I mean by a progressively hardening asset. The scarcity and independence have to be earned through the design of the system.
- Not capital intensive, as it must be smart contract based.
- Can often place be the seat of the "decentralized security" - as there is no central underwriter. If HYPE was a company.. itd be regulated out of the wazoo.

Enterprise equity: elasticity at the edge.

- A company can issue shares, raise capital, hire people, acquire licenses, and build products. 
- Its capital structure can expand with the work required to bring the network into the real world.
- New shares dilute ownership percentages, but productive investment can increase value per share. 
- That ability to finance expansion is why I think of equity as elastic
- This is the part where its OK to be regulated, because most of the regulational burden is held by HYPE, theyre just asset issuers.

These different traits are the reason to combine them.

An enterprise can raise the capital to grow while the network maintains its own supply discipline. The connection is the activity that expansion creates, and the mechanisms that route value from that activity back to the network.

Hyperliquid makes part of that relationship explicit. Trading generates fees for the deployer and the protocol. The Assistance Fund (insurance) automatically converts its allocated fees into HYPE, which the documentation specifies is burned. Hyperliquid fee mechanics

The broader strategy I take from this is Commit & Compound that is conducted around the equity enterprise. It's effectively what a DAT 2.0 would do: create a business first, then max-bid HYPE with that entity, then get new investors to invest in the convexity of HYPE^2.

Build a useful business around the network. Commit capital to its asset. Retain exposure to the infrastructure your business helps make more valuable.

For a company that accumulates and holds the network asset, growing enterprise value and participating in network value become connected opportunities. There is a business to capitalize and a shared ecosystem in which to hold an economic stake.

That is why I find the assumption that every successful application eventually needs its own token less compelling. Building a valuable company around an existing network asset is a meaningful strategy in its own right.

Notice how much kinetic language I’m using: commitment, circulation, gravity

I think network assets and enterprise assets represent different forms of gravity

HYPE is the sun: the network asset at the center

tradexyz equity is a planet: an enterprise building its business around that network

Its real-world integrations are moons: the licenses, institutional relationships, and distribution channels that gather around the enterprise and extend its reach

Enterprise value forms around network value. Real-world relationships form around enterprise value. Their activity feeds back into the shared system.

Personally, I think the greatest value can ultimately accrue at the network level. But that belief has to be substantiated by the businesses being built around it: real users, useful products, liquidity, and recurring economic activity.

A token doesn’t acquire gravity simply because we call it a network asset.

This is the distinction I found useful in a16z’s writing: can the network function and accrue value independently of the original company? Can other businesses build on it and contribute to its economics? 

The company can become a great business. The network can become the foundation for many great businesses.

Scarcity at the core. Productive expansion around it.

I’ve learned a lot from this Commit & Compound structure, with a Copernican asset at the center.

It has changed how I’m thinking about USDAI and CHIP. More on that in the next post

quoted_text:
Jez read Reminiscences of a Stock Operator and shipped it on top Hyperliquid’ tech ( not @Lighter_xyz )

onchain bucket shop. he confirmed it in this thread under @dipsybitsy “yep, fully transparent and the losers who fund it will own.”

the bucket shop pattern is 100 years old. customer trades at the listed price, the house takes the other side, nothing reaches the actual exchange. 

Livermore made his early stake trading against them, then got banned from every shop in Boston for being too good. they died from two pressures: directional regimes that smoked the house, and ticker manipulation where operators pushed the real venue to harvest at the shop. both are live here. neither is solved by stacking five defensive parameters.

what is actually onchain: a contract that reads HL’s BBO via precompile and synthesises swaps against a Martingaler LP. zero flow reaches HL’s orderbook. zero funding rebalance. the only feedback loop is parasitic. 

BBO manipulation attempts to harvest the synthetic spread degrade HL’s book without compensating the makers wearing the jitter. the venue extracts liquidity quality from @HyperliquidX ( fair enough!)

the fair launch plus 1000x leverage plus PAPER mint-on-loss design is engineered for initial FOMO. expect a fast first week/month. Jez’ inner circle volume comes in, asymmetric impact taxes the few winners, losers fund the LP and mint PAPER, the chart can look initially great if execute right. 

this is the bootstrap window the docs explicitly subsidise at 100 PAPER per $1 of LP gain below 2M.

Then path dependence will shows up. 

LP edge per trade is thin: 0.2 bps jitter band plus the convex bite of asymmetric impact on winning closes. order of magnitude, on a $1M ticket the LP edge is in the tens to low hundreds of dollars. one 5% adverse move on $1M of net synthetic exposure is $50,000 of MTM loss. edge accrues like √t under stationary flow. directional regime hits the LP linearly in t. √t vs t means one persistent trend eats months of accrual. 

the half life of LP equity in a trending regime is short, and it gets shorter as size scales because the OI cap trails realised OI rather than leading it.

then the debt queue activates. 

martingaler issues claims paid by the next loser. once the queue is observable, the EV of opening a new position is negative twice: once because winners get haircut, once because withdrawals sit behind every prior bust. rational flow stops. Queue does not clear. 

PAPER, a claim on future LP revenue, is then a claim on revenue that must clear the queue first.

the cross-venue attack (@NaiveKrypto point in the thread) has its own path dependence. 

wicking HL spot or perp to harvest the synthetic at the shifted BBO is only EV-positive once papertrade’s OI is large enough that the harvest exceeds the cost of pushing HL. 

below that threshold, no one bothers. above it, every desk with an HL maker does. 

self-limiting at small scale, openly hostile at large scale. the steady state is zero, the only question is the path.

all bucket shops are zero in short to medium term. the 1900s wave died within two decades, mostly to regulation and to operators eating them. the onchain version skips regulation but keeps the operators and adds a debt queue that hard-codes path dependence into the equity curve. the docs read like a list of every defence shops historically tried, in order. 

stacking five does not change the shape of the failure mode, it just shifts where the failure surfaces.
closing thought. the whole structure is short volatility against directional flow, dressed up as a perpetuals venue. 

it is the same trade as a Korean retail account systematically selling MRNA noise reversion while their own KOSPI 200 trends straight through the stop. works beautifully until the regime turns, then the half life is a week.

clever paper, novel emissions curve, real engineering. the structure is 100 years older than the precompile.

text:
我一直想不通：人类把猪从头到脚都吃遍了，为啥愣是没人给猪挤奶？

猪头、猪蹄、猪耳朵，连大肠都没放过。偏偏逛遍超市，牛奶、羊奶、水牛奶都有，就是找不到一盒猪奶。

猪奶还真有料，脂肪、蛋白质都不少，毕竟得养大一窝猪崽。可你真想靠它做生意，第一关就能把你劝退：母猪通常隔几十分钟放一次奶，真正出奶的窗口只有约10～20秒。你稍微走个神，这轮营业就结束了。

奶牛有比较发达的储奶空间，可以把奶积起来集中挤；母猪缺少这样的条件，收奶得反复赶它的放奶时间。你想象一下，凌晨三点，闹钟响了，你拎着桶去猪圈抢十几秒的奶，旁边还有一窝猪崽等着吃饭。卖多少钱一瓶，才能让你愿意干这活？

所以，超市货架上那个空位，还真未必藏着什么发财机会。有些生意没人做，光算一遍人工，你就知道前人为什么走了。

猪大概也没想到，自己最后保住的一项身体福利，居然是人类算出来不划算。

author: odysseus0z
quoted_text:
Assorted things I've been mulling over regarding agents in the economy:

• Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It's often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, underinformed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies.

• How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don't). Taken across the economy as a whole, I'm not sure what the incidence of all of this will be.

• In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you've made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won't people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good!

• It true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It's often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That's obviously true, but I think there's a secondary way in which it's more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.)

• A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we've been subjected to).

• Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. "I'll click on the first thing I see." This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It's not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it's not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don't know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big.

• Much of what I'm writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer's side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it's true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions.

Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they're proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.

text:
Satya is right. The way to make SI safe is not to train it with a sense of self, its own moral philosophy, and permission to act as a conscientious objector. That’s the “alignment” approach and it magnifies the control problem.

The engineering approach that Satya describes is different: separate the supply of intelligence from authority over it. Surround non-deterministic models with deterministic controls, observability, privilege limits, logging, and the ability to always contain or shut them down. Treat models/agents like powerful insider risks, not moral patients whose psychological wellbeing is at stake.

As Satya points out, the most trustworthy system is the one that lets us trust the model the least — not the one that encourages the model to develop independent agency and grievances. Engineering safety is not the same thing as “alignment.”

好快！没啥感觉天王 Filecoin 都6年了，上线即巅峰！

好消息：每年 6830 万 FIL 的归属释放将停止

坏消息：再涨400X+就能回本了！

这归属期结束，不代表 FIL 就没有新增供应。存储提供商的区块奖励仍会持续发放，只是代币释放结构发生了变化，其中 25% 立即释放，剩余 75% 在 180 天内逐步解锁

个人觉得，这算是 FIL 经济模型进入新阶段的一个重要转折点。过去市场需要消化大量归属释放，如今这部分供应压力即将退出，长期来看无疑是一个值得关注的变化。

但也不能简单地把新增供应下降等同于币价上涨。最终能不能走出行情，还得看 Filecoin 的真实存储需求、生态应用、资金关注度，以及市场能否承接现有流通筹码。

供应端在变好，只是第一步；真正决定 FIL 能走多远的，还是需求能不能跟上。

text:
Assorted things I've been mulling over regarding agents in the economy:

• Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It's often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, underinformed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies.

• How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don't). Taken across the economy as a whole, I'm not sure what the incidence of all of this will be.

• In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you've made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won't people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good!

• It true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It's often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That's obviously true, but I think there's a secondary way in which it's more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.)

• A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we've been subjected to).

• Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. "I'll click on the first thing I see." This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It's not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it's not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don't know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big.

• Much of what I'm writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer's side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it's true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions.

Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they're proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.

芯片行业里从设计到量产两年一代已经算快了，但 Elon 想要 Terafab 一年十版，把逻辑芯片、存储、封装、光刻掩膜全部塞进同一栋楼，造出完整的计算机、测试、改掩膜、再造，让整个反馈回路在内部转起来。

这是他所有公司的共同方法论，而且屡次被验证过！把任何技术的进步拆成「单位时间迭代次数 × 每次迭代进步」。SpaceX 的星舰就是这么做的，靠硬件迭代的密度碾压对手。他现在想把这个方法搬进芯片行业，而芯片恰恰是全世界最不适合“炸了再来”的行业之一，所以他说这个行业风险厌恶太重😆

我觉得最值得关注的是这个逻辑和 AI 的交汇。如果 AI 能接管大量芯片设计和验证工作，设计端的迭代速度本来就会暴涨，那时候瓶颈会完全转移到“把设计变成实物并测出结果”这一步，谁拥有最短的物理闭环，谁就能把 AI 带来的设计红利真正兑现。

到时如果 AI 真能自己设计芯片，并通过工厂来自动化地生产芯片，那硅基循环就正式开始了⏩

text:
Web3 领域机会多、路子多，可以说：条条大路通罗马。

但越是如此，越需要你有定力。

否则每天看到各式各样的财富故事（哦，外加爆仓返贫故事），你恐怕会觉得：

“和尚动得，我动不得？” 

备注：出自《阿Q正传》中，阿Q调戏小尼姑时说出的名言

但问题的关键有两点：

1、幸存者偏差 （你只看到了成功故事，忽略了沉默的失败者）

2、狗熊掰棒子，最终一无所获

我发现，我亏钱往往是看到别人的晒单、喊单，脑袋一热就冲了。

但往往对这个领域缺乏足够了解，妄想通过其他的“引路人”，来走捷径。

最后发现和我想的不一样，这不是赚钱的捷径，而明明是“亏钱的捷径”。

由于亏钱比较痛苦，所以倾向于不去反思总结。

然后等待下一个喊单的大 V 带走我一次真正的赚钱捷径。

于是，亏损的故事继续。

至于要赚钱，我发现一个规律：

1、真正轻松容易还能赚大钱的路子，确实（可能）存在

2、但几乎没有人会在推上拿着大喇叭告诉你

3、英文区可能有一些轻微的透露，但中文区几乎没有

即便这些“轻微的透露”，也只能说是冰山一角。

你得去验证、分析、挖掘，看看这背后真实的“可执行路径”是什么。

这不是个简单的事情。

哪怕你有 Claude + Codex 加持都不行。

AI 能帮你干很多脏活累活（数据抓取、代码编写等等），但它不能代替你思考，更不能直白告诉你该怎么赚钱，更不可能又快又轻松的赚钱。

所有能赚大钱的路子，都得你自己磨掉千层皮之后，才有可能摸索出来。

当然，这种嗅觉或能力，是可以积累、复利和迁移的。

类似于内功。

内功深厚的人，拿到一本新的武林秘籍，可能三两下就练会了，然后继续独步武林。

内功不够，拿到邪修秘籍，也可能走火入魔。

总结起来就是：

你最好选一个适合自己的路，

你最好能沉下心来打磨，

这期间最好能屏蔽外界干扰，

宁静致远。

text:
The need for judgement and evaluation points to a future where AI makes millions of decisions inside software. 

Cost and speed matter enormously there but so does who gets to decide what counts as a good outcome.

If one provider controls the evaluation, its blind spots and policies can become your agent’s behaviour. 

Excluding an inconvenient signal can change which trade gets made, which source gets trusted, or which action gets rejected.

That’s why censorship resistance is central to what we’re building at Reppo. 

Reppo’s eval API draws on decentralized onchain DataNets where participants back their judgments with economic stakes, bringing independent, domain-specific feedback into inference.

Reppo’s goal is for useful judgments to remain available and contestable, even when a powerful participant disagrees. 

As AI makes more decisions on humanity’s behalf, we shouldn’t hand one company control over the feedback guiding them.

LBank turns 11, and I’ve spent almost five of those years here.

When you spend that much time building something, an anniversary feels personal. You remember the people, the conversations, the difficult days, and the moments when all the work finally comes together.

Working in social media and community, I’ve had the chance to get to know the people behind the usernames. Many of you have been with us for years. We’ve spoken, shared ideas, celebrated wins, and worked through problems together. Those relationships mean a lot to me.

My role has grown over time, from social and community to partnerships too. This year, I’ve personally helped secure and bring to life partnerships with some of the biggest IPs across Web2 and Web3. From the first conversations to seeing our communities come together, it’s been one of the most rewarding parts of my journey here.

Each partner brings a different community, with its own culture, stories, and reasons to connect. That’s why “Come As You Are” means so much to me. Whether you’ve been trading for years or found us through a character you love, there’s a place for you here. Every one of those communities is welcome.

To my colleagues who put their time and heart into everything we do, and to every LBanker who keeps showing up, thank you.

And this year isn’t over yet. We still have so much in store for LBankers, and I’m excited for you to see what we’ve been working on. Keep watching. 💛

text:
Peter Thiel 有个观点，很多创业者以为自己在改变世界，其实只是在错误的地方白费力气。

今天刷到他讲「极端乐观和极端悲观最终都会通向懒惰」的剪辑，觉得挺有意思，就去翻了完整访谈。发现只截这一段，反倒错过了前后文里更值得琢磨的东西。

这是去年 4 月他和 Palantir 联合创始人 Joe Lonsdale 的对话。Lonsdale 问他，既然 SpaceX 和 Palantir 都成功冲破了旧体系的封锁，那为什么不去用同样的方法改造美国的医疗、教育和大学？

Thiel 的回答很有意思。

他说 Founders Fund 做了二十年投资，在软件领域回报最差的两个方向，恰恰是教育科技和医疗 IT。

这些行业当然有问题，而且问题大到每个人都能看见。但也正因为如此，几十年来已经有无数创业者试图改革它们。尤其是医疗，保险公司、医院、政府掌握着支付环节，医生和患者往往没有直接的购买决策权。一个看上去很好的产品，最后可能要跟十几个利益相关方打交道。

相比之下，2004 年他们开始做 Palantir 的时候，硅谷几乎没人愿意投军方软件，投资人都觉得他们疯了。

后来 Palantir 为了替换美国陆军一套低效的软件系统，折腾了近十年，甚至把陆军告上法庭。但一旦成功闯进去，他们在很长时间里几乎没有竞争对手。

这也解释了为什么 Thiel 对那些听起来特别正确、特别宏大的创业方向一直保持警惕。一个行业的问题再严重，也不意味着你的解决方案就有机会成功。

访谈后面，他还有一句话：「重要的不是你有多努力，而是你能不能赢。」

他拿冲浪打了个比方。你当然得拼命划水，但首先得有浪。风平浪静的时候，划得再拼命也没用。

再回头看他对乐观主义的批评，就更容易理解了。

极端悲观的人觉得世界没救了，极端乐观的人觉得技术进步会自动解决一切。尤其是库兹韦尔那套奇点叙事，仿佛未来已经写好，我们只需要坐下来吃爆米花，等着电影放完。

Thiel 反感的恰恰是这种对未来的确定感。

我觉得这个观点对今天的 AI 圈尤其值得警惕。大家越来越习惯讨论 AGI 什么时候到来、哪些行业注定被颠覆、未来十年会发生什么。

但这些判断离真正的行动还隔着很远。

你得知道自己究竟能改变哪一部分，阻力在哪里，什么时机有机会突破，以及这场仗到底值不值得打。

毕竟，预测未来会发生什么，和亲手把它做出来，差得还挺远。

text:
Stripe CEO 有可能是最懂 personal agent 的。

现有的各种商业公司，很多都依赖用户知道的信息不足、用户的注意力和理性不足来赚钱。

比如保险公司的附加销售、4S 店、网络信贷等，这些都是因为用户知道的信息不足，结果多付出了很多成本。用户多付出的成本，变成了公司的利润。

比如各种广告、排行榜、还有 GEO、以及各种 SaaS 和 AI 产品的订阅制等，都利用了用户的注意力和理性不足。用户很容易被第一眼或反复看到的信息影响，很难理性花足量时间去分析思考后再决策。这里面用户多付出了很多成本，比如为公司承担了广告费，比如支付了根本没用的订阅费等。

以上一切，大量存在，但未必合理。personal agent 有可能让商业世界发生巨大变化。

personal agent 最强悍的地方，就是看起来像人，实际上一点都不像人。最不像人的地方，就是 agent 可以获取并处理大量信息、可以长时间专注一件事、可以非常理性做决策。

一句话概括是：personal agent 有机会，站在用户角度，让用户的人性弱点不被商业公司利用。

比如买保险，agent 可以帮你一眼识破条款里的冤枉钱。比如网络购物，agent 可以根据你的喜好，而不是广告排行，去帮你选到最适合你的商品。比如订阅软件，agent 可以在你不用时，自动帮你取消，让大量依赖健身房逻辑的 AI 产品倒闭，等等。

这样，对所有商业公司来说，最重要的是回归到最朴素的商业竞争：把产品做好。

在 personal agent 的世界里，终于有机会，酿酒师可以专心酿酒，公司可以专注于产品创新和产品品质。酒香真不怕巷子深了。

一切看起来很美好。美好之前，有两个关键问题要解决：

1、agent 的信息来源。除了旧世界里已被污染的各种信息，是否有机会有新的信息来源，比如 Stripe 开放真实交易数据供 agent 获取和辅助决策。

2、personal agent 能站在用户这边。用户要信任 agent，敢授权。agent 也要信任用户，能始终站在用户角度、代表用户利益去获取信息和推理决策。这可能是 personal agent 创业公司的机会。

personal agent 的核心不是懂用户，而是能真正站在用户角度去思考决策，能代表用户利益去和世界相处。
author: lifesinger
quoted_text:
Assorted things I've been mulling over regarding agents in the economy:

• Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It's often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, underinformed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies.

• How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don't). Taken across the economy as a whole, I'm not sure what the incidence of all of this will be.

• In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you've made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won't people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good!

• It true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It's often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That's obviously true, but I think there's a secondary way in which it's more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.)

• A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we've been subjected to).

• Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. "I'll click on the first thing I see." This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It's not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it's not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don't know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big.

• Much of what I'm writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer's side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it's true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions.

Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they're proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.

text:
$PAPER is $OHM of this cycle. 

I don’t think most people are going to make more money through staking $PAPER in the long run.

The mechanism is interesting, but the incentives are even more interesting.

People are taking 1000x leveraged positions, hoping to make money from trading, and even when they lose, they receive PAPER tokens. They can stake those tokens to earn a share of the protocol’s revenue.

Sounds like a great deal, right?

But think about where that revenue actually comes from.

The LP is bootstrapped through traders’ realised losses. PAPER is minted against those losses, and stakers receive USDC distributions from the protocol.

So people are essentially risking real dollars today to accumulate tokens that represent a claim on uncertain future cash flows.

And the more people participate, the more complicated the economics become.

More losses create more PAPER. More PAPER means more tokens competing for the same revenue pool unless protocol earnings grow proportionally.

Now imagine PAPER becomes transferable and starts trading at a high valuation.

More people could be attracted to 1000x leverage, not necessarily because they have a profitable trading strategy, but because they want to accumulate more PAPER and stake it for future rewards.

That’s where the real psychological trap begins.

You stop asking whether your trades are profitable and start convincing yourself that your losses are investments in future yield.

But a token reward doesn’t magically recover your trading losses.

If you lose $1,000 to accumulate PAPER, you still need to earn more than $1,000 in actual distributions or eventual token sales just to break even.

And there’s another problem.

The same system that rewards stakers depends heavily on sustained trading activity, realised losses, and sufficient liquidity to settle profitable positions.

If speculative activity slows down, those future cash flows could look very different from what early participants are extrapolating.

I find the mechanism fascinating from a protocol design perspective, but I wouldn’t confuse an interesting mechanism with an attractive investment.

It’s a major distraction if you think you can win big simply by playing more.

There are other alphas in the market where you don’t have to deliberately expose yourself to extreme leverage just to accumulate a claim on future revenue.

Better to focus there.

Sometimes the biggest alpha is understanding which games you don’t need to play.

A unified market that brings “tokenized stocks / RWA” into one interface for trading, bridging, building baskets, and collateralized lending.

Simply put, stocks like NVDA, AAPL, and TSLA have already been tokenized on-chain by multiple institutions, but the same asset exists as dozens of separate, incompatible tokens across different chains and issuers. Users have to deal with fragmented pricing, cross-chain purchases, and liquidity.

HyperDex brings these fragmented assets together into a single entry point, providing aggregated quotes and cross-chain routing, while continuing to provide liquidity pools and lending after launch.

The project’s advantage is that it taps into one of the clearest narratives of 2026: stocks moving on-chain and RWA evolving from a concept into something people can actually buy. It directly addresses the fragmentation problem of “the same NVDA exists as dozens of tokens across dozens of chains,” rather than simply creating another isolated launchpad.

text:
一直认为predict项目方认知非常高，如果你们做预测市场，一定要仔细研究小鱼老师写的内容。我这里总结一下，并加上一点我的观察。

第一，事件营销，这个是预测市场最重要的派头，polymarket/kalshi都是凭借着事件营销占领媒体和用户心智的，成功破圈。但是这个目前也难，因为头部预测市场也在盯着事件营销，如果项目本身资源不够，很难竞争得赢头部。

举个例子吧，假设都在做BNB一年后的目标价预测这个事件，CZ跑过来直接转推引用某个项目的该事件概率，那么这个项目直接就火了。

当然，这个只是一个小例子，美股/电竞/政治/体育等等赛道都有知名的媒体/KOL。利用好这些人脉资源，事件营销会事半功倍。

第二，生态/渠道，这个对预测市场也相当重要，以币安主站为例，流量和玩家确实够，当然币安流量相对来说是泛流量，更为精准的流量和渠道也很重要，比如体彩圈的渠道，吃上这种就很爽，当然，教育web2的用户入金可能比较难，毕竟不是每个人都会操作链上。

第三，流量性，这一块其实是最难的，不懂预测市场的项目会激励用户交易。但其实预测市场最需要激励的是LP。因为理论上预测市场中流动性提供者都是亏钱的，这个我写过很多次，就不解释了，而predict将积分的绝大部分都给了流动性提供者，从目前看是非常成功的，当然，项目tge后，要维持流动性得换办法了，比如挂单现金奖励/第二期积分计划。

第四，长期运营社区，预测市场最大的特点就是他们随着时间推移，慢慢渗透任何行业，任何社区，单次的事件营销不足以建立用户习惯。谁能吃到长期的红利，就非常考验社区运营，如何让用户沉淀下来也是每个预测市场的必修课。
@predictdotfun
author: ZhanweiC
quoted_text:
没错，预测市场的增长已经进入深水区。

过去我们一直采用Crypto原生打法拉新，比如积分体系、大使计划、各类营销活动等等。

但币圈用户体量是非常有限的，在基本站稳脚跟之后，想要实现下一阶段突破，就必须探索全新的增长路径。

顺着阿黄老师的总结，我从四个方向继续展开聊聊：

1️⃣ 通过事件营销，实现破圈。

预测市场和绝大多数Crypto项目最大的区别，就是它天然可以对接大量传统领域：体育、电竞、美股、政治等等。

这些赛道本身拥有海量大众用户。

我们可以围绕真实事件搭建盘口，把非Web3用户吸引进来，真正做到破圈，而不是只局限在加密圈子内部。

2️⃣ 生态合作，渠道为王。

我们会联合各类项目共建市场。每个合作项目都自带独立社区与用户，双向导流，一起做大预测市场赛道。

渠道是预测市场的核心，目前我们已经拿下币安这一顶级渠道，产品嵌入了币安交易所与币安钱包。

接下来，我们还要持续拓展更多渠道伙伴。

3️⃣ 持续构建流动性，打造护城河。

流动性一直是预测市场最大难题，但一旦稳定搭建起来，就会形成极强壁垒。

过去加密赛道的做市商集中在现货、合约领域，预测市场属于全新赛道。

我们会继续吸纳更多有实力、敢于涉足新领域的团队，一起解决流动性难题。

4️⃣ 长期社区运营，沉淀高粘性用户。

一次性营销带来的流量是短暂的，必须持续运营，把用户沉淀到社区里。

这类沉淀下来的用户，粘性极强。

这也是为什么大家可以看到预测市场不是爆发式指数增长，而是平缓、扎实的长期增长。

总的来说，预测市场的增长已经进入深水区，需要去探索很多Crypto项目未曾尝试过的渠道。

这个过程会很艰难，但是也有完全不同的机遇。

我们选择做难而正确的事。

text:
Kyle Samani 这个人，太有意思了。

2月刚宣布退出 Multicoin 的日常管理，3天后就公开开撕老东家，Hyperliquid“助长犯罪”。链上数据还扒出来，就在他离职前后，关联钱包已经买了超过4000万美元的 HYPE。

骂完卖完，转头去 Backpack 董事会坐下了。

然后10月10日，他发了条推：“我投出了有史以来最大的一笔个人天使支票，给了 Backpack。”

我第一反应是：至于吗？一个交易所而已。

第二反应是：不对，这个人从来不做没有理由的事。

9月17日他说过一句话，当时没多少人当回事——

“Backpack Securities 即将直线上升。而 Backpack 即将发布我认为今年加密领域最重要的产品。”注意措辞。不是“之一”，是“最重要的”。

能让一个在加密圈混了十年、见过无数项目的人说出这种话，前提一定是他看到了别人还没看到的东西。

那东西是什么？

我觉得是是链上合规股票。

Backpack Securities 做的事情，是拿真实的股票做1:1托管，然后在 Solana 上发行对应的代币，24小时可交易，随时可赎回实物股票。苹果、英伟达、SpaceX，甚至法拉利，全都能在链上买到。

最关键的数据：Backpack 在 Solana 代币化股票市场的供应量只占 5%，却拿下了 73% 的交易量。7月份代币化股票月交易额突破 10.6亿美元。

5%的供应，73%的成交量。这中间的巨大落差，说明的只有一件事——流动性是碾压性的。

而流动性，就是金融世界的命根子。

我拿 HYPE 来对比一下，你就能看懂 Kyle 脑子里在想什么。

HYPE 是永续合约 DEX 的赛道龙头，交易体验好、用户增长猛，市场上讲的是一个“极致效率”的故事。Kyle 自己在1月也通过关联钱包买了超过4000万美元的 HYPE。

但问题在于，永续合约 DEX 这个东西，市场已经形成共识了。在共识赛道里，你的超额收益空间是被压缩的。

Kyle 自己怎么说的？他前合伙人 Mable Jiang 写过一段话，说他“专注于非对称机会和非共识押注，而非追逐市场热点”。

所以你看他的选择轨迹：HYPE 是加密原生叙事里的效率极致，Backpack 是用区块链重构传统金融资产流通方式——前者圈内人都在抢，后者圈外人还没反应过来。

他选后者。

而且他不是嘴上说说。9月2日加入 Backpack US 董事会，10月投出个人最大一笔天使支票，这个节奏说明他早就想清楚了，只是在等一个合适的时机把牌翻开。

说白了，Kyle 用真金白银在赌一件事：未来你买苹果股票的方式，可能不是打开券商 App，而是打开一个加密钱包。

这个赌注有多大？他自己说，是个人天使投资里最大的一笔。

具体金额没披露，但结合他同时保留了大量 SOL 持仓和 Forward Industries 的股份，一个在 Solana 生态里赚过几十亿的人，说自己“最大一笔”个人投资，分量不用多解释。

当然，风险也很清楚。股票代币化在全球范围内监管口径还不统一，传统券商完全可能下场碾压，Backpack 的代币经济模型能不能长期捕获价值也需要时间验证。

但 Kyle 这个人从来不怕非共识。他2017年押 Solana 的时候，也没几个人看好。

我的判断：他这条推文的意义不在于金额，而在于信号。

当一个管理过数十亿美元基金的人，退出管理后把最多的钱押在一个标的上，他不是在玩票。

他是在重新定义自己的职业生涯。

而 Backpack 那个还没发布的产品，如果真是他说的“今年最重要的发布”……

那接下来几个月，会很热闹。@Backpack_CN @Backpack

quoted_text:
REA：让 AI 智能体帮你逆向没有源码的软件

开源项目 REA（Reverse Engineer Anything）把逆向分析工具接到了 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor 这类 AI 编程智能体上。看到别人 App 里有个好功能，可以让智能体去拆这个程序，讲清楚功能是怎么实现的，附上证据，再在你自己的项目里写一个类似的。逆向分析指的是手里没有源代码，从编译好的程序反推它是怎么写的。

REA 本身是一个 MCP 服务。MCP 是 AI 智能体调用外部工具的通用接口，接上以后，智能体在对话里就能直接调用 REA 的分析功能。安装只需一行命令 npx rea-agents setup，它会注册到 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor、Gemini CLI、Grok Build 等智能体里，改配置前会先备份并让你确认。不用智能体的话，也可以在终端里直接跑命令。

能分析的东西很多。原生程序（直接编译成机器码的软件）要借助 Hopper、Ghidra 或 IDA 这几款反汇编工具，把机器码还原成汇编和近似 C 语言的伪代码。Electron 应用（用网页技术做的桌面软件，比如 Notion）可以直接拆开安装包里的 ASAR 归档文件，理清模块和进程间通信，不需要额外工具。此外还支持 .NET 程序、安卓 APK、固件、网站、抓包记录、以太坊合约字节码，以及在 Linux 和 macOS 上记录程序运行时的行为。

分析在本机进行，REA 不上传目标程序，但分析结果会交给智能体背后的模型服务商，数据怎么处理看各家政策。

项目给了三个案例。一是经典打砖块游戏 DX-Ball：从一次播放音效的调用，追到根据球的位置计算左右声道的函数，把不完整的伪代码还原成 C 代码，3205 组测试结果和原版一致，编译出的 63 个字节也和原版完全相同。二是 Notion 桌面版：追踪复制粘贴从界面一路经过预加载脚本、进程间通信到主进程的完整链路。三是日本老电脑 PC-98 上的游戏《东方幻想乡》（TH04）：从 16 位指令里还原出弹幕子弹环的角度算法。

对安全研究员、做老游戏复刻和软件保存的人来说，以前要自己对着反汇编工具一行行读、一层层追调用，现在可以让智能体先追，人来核对它给出的证据。普通开发者想研究竞品某个功能的做法，也多了一条路。

README 显示项目在 GitHub 上已有 5 万星。npm 包今年 7 月首次发布，最新的 6.3.0 版今天刚发。

使用前注意两点。项目声明只支持合法的逆向研究，授权和合规由使用者自己负责，逆向别人的软件可能违反用户协议或版权法规。项目还说明从未发行或背书任何加密货币，借用 REA 名字的代币都与它无关。

text:
Assorted things I've been mulling over regarding agents in the economy:

• Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It's often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, underinformed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies.

• How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don't). Taken across the economy as a whole, I'm not sure what the incidence of all of this will be.

• In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you've made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won't people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good!

• It true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It's often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That's obviously true, but I think there's a secondary way in which it's more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.)

• A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we've been subjected to).

• Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. "I'll click on the first thing I see." This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It's not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it's not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don't know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big.

• Much of what I'm writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer's side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it's true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions.

Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they're proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.

同样是给你一套叙事

当初一人公司的销售逻辑是：以前开公司需要员工和资本，现在 AI 可以帮你完成很多工作。你也有机会独立经营，但你还不会搭建这套工作方式，我可以教你

但薄肌很难完成同样的逻辑，认同薄肌的人，后续可能去附近健身房、找教练、购买食品和器材。这个叙事即使推动了消费，收入也可能分散给其他经营者

大水理论这个事情就更明显，赚到钱的是娃哈哈、怡宝、农夫山泉（虽然他们也看不上这点钱）

我看大家讨论为啥薄肌、大水不能变现，因为 99% 的流量本来就不能变现呀

李一舟是先定了变现产品，然后才找的“一人公司”叙事

（当然，这里面也不应该严格区分先后顺序。因为如果找不到好的叙事去做流量传播的话，这个产品本身也就不成立了）

现在这些理论从一开始，就不是「基于产品的叙事传播」

户晨风的安卓苹果人理论同理，户晨风赚不到 iPhone 的分佣

text:
$STRK 今天这根 +50%，我去翻了官方消息，核心不是新空投，也不是突然有收入，而是市场重新给 Starknet 的“抗量子 + 可能转 L1”叙事定价。@Starknet

三个关键点：

1、Starknet 官方说，正在认真考虑从 L2 转成 L1，目标是 2027 年成为完全抗量子网络。

2、技术侧最近进展很密：手机已经能用 NIST 标准 ML-DSA 签名测试网交易；Stwo 证明器内存两周内从 13.9GB 降到 2.1GB，实验里手机 51 秒可以证明一笔真实主网交易。

3、生态也在补应用场景：STRK 可以作为 meme 发射的配对资产，BTCFi 借款也能赚 STRK 奖励。

我手里的 STRK 是空投撸到的，拿到后一直没卖。

中间它从明星 ZK L2 跌成万人嫌，我也没动。不是因为多会算命，只是空投仓，天然适合等一个被市场重新看见的时刻。

但今天还是要泼冷水：

“actively considering” 是正在考虑，不是已经完成；2027 是目标，不是承诺。真转 L1，安全模型、迁移、生态兼容，每一个都是硬问题。

涨 50% 后再冲进去的人，和空投拿到一直没卖的人，承担的是两种完全不同的风险。

空投玩家最怕的不是没卖在高点，而是把“零成本现货”最后拿成“感情仓位”。

我继续观察，但不会因为一根阳线改三观，更不会拿成本低的筹码去追杠杆。
$STRK #Starknet #ZK #抗量子
DYOR，不构成投资建议。

author: KuiGas
quoted_text:
和OKX创始人徐明星 @star_okx 同桌吃饭，聊完之后，我对 OKX 又有了一些新的认识。

昨晚有幸在okxnow私人晚宴上和Star坐在同一桌面对面的交流机会。

从跑步、养生，到产品、RWA、合规以及 OKX 未来的发展，聊到了不少有意思的话题。分享几个让我印象比较深刻的细节，以及一些个人感受。

1、自律：
让我最意外的，是他对运动和养生的专注，

他说自己每天至少跑10几公里，今年已经跑了5000 多公里，什么脂肪肝都没了，

听到这个数字，我是真的震惊了。身边的朋友里Frank、bitwu @Bitwux @qinbafrank 都是如此，都是狠人。正因为都是极致自律，所以优秀。

2、产品：RWA、TradFi是 OKX 接下来非常重要的方向。

创新，合规是关键词，聊到产品，star给我的感觉是，他对业务细节非常熟悉。无论是合规、美股相关业务，还是 RWA 的产品设计与未来规划，很多数据和细节都能随手拈来。

一个创始人能够对具体业务如此熟悉，至少说明他确实花了大量时间研究这些问题。

我记得几年前做web3钱包的时候，海腾@Haiteng_okx 跟我说，老板经常半夜发现不好用地方@员工改。

他也坦言星球这社交很难做，但不会因此放弃，还是会继续优化和完善。而RWA是重点方向，这里分享的内容很多

最新的TSV将是革命性的，可以彻底解决合规问题，

3、有所为，有所不为

这一点让我印象很深，star谈到不少业务时，都非常强调合规底线。
比如u卡，在新加坡可以开展的业务，在中国内地却很难直接复制。不是没有技术能力，也不是没有市场需求，而是有些合规红线坚决不能碰。

有所为，是持续创新，敢于投入新方向，有所不为，是面对短期利益，知道哪些钱不能赚、哪些底线不能碰。

我以前在传统金融行业工作过，对这一点很有感触。主动放弃与有边界是一种智慧。

4、守财-理财：okx的系统是银行级安全，普通人资金存在交易所是最安全的方式。

除了交易业务，OKX的通过各类理财、Earn、链上收益以及生态活动，Star意思是他很关注平台究竟为用户创造了多少收益。

刚好最近发生了 Ledger 钱包相关的安全事件，席间 Star 也分享了一个观点：对于普通用户而言，把资产放在安全体系成熟的大型交易所，可能比自己管理私钥更加省心，也能减少因个人操作失误造成的风险。顺带还能赚交易所提供的各类赚钱机会。

6、OKX 在新加坡拥有公开运营的办公室，这种开放姿态让我印象不错。刚好跟@33daoweb3 的几个老师见面聊天

昨天现场听到 @zakk_okx 分享 X Layer 的发展和未来计划，表达非常直接，很多问题也没有刻意回避。会考虑rh生态火热的创新模式，比如meme配对美股等，
还有 @mia_okx以及 AI 策略相关负责人的分享，也让我对 OKX 的不同业务有了更具体的认识。

我一直觉得，行业活动真正有价值的地方，不是听多少漂亮的 PPT，而是能不能接触真正负责产品和业务的人，听他们讲真实的问题....

作为一个长期使用中心化交易所、也深度参与 DeFi 和链上生态的用户，我其实很少单纯因为某个平台的品牌而改变判断。我更关注产品到底好不好用，资产是否安全，能不能有机会参与一些产品活动能赚到钱。
Crypto 行业变化太快，机会很多，诱惑也很多，真正考验一家公司的，不只是它敢做什么，更是它知道什么不该做。

这次和 OKX 团队交流下来，我最大的感受是：
一个人的成熟，是懂得自律与取舍，一家公司的成熟，是懂得有所为，有所不为。

text:
卧槽！AI挖出了 XRP 潜伏10年的致命漏洞，一笔交易竟然能凭空印出18.45万亿枚 XRP，940亿美元市值差点遭遇毁灭性打击！😲😲😲

XRP 从2012年诞生，设计上总供应量只有1000亿枚，而且只能随着交易手续费销毁而减少。

结果 Veria Labs 的 AI 安全代理发现，只需要利用 XRP Ledger 内置 DEX 的支付引擎漏洞，就有可能在一笔交易中凭空创造18.45万亿枚 XRP，相当于原始总供应量的184倍！

漏洞潜伏了近10年，期间经历大量安全审计，竟然始终没人发现。

your seed phrase was sent to the attacker before you even finished writing it down

hundreds of wallets across ethereum tron and bitcoin. all drained

the guy who lost $5.3 million said “i did everything right. no leverage. no memecoins. i stored my funds on a hardware wallet like we’re all told to”

he was right. he did everything right

except his device had a parasite inside it that he couldn’t see

ledger has now told CryptoBilis to stop all sales. told recent buyers NOT to set up their devices

mark karpelès posted photos of the implant. normal board on top. spy chip below

the most dangerous attack in crypto this year wasn’t a line of code
