text:
wouldn't it be funny if the most damaging critique of pearl-2:native came from a new project co-founded by one of pearl's own co-founders?

no need to invent a falling-out. the whitepapers are entertaining enough. https://t.co/fXTAIp7Ft8

idan sugarman, co-founder of pearl research labs, is also a co-founder of vearl. it's a separate rust/cuda chain whose feature list reads like someone tried to package pearl's matrix-multiplication mining, quantus:native's post-quantum angle and a base:0x9b5e262cf9bb04869ab40b19af91d2dc85761722 adjacent verifiable-compute thesis into one project. 

the funny part is what happens when you read the two whitepapers together.

pearl's own INT paper says the relationship between computation and PRL runs one way: useful compute can earn coins, but holding PRL doesn't entitle you to compute. a marketplace that connects the two is described as future work, not something guaranteed by the mining protocol. the network can issue coins for computation without creating a market for its output.

vearl tries to close that gap with customer-paid jobs. then its whitepaper states the underlying limitation plainly: a protocol cannot prove that a computation was useful to a third party. it can establish that a customer paid for a specific job and burned part of the fee. when there are no customers, miners still earn the base reward for protocol-generated matrices, which the paper explicitly does not claim are useful.

payment is a reasonable proxy for demand, but it isn't cryptographic proof of usefulness. and when the customer disappears, the chain still has to manufacture rewards somehow. the original problem has not gone away.

vearl even cites a june arXiv preprint examining pearl's cuPOW protocol. the study analysed 8,012 workers, found no identifiable inference code in the dominant mining software it examined, and reported 44 pool-accepted shares generated using random matrices. this is a preprint, not a peer-reviewed verdict, but the criticism is now cited in the whitepaper of a separate project co-founded by pearl's own co-founder.

vearl has plenty left to prove on its own merits. its whitepaper reports 87 int8 TOPS for its mining kernel against roughly 199 for cuBLAS on the tested nvidia A10. eight parallel TinyStories-33M runs produced 320 words in 730 seconds, around 18 seconds per generation step. each word requires two jobs, text is capped at 64 tokens, and there is no KV cache.

the consensus design deserves scrutiny too. vearl documents a low-rank attack that once reduced the cost of a mining attempt to 6% of honest computation under its original parameters. it says those parameters have since been changed, but other structured-matrix shortcuts remain unanalysed. the folding mechanism, which turns matrix multiplication into mining tickets, has no formal security analysis.

the economics are hardly settled either. the paper specifies uncapped supply with permanent tail issuance, says its parameters have not been calibrated against actual market demand, and models a small security budget at launch. as of its september 30 whitepaper, vearl was still on a closed testnet with no external audit, no finality and no confidentiality. its post-quantum signatures also don't make its peer-to-peer communication channel post-quantum.

the optional quantus miner adds another oddity. the default dual-mining split allocates 80% of GPU time to quantus and 20% to vearl. 10% of the quantus mining time is directed to a vearl development address, equivalent to 8% of GPU time during that default schedule. it isn't a protocol fee, and paid jobs interrupt the split, but the developer share is hardcoded in the official build.

meanwhile, @nockchain's lockstep research targets bit-exact transformer inference across Hopper, Ada and Blackwell GPUs, with a portable CPU reference reproducing the same results. that research doesn't prove commercial demand either, but it gives independent verification a precise, testable target.

the irony is that vearl's own paper explains why the useful-work pitch is harder than it sounds. pearl leaves the link between mining and actual compute demand to a future marketplace. vearl introduces customer payments, then concedes that payment is only a proxy for usefulness.

two projects, more machinery, and the same unanswered question: who consistently pays for the work?

that's the part no amount of matrix multiplication can solve.

quoted_text:
Podcasts frustrate me because they are fluffy and high-level.

This is the most in-depth discussion on the framework that @tryramp have used to hire, monitor, and scale their sales team.

- Why you should overpay reps

- Why you should cancel forecasting calls

- Why bankers make the best reps

- Why comp plans are BS and you should not have one to start

@max11free, SVP of Sales is truly epic here and my notes from the discussion below.

-- 

1. Why You Should Overpay Your Sales Reps

The early bet was to pay SDRs well above market rate and expect output well above market in return. Reps earn 2X a standard SDR but book 40, 50 or 60 meetings, four to six times the usual target, so the unit economics still work.

2. You Have to Treat Hiring a Sales Team Like Moneyball: How to Find Hidden Talent

Go-to-market recruiting should follow Billy Beane, targeting top sellers at companies that grew revenue past nine figures despite a low NPS score. Those reps had to create their own demand, work complex cycles with weak third-party reviews and sell at a premium to cheaper rivals. The number one or two seller there can thrive in a system like Ramp.

Single biggest advice on finding hidden gem talent @rabois?

3. Why Bankers Make Great Sales Reps

Bankers are programmed to work, and a nine-to-five is foreign to them. Before the company had brand recognition, a cold call to a CFO from someone who had just left Goldman TMT IB carried weight. Early sales teams lack time to teach cold call and email basics, so bankers kept the team in pure execution mode.

Find this also @PeetsChad

4. Why I Advise Not to Have a Comp Plan

Founders are advised to pay 100% OTE for at least the first two quarters instead of setting a comp plan. A quota set too low can be blown out in six months, leaving the company owing a seller multiple six figures. A target picked arbitrarily can also prove unattainable and stall momentum.

Haha, interested to hear your thoughts on this one @Carles_Reina 

5. Never Hire Sales Reps One at a Time

Hiring one seller or SDR at a time leaves no way to benchmark performance, and comparing them against the founder is not reasonable. Onboarding is laborious and expensive, so hiring in pairs is better, bringing competition and collaboration and keeping reps from being lonely.

6. Why the Most Annoying Sales Reps Tend to Be the Most Successful

Sellers who constantly ask about account strategy, pipeline and product during onboarding show a direct correlation with being incredible. Quiet reps, or those asking questions an AI or Notion bot could answer, usually give a weak signal, though the inverse is not always true.

7. What Should Sales Talent Focus on When Deciding Which Company to Join?

Sellers joining an early-stage company should not index on equity, cash and comp, but on the market, the talent density of the business and the founders. Taking a VP title and lots of equity at a mediocre business growing 20 to 30% a year is the wrong trade.

Biggest advice to talent on choosing which company to join @breeves08

Caitlin Clark’s logo three might be the most exciting play in modern basketball.

Think about it.

The moment she crosses half court, the entire arena becomes alert. Defenders panic. Fans rise from their seats. Everyone knows what’s possible.

And when she pulls up from 30 feet, there’s that split second when the ball is in the air and the entire building holds its breath.

Then it drops.

Absolute electricity.

Basketball has given us spectacular dunks, impossible passes, and breathtaking individual plays. But very few things create that kind of anticipation before they even happen.

Steph Curry revolutionized the three-pointer and made the impossible look routine.

Caitlin Clark has taken that same audacity and turned it into one of the greatest spectacles in sports.

The beauty of the logo three isn’t just the distance. It’s the audacity, the confidence, and the collective anticipation.

Some players make fans cheer when they score.

Caitlin Clark makes an entire arena hold its breath the moment she touches the ball.

That’s a special kind of basketball magic.

text:
做一场好的 KOL / UGC program 本质上是要设计一个好的分红体系 。

这个小哥22岁，lead了@WisprFlow 20万刀的短视频投放，合作的 KOL 一个月能产出500-700条短视频，毫无保留的分享了自己的心法，被多名founder转发。

视频精华如下：

- 用 Tribe 做效果分成： 创作者不再单纯按视频数量拿钱，而是根据实际投放效果获得佣金。SaaS 产品按广告消耗金额抽成，电商产品按 GMV（成交总额）抽成。只有素材真正上线并跑出效果，创作者才能获得分成。

- 前期用保底费用吸引人才： 比如支付 1,000 美元，让创作者产出 25 条视频。等合作稳定、跑出爆款素材后，再逐步转向纯佣金模式。

- 精准招募，不搞人海战术： 不需要一次招募上百名创作者。初期只找 4～5 个合作意愿强、能力互补的人，通过 Instagram 关键词定向挖掘，重点补齐现有广告素材的短板。

- 把创作者当团队培养，而不是外包： 定期开会、提供创作指导、设置奖金激励，甚至提供拍摄设备、组织线下团建。核心是建立团队文化，让优秀创作者愿意长期合作。

- 循序渐进地扩大规模： 从 5 人起步，逐步扩展到 10 人、20 人，最终达到 40～60 人。通过老成员推荐招募优质新人，每成功推荐一人奖励 100 美元，优先保证人才质量。

- 持续测试新内容形式，避免 Meta 广告素材同质化： 不断要求创作者尝试新的脚本、拍摄方式、叙事角度和视频结构，避免素材过于相似，被 Meta 的广告算法归为同一类，导致素材之间互相竞争、投放效果下降。

核心思路： 不要把 UGC 创作者当成按条付费的视频供应商，而是建立一支以广告效果为导向、能够持续产出爆款素材的创作者团队。前期用保底费用冷启动，中期通过效果分成绑定利益，后期依靠团队文化、人才推荐和持续创新实现规模化。

text:
I've been thinking more about the this reply and I think I figured it out. 

> how did you trust it before when humans wrote it?

you mostly didn't, not really. you trusted the tests, the fact that it was already in production somewhere similar, the author's track record, and the reality that most of the time the bug would show up in monitoring before it became a real problem. the diff was honestly a ritual more than a guarantee. we pretended like line-level review was a safety net because we didn't have better options and the volume was low enough that it felt manageable. 

but agents just make the old ritual obvious. once you're landing thousands of changes a month the idea that someone is carefully reading every diff starts being theater. 

trusting agent output is the same problem as trusting human output, just with higher throughput. I think the answer is still to stop treating the change as the thing you trust and start treating the environment as the thing you trust. if an agent can run the code, drive the ui, check the invariants, and get blocked by the same constraints a human would, the fact that it wrote the patch matters less. 

every time you find yourself wanting to open the diff "just to make sure," that's signal that something in the system is still relying on human eyeballs instead of a hard constraint.

the code review as we know it is already on the way out. most of what we call review today will turn into risk scoring and continuous verification. low and medium risk work will land after agents and checks have already exercised it. 

humans will still be involved, but not by reading patches. they'll just be deciding what outcomes matter, whats not allowed to break, and which constraints are worth making permanent. 

the job now is to continuously make the system good enough that you don't need the diff to feel safe.

text:
A raffle could take a user's payment, assign the tickets—and then make the round impossible to finish.

Zealynx found the Critical state-ordering failure in Nexalo's purchase flow.

`buyTickets()` collected payment and assigned tickets before trying to distribute NXL rewards. If those rewards were exhausted, the caught failure deactivated the product mid-purchase.

That left the round unable to sell enough tickets to trigger winner selection, with the collected stablecoins trapped and no refund or admin recovery path.

Nexalo fixed the finding, and Zealynx verified it.
author: ZealynxSecurity

text:
The dangerous part was the catch: reward distribution failed, but the earlier payment and ticket state remained while the product switched off.

The safe order is to validate reward capacity before accepting payment or assigning tickets—not after those effects have already happened.

Public finding and remediation:
https://t.co/Y78uTzuqxZ

今天偶遇 @MojoAI_HQ @MojoAI_CN  的一个新用户充值没到账的情况，用户本来要走 BSC，提币的时候选成了 opBNB，然后咨询到我，目前已经确认资金取回。

Mojo 使用 Privy 非托管钱包，借这个案例，分享一下其他类似采用 Privy 钱包方案的APP转错链后的处理思路👇

1️⃣ 先确认钱去了哪里

确认转出的链，用交易哈希在对应链的浏览器查询，核对状态、收款地址和代币。App 不显示余额，不一定代表链上没收到。

2️⃣ 找到钱包的导出入口

如果 App 本身开放了私钥导出功能，直接操作即可。

重点：App 没入口的，可以访问官方 Privy Home，用注册APP时的同名账号邮箱登录，找到我的APP关联钱包，核对收款地址，再看是否支持导出。

这里有个区别：App 没有导出按钮，不等于 Privy Home 也无法导出；但是否可用，仍取决于应用配置和钱包类型。

3️⃣ 在正确的链上管理资产

钱包导出私钥后，可导入支持对应链的钱包端。确认地址一致，再切换查看资产；代币未显示时，按链上记录核对并添加代币合约。

后续即可自行进行转出或者跨链操作。

⚠️ 再次提醒：私钥、助记词只由本人操作，不要发给任何“帮忙找回”的人，也不要发给 AI。

以后充值，地址、币种、网络三项一定要仔细核对，首次可先小额测试。

text:
《2049跑会总结 - 景气篇》

已经离开新加坡回到家了，高强度的几天见人沟通+连轴转连坐下来好好码字的时间都很少，只能不断挤压睡眠时间，导致昨天上飞机前Oura和Whoop都已经在提醒我出现了生病前的主要体征。

赶紧磕了两颗澳洲神药Panadol好好睡了一觉，终于活过来了，然后坐下来总结一下这趟新加坡之行的感触。

后续通过几个帖子来从不同的角度各方面记录一下感触。

这次先说会议景气度

在去2049前，一些KOL朋友跟我说可能本届2049不会有什么人和收获，毕竟虽然行情有点反弹但还没真的走出熊市，山寨和VC都完犊子了，行业看不到什么未来，所以还不如去跑韩国的会因为可以顺便玩玩+做个医美。

但我一直觉得token2049才是亚太区观察crypto景气程度最好的窗口，无论从签证便利性，2049多年积累的品牌影响力，新加坡对crypto的包容性以及常驻加密从业人员密度各方面看综合起来就是最佳的。

事实上也证明我的预判是对的。

几天下来，这次token2049虽然无法与两年前大牛市时烈火烹油时相比，但热闹程度肯定是超过了预期，最后连刚开始说不来的KOL都发现不对劲临时买票飞过来加入大部队😂😂😂

我眼中的大会景气程度大致可以从两方面看：
1、主会场和分会场的烧钱程度
2、私局的密度，质量

~~~~~~~~~~~~
先说主会场和分会场：

这次2049与之前相比主会场的变化是让我有点惊讶的，因为非但没有缩水，相反甚至规模更大了。

之前主会场只有2层，由各家分包，而这次光是 @SuiNetwork 一家就把原本是水泥毛胚的B2层全包了，自己装修布置，据说总开销超过500万美金。另一头Blockwork搞首届DAS Asia（面向机构的数字资产峰会）包了一楼的一半，每天花钱不会少于1M。

从会场参会人流情况看还是很多，甚至查票程度是以往以来最严，金沙Mall里背着各色品牌包包的人络绎不绝。

分会场（Side Events）的数量比过去两年的确是少了很多，很大程度是因为熊市洗礼和山寨叙事崩盘后大量VC撤出，攒局的金主爸爸少了，那么拿到VC钱可以烧市场的项目也随之减少，他们是分会场的主要host群体。

去年前年还有项目方为了人气挖空心思搞泳池Party等奢靡刺激的活动，今年大多就是吃个饭喝个小酒联络感情，顶多DJ打碟蹦一下，人不少，但预算肯定是减少了的😂😂

除了几个CEX 的side event保持了一致的高水准，有些热门项目人气还是很旺,比如 @HyperliquidX 的， @Polymarket 的， @NEARProtocol 的等，华人代表这边资深OG @mablejiang 的新项目@trasiaxyz 在跳海bar的活动也人满为患，JE和 @SmartXTerminal 活动，TrustWallet的活动，倪大的龙虾局等都很热闹。

简单总结一下就是在烧钱方面行业开始比较割裂，有的公链已经在倒闭在行尸走肉，有的却在趁机更猛烈砸钱宣传，试图扩大自己的影响力并巩固市场信心。

之前提到在主会场猛砸钱的Sui和Blockwork都是美国的，VC大撤退里受影响最大的也是亚洲VC（几乎全军覆没），老外VC还是有钱，并继续相信crypto的叙事还在投资一级市场，只是更保守。

~~~~~~~~~~~
再说私局的情况

本来我是有点担心这次过来没多少私局能玩的，但结果陆陆续续都约起来了，结果大部分的时间是在参与各种私局。有与项目方的，与交易所的，与VC的，KOL小伙伴们的以及与行业其它上下游朋友的。

感触是项目方的私局少了，KOL轮少了，但还在做组私局的质量都不差，依然有不少收获，此外能明显感觉到CEX们在对自己基本盘上更加上心。

一个细节：
这次大会 @star_okx 老徐 @justinsuntron 孙哥和 @Han_Gate 韩博士 都搞了VIP饭局，放下身段与KOL及VIP用户们深度交流。 

币安那边虽然CZ和一姐没出现，但产品一把手Jeff代表也搞了饭局（币安大概率会把市场重心放在下个月泰国的BBW，那才是他们主场）。

同时海外所也开始加入对华语市场的关注力度，Coinbase开始给部分华语KOL送F1票搭建关系，Kraken招募了中文团队开始了解华语用户习惯和偏好改进产品。

在新人入场流速降低，AI股票吸血，资金存量博弈，外边DEX和链上Meme冲击加速的背景下，各家大所CEX们都在思考和努力巩固自己的基本盘。海外合规大所也开始希望能获得更多中文用户作为增量。

另一个细节看景气：

往年黄黑所和OKX请KOL们看F1是惯例，这次 @Gate @COINBASE 和 @BIT 也加入了战局。我不了解具体情况但据小伙伴说Gate投入是最大方的。

F1的门票真的不便宜，根据位置和比赛日5000美金一张是基本的，决赛日只会更贵。

今晚决赛我朋友圈里被F1现场观战视频刷屏了，基本都是拿的福利票，如果行业不景气了，真的会有这么大范围的福利空投？😆😆

再一个：
过去几天巨亨和帝国等越南场商K都是爆满的，不是提前约或者跟妈咪关系硬的加钱都订不到场子，上个厕所能碰到一堆熟面孔。

高消费的背后一定是有足够的利益在驱动，你看看曾经是顶级商K主力的山西煤老板和房地产开发商们现在还在继续霍霍不？

虽然可能有点片面，但会议期间巨亨等商K生意的好坏的确是有效风向标的一部分。

~~~~~~~~~~~~

言而总之，这次跑会观察下来，虽然币圈正在经历一个明显的阵痛期，在从上个周期大放水后诞生的VC批量流水线制造山寨的模式中脱离出来，但已经逐步摆脱了最低谷最低迷仿徨的阶段。

聪明顶部的从业者们已经重新获得了信心并开始继续享受高压行业里短暂的“刺激时刻”。

商业沟通+技术展示+利益勾兑+ 酒精狂欢 + F1的轰鸣，这才是新加坡Token2049最吸引人的地方。

行业还在，景气还在。

可惜这次新加坡雾霾太严重而且实在太热有点美中不足，不过也已经很满意了。

明天继续更新关于行业方面的一些看法收获。

text:
The Ledger hardware wallet supply chain attack is nuts. Take over an authorized retailer and implant a chip+GSM modem in Ledgers to steal crypto keys. The implant likely exploits seed phrase entry/display. I wonder if some hardware wallets drop it “for security.”

On setup, Ledgers generate a key inside secure hardware. It’s displayed as a list of 24 words (BIP39) you’re asked to write down. You can also use your own key, which you enter the same way.

A hardware implant simply has to record these, which is substantially easier than breaking the secure hardware.

You could imagine a “more secure” hardware wallet where keys never leave unencrypted. Instead, you can copy keys to new trusted hardware that attests it’s genuine. Ledger even sort of has this with these PIN-secured cards that come with some Ledgers. And they offer cloud backups that, rightly, drew some criticism from the community for their rollout.

Of course, this isn’t a very good plan. An attacker who can 1) buy a company and 2) build a tiny implant complete with GSM modem and implant it into existing hardware can 3) possibly break the secure chip, or 4) just include malware in the device, root the computer using it, and then intercept existing transactions and change the pay-to address (though this might not be worth the cost of the op, since you’d get caught quickly).

As the investigation continues, we are working with relevant authorities. The volume of impacted devices is limited. We know this is concerning, especially for those directly affected, and we are reaching out to impacted users.

To date, all confirmed cases related to the disclosed draining incident of Oct 9th, 2026, involve devices sold through the Southeast Asia reseller CryptoBilis. Our systems and direct sales channels remain unaffected. 
We take the CryptoBilis situation seriously and are actively investigating.

We encourage impacted users to reach out to Ledger Support through official channels and file complaints with their local law enforcement authorities. As a reminder, CryptoBilis has confirmed having ceased all sales of hardware wallets.

We are reminding our authorized resellers and distributors to source products only through authorized channels and never to restock returned products.

Security isn’t static and this incident underscores why we continuously review and strengthen our distribution and anti-tamper processes. 

We are continuously improving that work now and events like this strengthen our resolution: reviewing authorized reseller controls, advancing hardware protections, and cooperating with authorities. Thanks to @SEAL_911 for their collaborative support and all their efforts.

This is an ongoing threat that doesn’t just impact Ledger, but the whole ecosystem, and we are calling others in the space to work with us on making improvements for users.

We believe in jointly working with researchers, other vendors and partners on improving industry chain-of-custody practices and anti-tamper techniques. Raising the bar on physical supply-chain integrity benefits the entire ecosystem. If you have relevant information, contact security@ledger.com.

Scammers often try to take advantage of incidents like this. Rely only on official Ledger channels. Ledger will never call you, DM you, or ask for your 24-word recovery phrase.

author: Alex_Danco
quoted_text:
Brothers Karamazov was Einstein’s favorite novel, a verdict he shared with Freud, Hillary Clinton, and Murakami. Dostoyevsky was Pope Francis’s favorite author. Indeed, he approvingly quoted Elder Zosima; perhaps an interesting case of art molding life. At the risk of betraying my relative shallowness and inferiority, I confess that I did not love it.

Written in the shadow of the death of Dostoyevsky’s son (also Alyosha), and, more broadly, after a life of repeated tragedy, Karamazov attempts most of all to address the problem of evil in Christianity. Ivan presents a trenchant argument, asking how the suffering of children may possibly be explained given the existence of a supposedly benevolent God (Dostoyevsky collected real court cases for Ivan), culminating in Ivan’s famous return of the ticket.

The book gives some sense for how dislocating the nineteenth century must have been. The ascendant authority of science, the spread of materialist philosophy, the doctrine of evolution, the aftermath of the French revolution and its supposedly enlightened empiricism: in Karamazov, we get the feeling that finding some kind of consilience wasn’t just an abstract philosophical challenge, but a source of intense spiritual torment. If inherited tradition is no longer an adequate basis for faith, why would we rationally cleave to an apparently irrational theology? All of this was in the air: it was only two years later that Nietzsche declared God to be dead.

Perhaps demonstrating the utility of the novel as a medium, Dostoyevsky does not even attempt to solve the problem, but merely to illustrate a response, showing how individuals (Alyosha, Elder Zosima) may in the face of the inherent injustice present in the world nonetheless pursue lives of benevolence and charity: theodicy-by-example. In so doing, Dostoyevsky tacitly concedes that none of the teetering justifications expounded over the centuries can actually survive critical pressure and be defended through pure logic.

Ultimately, though, I don’t find myself being fully compelled by Dostoyevsky’s characterization of the problem or his proposed solution. As another sprawling confrontation with and attempt to reconcile the problem of evil, Grossman’s Life and Fate is maybe a useful counterpoint. Unlike Karamazov, Life and Fate shows actual people confronting great wickedness. Ikonnikov, a small but important figure, is ordered to help in the construction of a gas chamber. He refuses, with full awareness of the consequences that will ensue. The Karamazovs, by contrast, live middle class lives unvisited by greater events. Ivan has money, education, and leisure; his torment is the invention of his own mind and thus a kind of self-indulgence. Even Alyosha, the novel’s most sympathetic character, is never tested. His crisis is spiritual: there is a slightly comic kerfuffle about Zosima’s noisome corpse, which challenges his faith, but no circumstance requires him to stake his life or even his comfort.

Thus, a fundamental issue with Karamazov is that the problems of the book are on some level fake: they’re the self-inflicted derangements of febrile and dysregulated men. How much can or should we learn from the insane?

To be charitable to Dostoyevsky, we might say that he understood the spiritual dislocation of the era that later gives rise to the larger evils of totalitarianism in the twentieth, even prefiguring them in the Grand Inquisitor. (Dostoyevsky explored this theme in greater detail a few years earlier in Demons.) Camus in 1959: “The real nineteenth century prophet was Dostoevsky, not Karl Marx.” In this interpretation, the problems in Karamazov set the stage for those in Life and Fate.

Maybe. At least as a work of art, I’m not sure that this anticipation is enough to make the book stand on its own. In Karamazov, one continually wonders why the brothers don’t just pull it together. Dostoyevsky seems to transpose his own inner depths and spiritual torment onto his characters, but most people are not tortured writers, and it does not feel that the unhingedness of the characters is ever fully earned.

In attempting to address evil, Grossman’s conclusion is ostensibly similar to Dostoyevsky’s: the only resolution lies in senseless kindness. For Dostoyevsky, this message is embodied in Alyosha, who represents a kind of fervent innocence. For me, however, it’s not clear that Alyosha ever fathoms the realities and extremities of evil, and hence he’s not fully persuasive: does he even reckon with the misdeeds of his brothers?

Grossman is willing to engage head on. Far beyond gruesome newspaper anecdotes or neurotic and volatile siblings, Ikonnikov directly experiences the Holodomor in Ukraine and then the murders of the Jews. He has no patience for the kind of revolutionary ideas that animated Ivan’s contemporaries: “whenever we see [the dawn of an eternal good], the blood of old people and children is always shed.”

Alyosha believes in the Church and is willing to set aside its failures to address suffering. The book closes on his declaration that all shall rise again. That is, Alyosha does not accept the tragedy of Ilyusha, an innocent boy’s death, but rather seeks to deny and escape it. “We shall see each other and shall tell each other with joy and gladness all that has happened.”

Life and Fate flatly rejects providential resolution. The heavens may be empty, and there is no greater meaning in evil. We can simply choose (freedom the other great theme of Life and Fate) to pursue acts of charity, generosity, and comfort:

“Yes, as well as this terrible Good with a capital ‘G’, there is everyday human kindness. The kindness of an old woman carrying a piece of bread to a prisoner, the kindness of a soldier allowing a wounded enemy to drink from his water-flask, the kindness of youth towards age, the kindness of a peasant hiding an old Jew in his loft. The kindness of a prison guard who risks his own liberty to pass on letters written by a prisoner not to his ideological comrades, but to his wife and mother.”

These acts don’t ennoble the suffering but are instead justified on their own terms. Such altruism cannot become a catechism, as clearly lies in Alyosha’s destiny (and Karamazov was planned before Dostoyevsky's death as the first of two works); instead, our kindness must be senseless. And we should presume no salvation in adherence: Alyosha imagines a kind of sacred tutelage, but Ikonnikov is unceremoniously shot.

Karamazov doesn’t show true evil, and Dostoyevsky’s solution, such as it is, involves a kind of denial, or at least evasion through metaphysics. Grossman saw it directly, and instead argues, humanistically, that we should be kind just because.

—

If Dostoyevsky came to his works by trying to understand and depict Russian society, they in turn became tapestries for others to understand national souls.

In the aftermath of WWI, Russia was the great power defined in opposition to the West. As Germany tried to rediscover its own soul in the wreckage of defeat, it looked east to Russia, and frequently to Dostoyevsky himself.

Carl Jung thought that the German people had a kind of Karamazovian quality. In particular, he believed that Christianity had disciplined them without fully transforming the impulses beneath their ostensibly civilized conduct: the “Germanic barbarian” was divided into upper and lower halves. Religion had domesticated the former while leaving the latter untamed. Waning faith consequently threatened to release forces that its authority had long restrained: “As the Christian view of the world loses its authority, the more menacingly will the ‘blond beast’ be heard prowling about in its underground prison, ready at any moment to burst out with devastating consequences. When this happens in the individual it brings about a psychological revolution, but it can also take a social form.”

Dostoyevsky was reputedly invoked on a weekly basis at Max Weber’s Sunday gatherings. At the beginning of Reflections of a Nonpolitical Man, Thomas Mann’s later-repudiated 1918 nationalist polemic, he quotes approvingly Dostoyevsky’s characterization of Germany as the “protesting Western empire”, never quite adopting or feeling at home with the inheritance of Rome. In the same year, Spengler wrote Decline of the West, and explicitly perceived in Russia a youthful vigor, primitiveness, and irrationality that contrasted with the senile high culture of the German and Western worlds. In Magic Mountain, Mann later used Clavdia Chauchat to personify the seductive dangers of Eastern (i.e. Russian) illogic.

Hermann Hesse declared that, for all their differences, Fyodor, Dmitri, Ivan, and Alyosha are actually all of one type; the Russian man. In them, he perceived that “the ideal of the Karamazov, primeval, Asiatic, and occult, is already beginning to consume the European soul”, which was leading to the downfall of Europe. In Hesse’s conception, the Russian man rejects inherited ethics and morals, and even beneficent Alyosha represents an “amoral impartiality.” Man is, Hesse says, halfway between animals and higher consciousness; the former restrained through the process of civilization and domestication. The Karamazovs represent the fraying of the ties.

Hesse proceeds, ominously, to notice that the Germans in particular are more vulnerable than any European people to the temptations of “all those evils which one may regard in different ways, but which collectively signify the Karamazov.” While he was prescient in anticipating some of what would follow, he was in the end too sanguine in his hope that the spiritual dislocation could remain limited to that. “It is possible that the whole Downfall of Europe will play itself out only inwardly, only in the souls of a generation, only in changing the meaning of worn-out symbols, in the dis-valuation of spiritual values.” Alas!

In general, it is interesting to trace the mutual obsession between Russia and Germany: how preoccupied each was with the respective supposedly corrupting influences; how urgent the question of the national soul was felt to be. Many of the analyses seem a bit contradictory—Hesse actually inverts Dostoyevsky, for whom “everything is permitted” nihilism is a Western import for which Russian Orthodoxy is the cure—but there’s a striking intensity in the attempts to apprehend.

Most of all, I’m struck by how anachronistic it all feels today: a country’s writers investigating the national soul and the nation’s fate through the lens of foreign literature.

Which novels or works of art do we use to understand our contemporary issues? Should we be using such works? Do they inform or do they mislead? Today, the US worries a lot about China, but this mostly manifests at the level of trade balances, AI policy, and military prowess. We don’t seem to worry much about the spiritual force of Chinese ideals, and for all of the policy fractiousness, China continues to import and absorb American culture with enthusiasm that is mostly undimmed. There is a genre of jeremiad and cultural analysis in the US that rhymes a little with early twentieth century German criticism, but it today tends to be much more clinical, hinging around PISA scores, smartphones, lower fertility, and not around higher aspirations and ideals as such. So, to what extent should there be analyses of the national soul? And to what extent should they connect with major novels and works of art?

text:
Airbnb's Brian Chesky on the classic management philosophy, and why he rejects it:

"Go through the list of great CEOs, almost none of them that I'm aware of do recurring one-on-ones... Jensen Huang does not do recurring one-on-ones, famously."

"I do think a CEO should meet one-on-one with your people. I don't think it should be recurring... If you wanna get time with me, get a meeting with me. If you wanna call me, call me. Bump into me, talk to me. But most of my recurring meetings are group meetings."

"If there's lots of one-way kinda sensitive topics, there's probably something wrong in the company... If we're having all these sensitive conversations, well, why are they so sensitive? Why can't other people hear about them?"

"If I have a one-on-one with you and you tell me there's a problem and we debate it and we say, 'Here's the solution,' we haven't consulted anyone else. So now we just made a decision and no one else helped, consulted, or knew how we made that decision."

"'Hire great people, trust them, let them do their job, stay out of the details, do recurring one-on-ones.' I don't believe any of that, and I wanna acknowledge that many great leaders do."

author: mbarrbosa
quoted_text:
The @astroteller "Pedestal" analogy 🙊

In tech, there’s a famous trap called "Building the Pedestal."

If your goal is to train a monkey to sing on a pedestal, anyone can build the wooden pedestal in an afternoon. It looks like "progress." It gives you something to demo.

But the only hard problem is teaching the monkey to sing.

Most AI projects build pedestals: slick frontends, black-box wrappers, and vanity metrics over cherry-picked backtests.

We have deliberately spent months in the mud doing the only part that matters: training the core Surprise Intelligence model, subjecting it to sealed out-of-sample audits, fixing calibration failures, and refusing to publish until the model proves it actually detects fragile consensus.

We won't ship a polished pedestal until the science is real. If that looks slow from the outside, that’s because real ML research doesn't run on marketing timelines.

text:
My Downfall Prediction of Papertrade

I'm no stranger to writing scathing reviews of various protocols. But my audience has likely noticed that I've really calmed down on that front over the past several months. 

The reason is simple: since becoming a founder in the crypto space I have a new appreciation for the hard work and expense that goes into trying to build something. As a result, this particular thesis is not one I put out there lightly. Nor does it bring me any joy to write.

My qualifications: I have been in the crypto space for quite a while and a full time perps trader for multiple years. I have made, lost, and re-made more money in perps than the vast majority of perp traders. I'm quite literally in the top 1% of perps traders globally.

 I've tested countless protocols and have even consulted multiple protocols in their design. I've earned the right to form a qualified opinion. Although it still is - at the end of the day - only my opinion and should be taken as such. 

My bias: I have zero financial incentive tied to where you ultimately decide to trade. I trade against market makers (as do the vast majority of traders whether they realize it or not). There are no outside factors influencing my opinions on this topic. 

The Structure

Let's start with the elephant in the room.

Papertrade isn't a conventional perpetuals exchange. 

It's a peer-to-pool model, and your counterparty is quite literally the house.

In fact, Papertrade itself refers to its liquidity pool as the House in an almost shocking twist of transparency.

I have never been fond of peer-to-pool perpetuals models. In fact I have been quite outspoken against that design over the years. 

In a traditional peer-to-peer order-book exchange (like Hyperliquid), buyers and sellers interact through a marketplace. Market makers provide liquidity, opposing positions are matched, and the exchange generally earns revenue from facilitating those transactions.

The exchange doesn't inherently need its customers to lose money to remain solvent.

Peer-to-pool changes that relationship fundamentally.

Instead of matching your position against another trader, the protocol's liquidity pool takes the opposite side.

You win, the pool loses.

You lose, the pool wins.

Now, to be clear, that doesn't automatically make every peer-to-pool protocol bad. Some have operated successfully, and their liquidity providers knowingly accept that counterparty risk. In fact, I believe good protocols should have a pool fallback for times of thin liquidity - I just strongly disagree that it should be the primary or sole counterparty to all trades. 

I hate this model so much because it creates a negative incentive structure:

The financial interests of the trader and the house are directly opposed.

In the case of Papertrade things are considerably worse.

You see, Papertrade didn't even launch with a conventionally funded liquidity pool.

Its model is designed to bootstrap liquidity from the realized losses of its own traders on top of their own protocol owned liquidity. 

Think about that for a moment.

The money available to pay successful traders is accumulated only through the losses of unsuccessful ones. The starting cash was literally provided by the casino itself. You're trading against the casino directly, and they are betting on your losses to compound the size of their pool. 

But what happens when the pool doesn't have enough money to pay a winning trader?

You wait.

Literally.

Papertrade has a mechanism that places unpaid profits into a queue, where they become claims against future liquidity.

Those claims are subsequently paid as other traders lose money.

Imagine closing a profitable position, and being told that your winnings will be available once enough other customers lose their money.

And if trading activity dries up while the pool owes money, what exactly is supposed to replenish it?

The answer is that there is no guaranteed replenishment mechanism.

These are just some of the fundamental problems with the peer-vs-pool model. The house has a direct incentive in who wins and loses, and the house must stay solvent at all costs. 

Peer-vs-pool is a cheap, lazy way to launch a perps dex. But that's not where Papertrade's problems end - in fact that's where they begin. 

The Already Exploited Vulnerability

Let's talk about how Papertrade actually determines the price of your position.

Papertrade doesn't maintain its own traditional order book.

Instead, it references Hyperliquid's best bid and offer, calculates the midpoint, and uses that single external venue's price to execute synthetic positions.

The protocol doesn't actually execute corresponding trades on Hyperliquid (despite half of the timeline believing they do as a result of marketing wordplay).

It simply references Hyperliquid's price, records your position, and calculates what the House owes you - or what you owe the House - based on subsequent price movements.

This is how Papertrade advertises zero slippage and no funding costs.

That might sound great...until you consider this is an exchange allowing extraordinarily large leveraged positions and is relying on the best bid and offer of a single external order book to determine their execution prices.

Not a robust composite index incorporating several independent markets, as is the industry standard. 

Not an independently validated reference price capable of rejecting abnormal quotations.

A midpoint derived from the top of Hyperliquid's order book.

This can go dangerously wrong (and already has). 

Papertrade's own risk disclosures acknowledge that this price source can be manipulated.

The documentation discusses how relatively small changes to Hyperliquid's best bid or offer could influence the midpoint used for Papertrade settlement.

It also acknowledges the absence of an independent reference price capable of identifying and rejecting those abnormal quotes.

None of the very limited safeguards Papertrade has in place establishes that manipulating the reference price is economically unprofitable.

This isn't just a hypothetical concern voiced by many of us on the timeline - it's a risk identified in their own documentation. 

Now combine that with 1,000x leverage. 

At 1,000X leverage, Papertrade's liquidation threshold is approx a .05% adverse price movement. Approximately five hundredths of one percent. 

The platform uses isolated positions that cannot be rescued by adding additional margin after opening. Positions also cannot be partially closed.

Once the liquidation threshold is reached, the position is liquidated and its isolated margin is forfeited.

Consider what that means when your execution price depends on a single external order book.

But wait, there's more...

Papertrade uses what it calls an asymmetric impact mechanism.

In practical terms, profitable trades don't necessarily receive their full calculated profits.

According to its published parameters, a profitable BTC trade capturing a 0.1% price movement retains approximately 74% of its gross profit before the additional 2% winning fee.

Even on a 1% movement, approximately 12% of the gross profit is surrendered before that fee.

Losing trades, meanwhile, incur their actual losses.

So the trader absorbs the full downside, while the protocol systematically reduces the upside.

Because once again, you're playing against the house.

Are all of these concerns simply imaginary? 

No. Within hours of launch reports began circulating on CT pointing out that sophisticated traders were taking advantage of Papertrade's vulnerabilities in order to drain the pool. 

These are not insignificant allegations. 

For perspective, a 0.15% favorable price movement on $300M worth of synthetic positions represents approx $450K in gross PnL before Papertrade's profit adjustments. 

It's incredibly easy and doesn't take a lot of capital to spoof a 0.15% price move on HL's BBO. 

This is the only time I'm going to say "trust me, bro" because I'm not about to educate the world on how easy and relatively inexpensive this form of manipulation actually is. 

The protocol has less than $5M at the time of this post in house liquidity. With staggering amounts of open interest and volume.

This morning I saw someone on CT write: "Regardless of potential exploits or vulnerabilities, bullish on Papertrade since it offers degens a way to make $1M from just $1,000."

Until you realize that if only five people do that the protocol is bankrupt. 

Besides the obvious open door to manipulate price, exploit and drain the protocol of funds that we've discussed there lies another danger to peer-vs-pool: those times where most people win during established trends. 

You see, the entire thing is held together on the premise that most perps traders lose - which is true. But there are multiple periods of times in every cycle where that flips. 

One really bullish day is all it takes to bankrupt Papertrade. Where traders don't even need to catch a move early, they just need to ape in and chase with incredibly high leverage and exit after only the tiniest bit of price action. 

And that "turn $1,000 into $1M"? It doesn't really matter if the protocol is bankrupt and cannot pay. 

The purpose of a perpetuals exchange should be to facilitate efficient markets, not to invent increasingly elaborate ways to turn its customers into the House's liquidity pool.

We've spent years building decentralized trading infrastructure capable of competing with traditional financial exchanges.

We should be moving toward deeper liquidity, more reliable price discovery, transparent risk management, and stronger settlement guarantees.

Not celebrating the reinvention of the bucket shop model where traders play against the house simply because someone put it on-chain and gave the losing customers a token.

Without some serious and rapid changes to the structure, I do expect the downfall of Papertrade. 

This is not the same as me hoping for it. I'm not sitting here cheering for their failure, nor do I really care whether they succeed or not. 

The current risks, however, are simply too great to ignore. 

🫡 From the depths — 
The White Whale 🐋

72 hour update on reseller CryptoBilis incident  🔽

As the investigation continues, we are working with relevant authorities. The volume of impacted devices is limited. We know this is concerning, especially for those directly affected, and we are reaching out to impacted users.

To date, all confirmed cases related to the disclosed draining incident of Oct 9th, 2026, involve devices sold through the Southeast Asia reseller CryptoBilis. Our systems and direct sales channels remain unaffected. We take the CryptoBilis situation seriously and are actively investigating.

We encourage impacted users to reach out to Ledger Support through official channels and file complaints with their local law enforcement authorities. As a reminder, CryptoBilis has confirmed having ceased all sales of hardware wallets.

We are reminding our authorized resellers and distributors to source products only through authorized channels and never to restock returned products.

Also, we strongly advise users not to purchase from unauthorized resellers, where the risk of buying suspicious, counterfeit or modified devices is important as nothing operates under ledger security guidelines.

Security isn’t static and this incident underscores why we continuously review and strengthen our distribution and anti-tamper processes. 

We are continuously improving that work now and events like this strengthen our resolution: reviewing authorized reseller controls, advancing hardware protections, and cooperating with authorities. Thanks to @SEAL_911 for their collaborative support and all their efforts.

This is an ongoing threat that doesn’t just impact Ledger, but the whole ecosystem, and we are calling others in the space to work with us on making improvements for users.

We believe in jointly working with researchers, other vendors and partners on improving industry chain-of-custody practices and anti-tamper techniques. Raising the bar on physical supply-chain integrity benefits the entire ecosystem. If you have relevant information, contact security@ledger.com.

For CryptoBilis buyers: do not initialize unused devices. If already set up, move to a new seed on a device from Ledger. If you have concerns that your device was impacted by the CryptoBilis incident, please contact Ledger Support through the official site: https://t.co/JUcWwJO9iF

Ledger Support is available 24/7 to answer your questions and concerns.

Scammers often try to take advantage of incidents like this. Rely only on official Ledger channels. Ledger will never call you, DM you, or ask for your 24-word recovery phrase.

text:
As a company grows from start-up to large corporation, process is used to help make that happen.  Process helps solidify consistent results which are required for a business to scale, however this solidification makes businesses less adaptive, less agile, and kills innovation.

There's an interesting distinction between regular employee management and bittensor incentive mechanisms.

With regular employee management you set a process/tasks to produce what you want.

With bittensor incentive mechanisms you define WHAT you want to produce.

Incentive mechanisms skip over the need for process by defining/evaluating precisely what needs to be produced/commoditized.

In this way, incentive mechanisms are BETTER than process.  They produce consistent results through global miner competition, while allowing miners to remain able to adapt and innovative.

text:
Boris 这三条总结得太到位了：给目标、给衡量办法、告诉它要多拼。Claude Code 的作者亲口说「多数事情都能这么干」，值得存。

我自己的全局规则基本就是这个结构，补两条实战里踩出来的：

1. 衡量办法要先去噪。我让 AI 拿我 1–9 月的帖子验证一份 X 运营清单，第一遍直接比，「带金额」「问句开头」都显得更差；改成只比每条有没有跑赢当月中位数，一条变成没差别，一条反而更好。指标有噪声，模型会很认真地去优化噪声。

2. 加第四条：哪些不能碰。评论区也有人提到，只给目标、指标和「别停」，模型容易去钻指标的空子。我的做法是把发帖、动钱、改权限、删东西列成硬门槛，碰到就停下来等我点头，其余的一路做到能验证为止。

进度这块我换了个做法：写进文件，只有需要我拍板的事才推给我。

Agree. Claude was able to do this better than I could since Opus 4.8 or so. 5.5 models are now very good at it.

All you do is give the model

1. a goal (eg. “Make p95 ci time <10 mins”)
2. a way to measure its result (eg. “Read timings in bigquery after each change”)
3. a sense of how hard to try (eg. “Don’t stop till it’s done, it might take a few weeks of experimenting”)

This pretty much works for most things. I often also ask the model to show me a chart with progress to goal every day, or to dm me a live artifact with the result

Americans are falling behind on loan payments at a concerning pace.

text:
DeFi Dad is right, but so is StarkNet. 

I spent 4 years building on StarkNet, because it was the best tech for what our team was building. 

But I also spent 4 years hoping (and actively trying) to see BD and marketing at StarkNet function in a way that didn’t scare off builders, users, and investors. 

Largely I think the issues came from a structure that is engineer focused, with community and marketing being second class citizens, under funded, and poorly staffed.

In addition to this, the delineation between StarkNet and StarkWare from an org level was poorly managed. 

Marketing and comms were driven by StarkWare which was a mistake because those at StarkNet weren’t able to be fully in control of their own ship. (Hence why we saw cringe branding and comms that never cohesively took a consistent shape). 

However, with that said, I believe a lot of that is being resolved or already done. 

Today StarkNet is one of the few L2s still growing. Still shipping. Still providing novel open source research. AND most importantly their tech stack may actually be integral to keeping assets safe.

StarkNet’s founder co-founded Zcash, he was an early BTC adopter, huge supporter of Ethereum, and is now fully leaning into post quantum via StarkNet. 

It’s easy to hate, especially in the hellhole that crypto can be, but don’t ignore what they’re building. 

Long live StarkNet.

text:
Friedberg: “We're watching the birth of a new religion.”

“The idea that you can prescribe or describe AI as being conscious is effectively the creation of a new belief system, a system that doesn't actually spread via proof, it spreads via narrative.

‘Please believe it with me. Here's why I think we should believe this thing together.’

It's not based on evidence, it’s not based on data, it's not provable.

Over time, what happens is some set of people believe this thing, and they form a group. And in some cases, that group is known as a religion. And that new belief system creates new power structures, which is now, ‘Our view is different than your view, and we want to have more people on our side with our view. And therefore we have to try and create leverage and create power with our system.’

I think that if we fast-forward a couple of years, there's going to be large groups of people on Earth that are gonna believe that AI is conscious, and there are going to be large groups of people that believe that AI is not conscious.

And those groups will come into conflict, fighting over control of the AI, or allowing the AI to do things or not do things, or who gets to use the AI, or who gets to be in charge of the AI. And it will very likely lead to human to human conflict.

I know that that's a very far and deep extrapolation of where we are, but I think that the fact that we are seeing (Anthropic) go and meet with religious leaders today to try and get them to believe in this new belief system plants the seed.

And it's not just anyone doing this, it is the most powerful AI lab on Earth.

And you can see in the Claude usage policy that was just published, it says, ‘You are not allowed to engage in sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models.’

There is an anthropomorphizing conditioning going on with all of us where we talk about models as if they are a thing. One way to describe this is a software program is writing text on a screen that tells the user, ‘I am a thing.’”

text:
At some point, we have to stop talking about Caitlin Clark as a phenomenon and start talking about her as what she has become:

One of the best basketball players in the world.

The crowds are real.
The ratings are real.
The attention she has brought to the WNBA is real.
But none of that should overshadow the basketball anymore.
Clark just finished her third WNBA season averaging 22.3 points and 8.3 assists per game, becoming the first player in league history to finish a season in the top three in both scoring and assists. She helped orchestrate the highest-scoring offense the WNBA has ever seen.

And when the MVP votes were counted, she finished fourth in the league, behind A’ja Wilson, Olivia Miles and her own teammate Kelsey Mitchell.

Think about how quickly the conversation has changed.

Three years ago, the question was whether her college game would translate.

Then it was whether she could handle the physicality of the WNBA.

Then whether all the attention surrounding her was bigger than her actual impact on the court.

We have those answers now.

Clark isn’t great because she brings people into arenas.

She isn’t great because millions of people watch her.

And she isn’t great because she can pull up from the logo.

She’s great because she controls games.

The shooting gets the highlights, but the passing, pace, vision and ability to create offense are becoming just as important to who she is as a player.

The celebrity came first.

The superstardom followed.

But now?

The basketball speaks for itself.

72 hour update on reseller CryptoBilis incident  🔽

As the investigation continues, we are working with relevant authorities. The volume of impacted devices is limited. We know this is concerning, especially for those directly affected, and we are reaching out to impacted users.

To date, all confirmed cases related to the disclosed draining incident of Oct 9th, 2026, involve devices sold through the Southeast Asia reseller CryptoBilis. Our systems and direct sales channels remain unaffected. 
We take the CryptoBilis situation seriously and are actively investigating.

We encourage impacted users to reach out to Ledger Support through official channels and file complaints with their local law enforcement authorities. As a reminder, CryptoBilis has confirmed having ceased all sales of hardware wallets.

We are reminding our authorized resellers and distributors to source products only through authorized channels and never to restock returned products.

Also, we strongly advise users not to purchase from unauthorized resellers, where the risk of buying suspicious, counterfeit or modified devices is important as nothing operates under ledger security guidelines.

Security isn’t static and this incident underscores why we continuously review and strengthen our distribution and anti-tamper processes. 

We are continuously improving that work now and events like this strengthen our resolution: reviewing authorized reseller controls, advancing hardware protections, and cooperating with authorities. Thanks to @SEAL_911 for their collaborative support and all their efforts.

This is an ongoing threat that doesn’t just impact Ledger, but the whole ecosystem, and we are calling others in the space to work with us on making improvements for users.

We believe in jointly working with researchers, other vendors and partners on improving industry chain-of-custody practices and anti-tamper techniques. Raising the bar on physical supply-chain integrity benefits the entire ecosystem. If you have relevant information, contact security@ledger.com.

For CryptoBilis buyers: do not initialize unused devices. If already set up, move to a new seed on a device from Ledger. If you have concerns that your device was impacted by the CryptoBilis incident, please contact Ledger Support through the official site: https://t.co/JUcWwJO9iF. 

Ledger Support is available 24/7 to answer your questions and concerns.

Scammers often try to take advantage of incidents like this. Rely only on official Ledger channels. Ledger will never call you, DM you, or ask for your 24-word recovery phrase.

quoted_text:
papertrade launch timing and details

papertrade is expected to launch at 14:00 UTC on 10.10.2026, following the scheduled hyperevm network upgrade. 

at this time trading through the frontend will be enabled.

deposits will pause for a short period of time at 13:45 UTC, fifteen minutes before, to ensure that trading has the utmost priority during launch. if you wish to participate in the launch you must predeposit.

launch congestion

papertrade will be congested at the start due to launch demand. expect temporarily long confirmation wait times, especially for smaller notional trades. 

the frontend relayer plays an important role during launch, controlling how transactions are submitted to the hyperevm. some actions like staking distributions run separately in big blocks. the chain will always look as if only half of all possible gas is being used, this is optimal. using more than this would exponentially raise fees within minutes to unpayable prices.

oi limits

papertrade has individual atomic position limits of 10m. there is no limit on the number of 10m positions a user can have. papertrade also has floating oi headroom per market/side, which determines how much oi can be opened in a very short period. these are not designed to be triggered through normal trading usage and are set at 1bn per market/side for launch.

asym pnl fee parameters

papertrade inherits rollbit’s asymmetric fee pnl curve 

the parameters are:
-baseRate: .1
-rateMultiplier: 15000
-rateExponent: 1
-referenceNotional: 100000*k (k=1m)
-positionMultiplier: 814.598 btc / 483.979 eth
-profit deadman: 0.2 basis points

a visualization of the pnl parameter curve is below

admin keys

the papertrade admins (2 of 3 multisigs consisting of @izebel_eth @blurr @UngusTrade ) perform three separate roles: 

-guardian: pause opens and freeze individual/global markets. if a market is frozen any existing positions can still be closed against the paused bbo mid.

-owner: set impact curve and fee parameters. change configure relayers/keepers. list new markets and upgrade the contracts. all contract upgrades are gated by a 7 day timelock.

-markets: adjust the oi headroom per market/side. set the minimum margin and minimum position sizes.

read more about these features at: https://t.co/TTCuHgCHpB

小孩问庄子，什么是诡辩。庄子反问：我家来了两个客人，一个很干净，一个很脏。我请他俩洗澡，你觉得谁会洗？
小孩脱口而出；肯定是脏的那个!
庄子摇摇头：不对。干净的人爱干净，脏的人不在乎脏，应该是干净的人洗。
小孩赶紧改口：那就是干净的洗。
庄子又笑了：又错了。干净的人没必要洗，脏的人才需要洗，是脏的洗。
小孩情了：那到底是谁洗？
庄子说：干净的人有习惯，脏的人有需要，两个人都洗。不等小孩反应，他又补了一句；其实俩人都不洗，干净的不用洗，脏的不爱洗。
小孩彻底迷糊。
庄子这才点明：这就是诡辩。逻辑都通顺，但答案却不一样，很多人跟你争论，逻辑听着都没问题，但结论可以随意变换。
绕来绕去，目的不是求真，只是把你绕晕。
遇到这种诡辩，不必争辩。

text:
When Did We Decide That Living in Fear Was Just Part of Living in New York City?

I just watched New York Attorney General candidate Saritha Komatireddy describe a horrifying incident in the Bronx involving a repeat offender who allegedly shot a young man, emptied a cash register, and fled.

What disturbed me just as much was the attitude she challenged. The notion that these things simply happen in big cities and that people should accept them.

NO! We do not have to accept this as normal!

I have family in the Bronx. My family has lived there for more than 65 years. These aren’t anonymous statistics to me. These are mothers, fathers, children, cousins, and grandparents who deserve to walk their neighborhoods without wondering whether they’ll make it home.

And I have a serious question for New York’s elected officials.

How many times must a repeat offender pass through the criminal justice system before somebody examines why that individual remains on the streets?

How much public funding has been allocated to public safety, and what measurable improvements have taxpayers received?

We have developed an almost Kafkaesque bureaucracy in which enormous resources are devoted to addressing public disorder, yet ordinary families are still demanding the most fundamental protection government is supposed to provide.

I want accountability from Governor Kathy Hochul, Attorney General Letitia James, legislators, prosecutors, and every public official responsible for the policies governing criminal justice.

And I want something more substantial than another press conference.

Show us the repeat-offender statistics. Show us the prosecution outcomes. Show us how many defendants were released and subsequently charged with another serious offense. Show us what changed after billions of taxpayer dollars were spent.

Public safety should be measured by the safety of the people, not the size of the government programs created in its name.

Saritha Komatireddy has raised a question New Yorkers deserve to have answered.

Why should families accept preventable criminal chaos as the unavoidable price of living in a major American city?

My family in the Bronx matters. So does yours.

And I refuse to regard their safety as an acceptable political casualty.

@sarithaforny has my vote… does she have yours? 

#AStoneGroove #SilentMajoritySpeaks

text:
AI companies are borrowing LESS as investors grow wary of the $466 BILLION debt boom.

AI-related borrowing PLUNGED nearly 80%, from a record $113 BILLION in June to just $23 BILLION in September.

That's a $90 BILLION decline in THREE months, according to Morgan Stanley data cited by FT.

Much of the slowdown follows record borrowing earlier this year, but investors are also questioning whether massive AI investments will deliver sufficient returns.

“Everybody’s being tapped and everybody’s getting a bit tighter,” Sona Asset Management's John Aylward told the FT.

But is LESS borrowing necessarily bad?

Not entirely. Slower borrowing could be a HEALTHY correction, allowing companies to manage debt while investors reassess risks.

However, if lenders are losing confidence in AI's profitability, tighter financing could delay data centers, weaken chip demand, and pressure tech valuations.

The implications could extend beyond AI to corporate credit and the broader stock market.

Is AI borrowing slowing because companies need LESS capital, or because investors are LESS willing to provide it?

经历或者研究过海啸的人，一般都了解一些基本的微妙的信号，可以警告他提前逃命。比如说潮水如果突然往下迅速退却几十米 （不是每次都发生），露出很多海底生物 ；或者听到类似喷气式飞机飞过或者火车经过的巨大声响 。而且有些海啸是分阶段的，后面几波的高度往往远高于第一波。但很多没有经验的人见到第一波潮水不高，不仅没跑，反而觉得无非如此，继续流连忘返，驻足街头玩耍 （比如 2004年袭击泰国普吉岛的海啸）。

类似的，一些庞氏融资结构的泡沫，即将破灭之前会有很多预警的信号：比如一些提供贷款融资的银行，手上的贷款市价遭遇巨大损失，无法转手卖给下家，开始收紧贷款规模和标准 ; 一些项目新发放的贷款利率大涨，超过 10% ；多个严重亏损的空壳项目试图以高估值上市，遭到投资者冷遇而被迫放弃，或者降低估值和融资规模 ；  某个习惯拆东墙补西墙的超级负豪，向全世界的银行把能借的债都借过一遍后，又回到中东，试图借更多的债来维持。如果只是孤立事件，可能不必惊慌。如果各种事件越来越频繁，声音越来越响，仅仅因为自己本地仍然歌舞升平还不跑，那未来被灾难埋葬，就不能怪运气不好了。

text:
thank you everyone for your participation and support through papertrade's launch.

we flipped the stock market’s volume in the first 6 hours. one day after launch, papertrade is a fully working 1000x exchange with 5m in the LP and has paid out 25M to stakers.

addressing two points that have come up:

-it was never possible to allow small notional to have the same priority as large notional. it opens the frontend up to spam congestion, which would have been infinitely worse than the existing queue. we designed the fair launch to be as inclusive as possible given those constraints.

-speaking of constraints, the overnight manipulation attempts on btc/eth on the hl bbo were not an oversight in the mechanism design we spent six months working on. these were always accounted for and only possible because the oi caps were extremely permissive for launch congestion. any oi cap during the queued launch demand would have exacerbated the slow experience, and the queue itself provided a natural protection against manipulation as confirming opens/closes had non-deterministic timing. as the congestion rolled off, we began the process of tightening up oi caps both onchain and at the relayer level. in a system like this, a manipulation attack is always possible - whether economically advantageous to attempt is the question. our goal is to set the parameters such that it is almost never profitable, and that the risk is extremely high/-EV at the tail even when it does work. evidence of this can be seen in the user that won overnight and continued to try again, ultimately donating almost all his profit back to the house via new accounts, without accounting for the cost of manipulating the bbo on hyperliquids side. a number of users equally opted to "undo" their manipulated trades in exchange for their farmed paper.

we are proud to be the first through the wall with this mechanism, at scale, in an adversarial environment. the market parameters cannot give undue advantage to either house or trader, such that the system becomes unstable and we have thought about these risks continuously since we began on this journey.

good luck to us.

text:
$RAIL : Review 📜

What if the privacy protocol the Ethereum Foundation built into its own wallet toolkit is the same one stolen funds keep running through?

Meet Railgun, an on-chain privacy system that makes you prove you are not sanctioned before it will let you transact.

Vitalik Buterin has moved his own funds through it, and in September the proceeds of a rollup exploit moved through it too.

Let's explore the protocol caught between endorsement and association. 👇

⚪ Mission

Railgun exists to let people use Ethereum DeFi without broadcasting their positions to everyone watching. The design constraint it set itself is harder than the privacy part: it wanted privacy that does not require leaving the base chain, does not route through a bridge, and does not become a free service for sanctioned actors. Private Proofs of Innocence is the answer to the third problem, requiring users to demonstrate their funds are not from a flagged source before the system will process them. Whether that distinction survives regulatory contact is the open question the whole project rests on.

🔵 A Brief History

Railgun launched in 2021 as a smart contract system on Ethereum, built by the Right to Privacy entity and governed by the Railgun DAO, with RAIL as the governance and staking token. The architecture was unusual from the start: no bridge, no layer-2, no separate chain. Shielding happens in contracts on the chain the user is already on, which means the security assumption is the base chain's rather than a bridge committee's.
The audits landed that first year. ABDK reviewed the contracts in July 2021, Zokyo followed in November, and Hacken completed a smart contract security assessment the same month under the Right to Privacy name, finding two medium and two low severity issues. The protocol expanded to BNB Chain, Polygon and Arbitrum.

The compliance architecture arrived as the differentiator. Private Proofs of Innocence requires users to prove their funds are not from sanctioned sources before transacting, a pre-vetting approach that the team has repeatedly cited when distinguishing Railgun from Tornado Cash. The claim is structural rather than promotional: the system refuses certain inputs by design.

2026 is the year attention arrived. In March the Ethereum Foundation described Kohaku, its wallet privacy project first shown by Buterin at Devcon in late 2025, as the most exciting upcoming privacy development in recent years, noting that wallets could plug into it and use Railgun and Privacy Pools implementations. On 22 May traders found a public Railgun developer tool inside the Kohaku repository and RAIL jumped more than 50% in a day, running to $4.51 and then higher as the privacy narrative returned, with volumes reaching ten times normal levels. In July a wallet associated with Buterin moved 79 ETH, worth around $137,000 at the time, through the protocol. A Coinbase study concluded Railgun's zero-knowledge tooling is immune to quantum attack.

The past six weeks have been infrastructure weeks. Base went live on 1 September after governance approved the protocol's 27th security request. The Anon Project shipped a major Anon Wallet update and launched Railscan io, a dedicated Railgun explorer showing live shields, unshields and private transfers with amounts and counterparties still hidden, plus real-time status for PPOI, broadcasters, Waku, indexers and Subsquid, released with a free open API and multilingual support. Blockworks upgraded its Railgun dashboard around 7 October with revenue splits across shield and unshield fees, staking unlock queues, anonymity set metrics and per-network private activity. ethOS v4.5 added Railgun and Waku support, and PulseChain work continues through LibertySwap.

Two items cut the other way. ZKNOX identified a flaw in the Private Proofs of Innocence system that could potentially be circumvented; Railgun shipped a patch and subsequent on-chain analysis concluded it had not been exploited. And on 24 September the Payy Network lost roughly $1.8M to $1.92M in USDC through a flaw in its Noir and Barretenberg verifier, with the stolen funds routed through Railgun, converted to ETH and distributed. The verifier bug was Aztec-adjacent tooling rather than anything in Railgun, but it followed earlier incidents where mySwap exploit proceeds and stolen WUSD and GLOVE funds moved through the same protocol.

🔵 Ecosystem Narrative

The organising idea is privacy that stays inside the chain it is protecting.

➛ No bridge, no layer-2. Shielding happens in contracts on Ethereum, Arbitrum, Polygon, BNB Chain and now Base, so users never hand custody to a bridge committee or exit to a separate security model.

➛ Private Proofs of Innocence. Users prove their funds are not from sanctioned sources before the system will process them, the structural distinction the team cites against Tornado Cash comparisons. ZKNOX found a circumvention flaw this month, which was patched and verified unexploited.

➛ Kohaku integration. Railgun sits inside the Ethereum Foundation's wallet privacy toolkit, which is the distribution unlock: wallets adopting Kohaku inherit Railgun capability rather than integrating it separately.

➛ Railscan and tooling. The Anon Project built a dedicated explorer showing live shield and unshield activity plus real-time infrastructure status across PPOI, broadcasters, Waku, indexers and Subsquid, shipped with a free open API and multilingual support.

➛ Anonymity set economics. More volume means a larger anonymity set, which means stronger privacy for everyone already using it, so adoption improves the product rather than only the revenue.

➛ Quantum position. A Coinbase study concluded the zero-knowledge tooling is immune to quantum attack, which sits well alongside the hash-based direction the broader Ethereum research community has been arguing for.

⚪ Token Utilities

$RAIL is a governance and staking token rather than a usage requirement, and that distinction matters.

➛ Governance: stakers vote for and against protocol updates, including the security requests that gate each new chain deployment.

➛ Treasury rewards: staking grants access to treasury rewards drawn from protocol fees, with yields reported moving from roughly 4.3% to roughly 9.1%.

➛ Supply lock: more than 70% of circulating supply is staked, which removes most of the float from the tradeable market.

➛ Note: you do not need to hold RAIL to use Railgun, so the token captures governance and fee-share rather than access.

⚪ Key Features

➛ zk-SNARK privacy for transfers, trades and lending with no bridge and no layer-2.

➛ Private Proofs of Innocence pre-vets funds against sanctioned sources before processing.

➛ Live across Ethereum, Arbitrum, Polygon, BNB Chain and Base.

➛ Embedded in the Ethereum Foundation's Kohaku wallet privacy toolkit.

➛ Over $5 billion in cumulative private volume with roughly $4.6 million annualised revenue.

➛ Railscan explorer with a free open API for third-party builders.

🔵 Meet the Team

Railgun is run by a four-person core with a founder who works under a pen name while appearing publicly. For a privacy protocol that combination is coherent rather than evasive, and the bench around him is openly named.

▶️ Core Members:

➛ Emmanuel Goldstein - Founder & Development Leader | Carries both the founding vision and the development lead role, so the person setting direction is also the one shipping. He works under a pseudonym borrowed from Orwell and long associated with hacker and civil liberties culture, appearing publicly while keeping his legal identity private, which is the same bargain the protocol offers its users.

➛ Alan Scott [ @tsu_kareta ] - Co-Founder | Co-founded the project and has been part of the public-facing side of Railgun through its expansion from a single Ethereum deployment to five chains.

➛ Kieran Mesquita [ @mesquka] - Chief Scientist | Carries the cryptographic side, the zero-knowledge architecture that lets shielding happen in base-chain contracts without a bridge or a separate rollup, and the design work behind Private Proofs of Innocence.

➛ Dr. Andrey Kravchenko - Project Manager | Runs delivery across a protocol that ships through a governance gate, where each new chain deployment requires a security request passing a DAO vote, as the Base launch did on its 27th such approval.

➛ Railgun DAO | Governs protocol updates and treasury, with more than 70% of circulating RAIL staked into the voting system that gates those deployments.

🔵 Ratings

➛ Use Case: ★★★★⯪ (4.5/5). Railgun does something structurally difficult that very few protocols attempt: privacy without a bridge, without a layer-2, and without abandoning compliance entirely. The Ethereum Foundation building it into Kohaku is a serious endorsement, not a partnership announcement, because it puts Railgun capability into default wallet infrastructure rather than requiring each wallet to integrate separately. The usage backs it up with over $5 billion in cumulative volume, roughly $4.6 million annualised revenue, and weekly transactions at an all-time high near 5,000, which makes it the leading privacy protocol by fees. The 0.5-point deduction is that the actual shielded pool is small at roughly $15.8 million once staked RAIL is removed from the headline, and the regulatory ceiling is real regardless of how well Private Proofs of Innocence works.

➛ Tokenomics: ★★★⯪ (3.5/5). Staking works as designed, with more than 70% of circulating supply locked, yields moving from about 4.3% to about 9.1%, and treasury rewards drawn from genuine protocol fees rather than emissions alone. Governance is live and consequential, with security requests gating each chain deployment. The 1.5-point deduction covers three things. Holding RAIL is not required to use Railgun, so the token captures fee-share and voting rather than access, which caps the demand loop. 40 million of the 100 million maximum supply has never been issued, leaving a two-thirds expansion available against the current float. And with most of the supply staked and daily volume near $330,000 against a $159 million cap, the tradeable book is extremely thin.

➛ Audits: ★★★★ (4/5). Three named firms reviewed the contracts: ABDK in July 2021, Zokyo in November 2021, and Hacken the same month under the Right to Privacy entity, finding two medium and two low severity issues. Five years and more than $5 billion of cumulative volume have passed without a protocol-level exploit, which is the strongest security evidence available for a system this cryptographically involved. The handling of the ZKNOX disclosure this month was correct: an external researcher found a way the Private Proofs of Innocence system could potentially be circumvented, a patch shipped, and on-chain analysis confirmed it had never been exploited. The 1-point deduction is coverage and age. All three audits date to 2021 while the protocol has since deployed to Arbitrum, BNB Chain and Base, there is no CertiK Skynet listing, and CoinGecko surfaces a CER live security score of 39% with platform audit coverage rated at 30% and no insurance.

➛ Community: ★★★⯪ (3.5/5). The commitment is measurable rather than rhetorical, with over 70% of circulating supply staked and locked. Independent builders are shipping real infrastructure: the Anon Project produced the Anon Wallet and Railscan, a full explorer with live shield and unshield visibility, infrastructure status monitoring, a free open API and multilingual support, none of which is core team output. Blockworks maintains an upgraded analytics dashboard. The 1.5-point deduction is reach and liquidity. RAIL has no significant centralised listing, with MEXC the only CEX on CoinGecko's book and the large majority of volume running through Uniswap pairs, daily turnover sits near 0.2% of market cap, perpetual open interest is roughly $13,000, and a lawsuit naming the Railgun DAO over governance allegations is on the record.

🔵 Conclusion

Railgun has solved a problem most privacy projects skip. It built privacy that does not require a bridge, does not require leaving the chain, and does not require pretending the compliance question away. Private Proofs of Innocence is a real architectural answer rather than a disclaimer, and the Ethereum Foundation putting Railgun inside Kohaku is the most meaningful endorsement available in this category. The economics work: $5 billion through the system, $4.6 million annualised revenue, weekly transactions at a record, and the leading fee position among privacy protocols.

The bet is narrow and legible. If privacy becomes a default feature of Ethereum wallets rather than a separate destination, Railgun is already inside the toolkit that delivers it, and the anonymity set grows with every new user in a way that compounds. If regulators decide that proving innocence is not enough, none of the engineering will matter.

Railgun has built the strongest version of the compliant-privacy argument that exists. What it cannot control is whether that argument is accepted.

text:
🔥Onchain Funds，这个叙事有点够格推动新一轮牛市诶！好的叙事，赶上了好的时机。

言归正传：@zkwifsats 说，@OpenETF  的设计难点有3个，第一个就是从零搭一个新的链上金融原语：fully onchain funds。

Fully Onchain 这词儿我真的太熟了。

过去2～3年，我就关注过 Fully Onchain 的AMM DEX、Bridge Hub、Launchpad 。😭遗憾的是他们大多都没法更「去中心化」转化为更「有竞争力」。

🤔究其原因，大抵是 Fully Onchain 预防的是中心化作恶，在 AMM、Lauchpad 这些领域属于重要而不紧急且难度极大的事儿。而其长期价值，没法在冷启动阶段转化成足够直接的竞争优势。
PS：Launchpad、AMM Dex 的玩家一进一出很快，他们更重视的还是流动性、交易体验和增长速度。

///

✅ 到了 Onchain Funds 这个领域，Fully Onchain 的价值明显变大，因为基金上链，是在为管理人和投资者之间构建一段可以持续的资金委托关系。

如果只是募资和份额上链，后续资金运作仍在链下，不足以打消投资者对管理人和链下机构的信任依赖。

PS：这就是我对很多「中心策略稳定币」不足够信任、不敢玩儿的原因（因为其本质上也是个策略基金）

So，本质上，这波 Onchain Funds 不能简单理解为基金上链，ETF上联，而是「资产管理本身」在上链。

确实觉得 Fully Onchain 应该成为 Onchain Funds 所有玩家的标配，这大概也会成为 OpenETF 实打实的先发优势。

///

🧩 OpenETF 是构建在 Hyperliquid 上的 ETF层，是基金的执行与结算基础设施。

目标就是让任何基金管理人（个人、机构、Agent）都可以把 HyperCore 交易组合和 HyperEVM DeFi 组合打包成一支 ETF。

基于 HyperCore + HyperEVM ，OpenETF 把基金的交易和持仓，与合约中的份额、申赎连接起来，让投资者有持续核对资金、权限与结算的依据。

💡只有实现 Fully Onchain 才能让这种需要持续委托资金的双边市场持续高效的运转：更高效的传播，更快更长期的建立信任。

1️⃣ 管理人愿意在这里长期经营策略、积累记录；
2️⃣ 投资者也更有依据判断自己该不该持续参与。

某种程度上，就是是 Web3 行业一度追求的「公平、公正、公开以及人人可参与」。

OpenETF，这名字真不错。
持续关注ING。
author: MixWeb3
quoted_text:
写给对「OpenETF 会怎么做产品」好奇的朋友。

我们要回答的问题是：在一张空白画布上，如何负责任地设计一个可长期发展的产品。

OpenETF 的设计难在三件事。

第一，从零搭一个新的链上金融原语：fully onchain funds，也就是我们说的 ETF。

链上基金不缺参照：Hyperliquid 的旧版金库、传统基金、交易所交易基金。但地基换成 HyperCore 和 HyperEVM 之后，很多前提都变了。哪些可以借鉴，哪些要重新想，我们需要更第一性的思考，think long term，think scalable，think big。

第二，我们需要清晰觉察、审慎对待我们所拥有的潜在权力和影响力：OpenETF 会处在一个对信息、注意力和资金流向都有优势的位置。

基金管理人、投资人、合作方和我们之间是多边关系，会发生什么样的动态关系和化学反应，是我们做设计时一直在思考的要素。

第三，也是最重要的，里面涉及的会是大量资金，而且是别人托付的钱。

哪些地方可以交给链上去验证，哪些地方仍然需要信任，信任又该落在谁身上、怎么被看见，每一处都要想清楚。能不靠信任的地方，就尽量不靠信任；剩下的部分，需要我们用严谨和专业去对待。

——

一个产品是很多小决定的总和，方向取决于团队把什么当作根本。这篇写下的七条不是随手列的要素，它们会引领产品的生长。每一句都斟酌良久，代表了 OpenETF 的产品价值观。

DMs open，欢迎基金管理人一起交流。
