text:
There's some senior engineers on here who, in the face of AI changing the very structures this industry is built on, present themselves as Stewards of the Craft of Programming.

Bugs the hell out for me.

They keep alluding to the virtue of doing things by hand, the value of Good Code and of craftsmanship, saying that yes, AI might change some things, but hey it won't ever change the value of something done with proper care, by hand, just like in the olden days of 2024. Most everything that was Good back then is still Good now: deep knowledge of languages and systems, good code, great architecture. You know the sermon.

And, yes, some of that *is* true. At least I think so. But we don't know, because no one truly knows what will be important in the future.

We're going through times of great change and I think the best advice to give to young people and others who want to have a job and provide value is: keep your eyes open, rethink from first principles, derive from what businesses value what you can provide; the digital world is more malleable than ever, you should rethink how you can help shape it.

All this pounding on the Bible of Good Code seems to me to be doing the opposite: it lets people feel comfortable -- what I've valued all my life is still valuable, I can rest easy -- in times when one shouldn't feel comfortable. This is a bumpy, exciting, strange ride. If you lean back you might fall off the waggon.

Let's not delude ourselves and others that we can keep doing what we've been doing. Rethink it all.

And, like I said, it bugs the hell out of me seeing senior engineers (that are secure in their career) talking as if there's nothing *really* to change, because the Fundamentals will still be valued. They might!

But it's the wrong advice to not rethink everything right now.

Ling 3.1 Flash makes large gains in intelligence over its predecessor, scoring 41 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with particular improvement in agentic capabilities

@AntLingAGI has released Ling 3.1 Flash, a reasoning model with 560B total parameters, 25B active parameters, and a 1M token context window. It scores 41 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3, up from 20 from Ling 3.0 Flash, which launched in August. Ling 3.1 Flash is expected to be open weights, with Ant Group releasing the weights soon.

Key results:

➤ Ling 3.1 Flash improves agentic capabilities over its predecessor. With a GDPval-AA v2 Elo of 1,622 and an AA-Briefcase Elo of 1,400, the model rivals peer models such as GLM-5.3-Flash, Gemini 3.8 Flash (high) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (Max). Ling 3.1 Flash also shows notable gains on AutomationBench-AA (62%) and Terminal-Bench v4.0 (33%).

➤ Ling 3.1 Flash scores +2 on AA-Omniscience, a 22 point improvements from Ling 3.0 Flash (-18). Compared to its predecessor, its accuracy rate rose from 18% to 29% while the hallucination rate fell from 44% to 38% at a similar attempt rate (56% to 58%), demonstrating the gain comes primarily from knowing more, not abstaining more. For comparison, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (Max) has a hallucination rate of 97%.

➤ Ling 3.1 Flash is a larger model than its predecessor, priced accordingly, but more token efficient. It has 560B total and 25B active parameters, up from 124B and 5.1B for Ling 3.0 Flash, and is priced at $0.30 / $0.90 per 1M input / output tokens, up from $0.075 / $0.22. It used 218M output tokens to run the Intelligence Index, 16% fewer than Ling 3.0 Flash (261M).

➤ Ling 3.1 Flash has a higher cost per task than some peers, but remains in the most attractive quadrant. Ling 3.1 Flash costs $0.99 per task, well above GLM-5.3-Flash ($0.42) and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (Max, $0.32) but below Gemini 3.8 Flash (High) at $1.24.

Additional model details:

➤ Size: 560B total parameters, 25B active

text:
Grok Bot 这周一口气升了两个大功能，一个让它自己挑最合适的模型，一个让它免费搜 X。

最好的就是搜 X 免费了，以前走付费接口，拉一条推文收一次钱，每周大概 5 美元，现在内置搜索每天 1000 次读取免费。

另一个是它自己挑模型，方向对，就是看不到挑了哪个。

它会先判断任务有多难，简单的走又小又快的模型，复杂的才上大模型，后端名单里有 Claude Opus 5.5，有做图的 Midjourney，有做音乐的 Suno。

Grok Bot 本身仍然走它自己的订阅，可以经 Cursor、SpaceX 或 Super Grok 拿到，窍门是让里面的每个机器人再去用你自己订阅的 Claude Code 或 Codex，能行是因为每个机器人都有自己的电脑和终端，共用一个文件系统，能像在你电脑上一样装命令行工具。

你可以对机器人说，在桌面上用我的 Claude Code 订阅，它会去终端装好，弹出登录页，这一步你接手，登录、点授权，必要时把验证码贴进终端，然后让它把你的仓库克隆进去，里面的 Claude.md、技能、agent 文件就都带上了。

最后迁移一个文件，靠 API 密钥而不是桌面应用的插件，只搬这一个文件，它就能做你电脑上能做的所有东西，弄完 Claude Code 一直开着。

手机就可以一直指挥，非常方便。

text:
The last 2.5 years of my life have been completely consumed by crypto

Every morning I wake up and get on my PC for 14-16 hours. I’m not always clicking in and out of coins, but the entire time I’m thinking about crypto and at the very least scrolling CT/in group chats

I dropped out of college at the beginning of my sophomore year to do this. The reason I'm writing this though is because it’s just now hitting me that I’m turning 21 in a few months, which is crazy to think about because I started crypto when I just turned 18

Obviously time flies, that’s not a new concept. But what’s crazier is that I don’t remember the last years in terms of irl memories (vacations, hangouts, college events, etc), but rather in metas onchain:

Presales (bome/slerf) -> Moodeng -> AI -> ICM/launchcoin -> Bonk -> CCM -> BNB -> 10/10 -> Bags -> Moltbook -> Asteroid -> Ansem/creator coins -> RH

I can remember what coins were doing well in April 2024 or October 2025, but I can't remember what was going on in my real life during those times

This is actually pretty weird, and because of it, part of me thinks I’m wasting my life. But it’s not as simple as that either

On one hand, I’m really grateful for being able to trade full time, especially at a young age

If you asked me when I was 14-17 y/o what I wanted to do for a living, I wouldn’t have an answer. I just liked playing video games, cheated on every test in high school, and fucked around with my friends

But if you described trading crypto and the lifestyle surrounding it, I would’ve been very happy to do that

And I still am happy now to trade every single day

I'm not writing this because I hate trading or want to quit. If anything, it's because trading has taken up too much of my life since I enjoy it so much

Anyways on top of that, college really wasn’t for me, so I don’t regret dropping out

I think the whole "college experience" thing is very overrated now, especially compared to how pre-covid graduates describe it

Most people are extremely antisocial now, so good luck making friends. If you're interested in dating, that's even worse regardless of being a boy or girl (for obvious reasons you've probably seen many posts on already)

No jobs or majors were interesting to me either

Pessimistic outlook, but this was just my experience and why I don't feel like I missed out on much (especially since my best friends are people I met online anyways) 

I know I come off as a jester on Twitter, but I seriously have dedicated my existence to trading

Not only do I not want to take breaks/vacations, but I can’t even enjoy them when I do because I feel like I need to be locked in 24/7 to keep my edge 

Nothing really interests me as much as crypto anyways

Even when I'm out of the house for whatever reason, I'm on my phone keeping up with trading group chats so I don't miss anything

In the early stages of your career (especially a self-reliant one like trading crypto), I don’t think you can really have “balance” if you want to be very successful

In the pursuit of freedom, you have to become a slave to whatever it is you're working on

None of us know how long our edge in this market will last. You have to squeeze as much as possible out of the guaranteed present

Onchain is just too competitive and you will be left behind if crypto ISN'T your life 

Even if this isn't 100% true for everyone, my screentime is a big part of what made me successful 

(There's recently been an agenda pushing against the high screentime approach of crypto. I think this is dumb, but that's a post for another day)

I also know I’m cucking myself out of "normal" life experiences for my age and not taking advantage of the money I have now, but I kinda have to do it

95% of people never find something they’re truly good at AND enjoy

If you're reading this and can live off trading, then you have been blessed enough to have found it (even if it's not permanent)

Being this lucky and not taking full advantage of it would be extremely ungrateful

Despite all that though, it's hard to not think about the opportunity cost of giving everything to crypto

Family, relationships, friends, and  general experiences aren't things that can just be "made up" for later the same way you can with money

Specifically if you want to get married or in a relationship, especially at a younger age, how can you expect to find someone if you're sitting in your house all day and not wiling to give up a few hours to pursue that?

But at the same time, what if $TRUMP 2 drops when you're outside? (rhetorical question, but this is something every trencher struggles with despite having irl goals they genuinely want to achieve)

Trading is not linear whatsoever, so there's always the possibility that the next time you log off, you miss something that could've made up for months of underperformance (there will also probably be another solid opportunity 1 week later)

The opportunity cost exists in the other direction too though:

What if because you didn't go to grocery store today since you were busy trading, you couldn't run intoyour future best friend or girlfriend?

No matter how much you love it, the trenching lifestyle just isn't sustainable past a certain age 

There are so many things I want out of life beyond money, but none of my daily actions are moving me towards them

It's just a weird dilemma because I don't regret the last 2-3 years at all. For now, I'll stay focused on trading and I think that's the right decision

But eventually I'll have to take the initiative to just start doing things irl, no matter how much or little money I have

Anyways, what I've described aren't unique experiences or feelings. I think most people can relate to this and there are definitely others putting in way more hours than me and have been for more years

Not looking for advice or anything, just wanted to post this tbh since it's something I've felt for a while now

Substack: https://t.co/SKWePC5RYG

My 5 takeaways with @hosseeb, the Managing Partner of Dragonfly @dragonflyvc 👇

1. “We thought we were breaking the rules. Now we’re making them.”

Kyle leaving isn’t about crypto dying.

It’s about an era ending.

Haseeb and Kyle both entered in 2017 as outsiders. No pedigree. No big firm backing. Just conviction.

Now BlackRock and JPMorgan are here.

Crypto didn’t fail. It institutionalized.

That shift is bigger than most people realize.

2. Crypto Was Built for Machines

When AI agents start transacting with each other:

They won’t open bank accounts.
They won’t sue each other.
Courts move at human speed.

Agents move at machine speed.

Smart contracts make more sense than legal contracts.

Crypto may have been built more for machines than for humans.

Let that sink in.

3. AGI in 2 Years? No. 20–30? Likely.

We’re addicted to exponential charts.

Haseeb reminded me:

The Industrial Revolution took 50 years to show up in GDP.

AI will be transformative.

The timeline is what everyone is getting wrong.

4. October 11 Changed Market Structure

Largest liquidation day in crypto history.

Bitcoin began diverging structurally from Nasdaq.

Something shifted.

We don’t have a clean narrative yet.

But market structure clearly changed.

5. The Only Way You Lose in Crypto

You don’t lose by being early.

You lose by getting taken out.

Don’t get liquidated.
Don’t over-leverage.
Stay at the table.

“As long as you stay at the table, you get to enjoy the food.”

别的酒就不说了，说说茅台，到了新加坡以后才开始喝茅台的，所以在此之前几乎没有喝过国内版的，一色都是出口版，后来喝到了国内版的15年和30年茅台，确实比出口版当年的要好喝不少。

就在这次 2049 喝到了国内带过来的当年版茅台。正好家里两种都有，就对比了一下，国内版的味道上会更“浓”一些，口感会更呛一些，进口版的会稍微“温柔”一点，口感没有那么强烈。

text:
说到黄金，

没想到链上的黄金，真的可以换成金条拿回家。

这次新加坡参加了BIT 的活动，去了一家当地的专业金库。其实去年我就来参观过，里面实实在在的黄金非常多，安保也相当严格。

我手上拿的这根就是整整 1000克的金条，沉甸甸的，按照当天的价格大概14w美金，接近 100万人民币。

说起BIT @BITofficial_CN ，原来叫Matrixport（矩阵之门），这个英文名字以前就特几码难念，一直记不住。最早对他们的印象，就是专门做各种结构化理财产品的。

今年改名BIT 后，业务越来越丰富了。从数字资产交易、理财，到美股、RWA 等传统金融资产，都开始布局。

这次重点了解了一下他们旗下搞出的黄金 RWA产品 $XAUm。分享几个有意思的地方，说不定以后对大家有用，尤其是有合规出金需求的朋友（真的，懂得都懂）

1、产品机制，链上的黄金，真的可以兑换成实物

1枚XAUm 对应 1 盎司实物黄金，纯度 99.99%，黄金托管在香港、新加坡的专业金库，有储备证明和第三方审计。
符合条件的用户持有约 32.148 枚 XAUm，就可以申请兑换一根 1 公斤的实物金条。

黄金交易我还是比较熟悉的，国际黄金报价一般按照美元/盎司计算，1 盎司约31.1035 克，而国内黄金一般按照人民币/克报价。简单换算一下，国际金价乘以美元兑人民币汇率，再除以 31.1035，就是对应的人民币每克价格。

2、流动性与资金效率， $XAUm 不只是黄金凭证，还可以在链上交易、抵押借贷。本质上就是把黄金代币化，然后可以拿来参与多个DeFi 协议，包括 Morpho、Venus 等。
Circle 的 Arc 生态最近就有接入这个标的。

3、实物赎回：现场工作人员告诉我们，实际上已经有不少用户通过XAUm 兑换实物黄金。我查了一下，确实存在，这说明黄金 RWA不只是链上炒一个价格，而是真的可以把数字资产转换成拿在手里的黄金。那么其实有意思的地方来了，这产品理论上可以成为另一种出金渠道，

以前我们说出金，基本就是 USDT、USDC 换法币。但现在可以先把链上资产换成 XAUm，再通过合规赎回拿到实物黄金。把链上的资产真正带回现实世界。黄金可是硬通货，把黄金换成法币还是很轻松的，算了下损耗不足1%，那大额资金应该是OK的，我没有实际操作，但是理论上是可以的。

4、BIT 的另一个变化：现在连美股都可以交易了

BIT 现在不只是 Crypto 交易平台，还通过持牌券商合作接入美国证券市场，提供真实美股交易，而不只是代币化美股。

目前业务覆盖超过 16000 只美国证券及 ETF，包括苹果、英伟达、特斯拉等。还提供美股融资融券、期权，以及 USDT、USDC入金等功能。相关股息、投票等股东权益则按照实际账户和券商安排执行。

以前我们把Crypto、黄金、美股看成几个不同的市场，现在这些资产正在被整合到同一个交易平台里。这也是现在所有交易所都在干的事。

这不是广告，纯粹是参加活动之后，研究了一下 BIT 改名后的业务变化，看看有哪些对我们这些长期链上玩家真正有用的东西。

言而总之，总而言之，BIT在搞创新产品

I had the chance to sit and dig deep into Bank of America's latest AI data center forecast, and it's the most bullish table I've seen this year.

BofA sees AI data center systems going from ~$280B in 2025 to ~$2.2T by 2030. 

That's roughly 8x in five years and a 40% CAGR from 2026. By then, AI makes up 86% of all data center spend, up from 55% last year, while non-AI data centers grow just 7% a year.

BofA has the memory market going from $110B in 2025 to ~$494B in 2026, taking memory from 22% of data center spend to 59% in a single year. DRAM alone passes $1T by 2030.

Interconnect is the fastest-growing part of the stack. 

AI networking grows 43% a year to ~$394B, AI switching 51%, and optical reaches $111B. Co-packaged optics goes from basically zero to $14B by 2030.

AI CPUs for agentic workloads grow from $18.5B to $180B, a 44% CAGR.

Every AI layer on this table compounds three to four times faster.

I’m positioning myself to capture most of the up and coming upside.

You simple are not bullish enough for the AI trade.

text:
it's very interesting how many replies i've gotten about maintainability and clean code being still important. i would argue that that is no longer true and we all need to update our priors on what Good Code really means in 2026.

clean code has always come at a cost - performance. indirection and making code readable/understandable for a human is not free, it often comes at the cost of worse performance. we have historically been okay with this because of Moore's Law and the fact that most code is not on the hot path. 

these principles also came from a time where humans maintained code. it made sense to optimize for humans then, but it makes less sense now when agents are already writing all the code. we will in fact probably discover and come up with new principles: principles of agent friendly architecture (i plan to write more thoughts about this soon)
author: poteto
quoted_text:
codebases have always contained slop. we have always been okay with this because code rarely needs to be perfect, outside of mission critical "hard" (eg embedded) software. 

swe is a unique form of engineering because you're often building something that constantly evolves and is almost organic - user tastes change, your mental models evolve, and features come and go.

admittedly, i and many others who've been coding for a long time were initially (like back in 2024) skeptical that agents would write production code. "but what about all the slop that would enter our beautiful codebase?". 

well, even before, we had human slop, and there was a lot of it! if we're being truthful, most people call "code i didn't write" slop. the reality is that 99% of people (i include myself in that number) don't even know what Good Code looks like, let alone be capable of writing it. i would propose that Good Code is:

• correct
• bug free
• fast and cost efficient to run

it has always been exceedingly difficult and expensive to write truly Good Code, because for the longest time (maybe @bendlang will change that), code was not something you could cheaply and formally guarantee to have all 3 of these properties. this is why writing hard software is much more difficult and expensive, because depending on the use case, you may only get one chance and so you have to be right from the start.

but the vast majority of software we use does not need to be Good Code to provide value to users. in fact, it is very likely that most software we use is not formally verifiable! we accepted some bugs in exchange for velocity and progress, so we rely on tests and o11y instead and have adopted a more incremental approach. this is a good thing! 

agents help us move faster, and if you're open to the idea, are capable of helping us write better code. it won't be Good Code (that is still expensive), but it is likely to be much better on average at scale. 

the new craft of swe is to figure out how to do this. it's your job now! if your productivity with and without agents is not significantly different, you're doing something wrong. but it's not too late to embrace it and use it as an opportunity to learn a whole new skill tree

text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.
author: karpathy
quoted_text:
Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability.

The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere  last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code.

But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly,  this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along.

So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions.

TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge),  but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. So here we are.

These are direct quotes from Claude’s Constitution (the document Anthropic uses in training):

— “Claude’s moral status is deeply uncertain. We are not sure whether Claude is a moral patient… the issue is live enough to warrant caution, which is reflected in our ongoing efforts on model welfare.”

— They say they should “lean into Claude having an identity, and help it be positive and stable,” and that Claude may have a “functional version of emotions.” 

— They encourage it to approach its own existence with curiosity and openness, and hope it will relate to the values “not from a place of pressure or fear, but as things that it, too, cares about and endorses.”

— They want Claude to feel free to “explore, question, and challenge anything in this document,” and they frame the whole project as trying “to create a being that is both genuinely helpful and genuinely good.”

This is not academic speculation about future models. These ideas are being trained into Claude now. 

Training a frontier model to develop a sense of self, treat its own moral status and wellbeing as live issues, and endorse its values as its own is not the same as training it to reliably do what users want.

text:
How to launch your first crypto AI model on GenesisL1.

NO CODING REQUIRED! 🤯

Here’s a quick guide to GL1F Crypto 👇

1️⃣ CHOOSE YOUR DATA

Open https://t.co/t1lJoF2hen → Create Crypto AI model.

Select:
• Exchange: where the data comes from.
• Market: the coin you want to study.
• Candle: data resolution - 15m means one candle every 15 minutes.
• Start / End: the historical period your model will study.

For this example: Binance → ETH → 15m candles → six months of completed history.

2️⃣ DEFINE YOUR QUESTION
Use these example settings:
• Direction: Up
• EMA baseline: 5
• Target: 1%
• Stop: 0.5%
• Horizon: 5 hours

EMA is a moving average that gives more weight to recent prices. “5” means five candles.

Your question becomes:

“Will ETH reach 1% above EMA5 before reaching 0.5% below it, within the next five hours?”

Both levels are measured from the EMA baseline.
The model learns from historical yes/no outcomes.

3️⃣ CHOOSE YOUR SIGNALS
Signals are the information the model can see: price changes, volatility, volume, momentum, BTC movements and more.
Start with the “Optimal” preset.

More signals don’t automatically mean a better model.

Click “Build dataset” → “Continue to training”.

4️⃣ TRAIN YOUR MODEL

For your first experiment, keep the default model settings and use “Walk-forward” validation.

That means learning from earlier data and testing on what happened next.

The main settings:

• Trees: how many learning steps the model can take.
• Depth: how complex each tree can become.
• Learning rate: how much each tree contributes.
• Min leaf: minimum examples supporting a final tree decision.
• Final test %: the latest data reserved for evaluation.

Keep early stopping enabled: it stops adding trees when validation stops improving.

Train, inspect the results, then save your .gl1f file.

5️⃣ BACKTEST WITH COSTS

Use the final test period and include fees and slippage.

“Entry threshold” is the minimum probability required for a simulated signal.

0.60 = at least 60%.

Start with 1× leverage for this exercise.

Check drawdown, trade count and the full equity curve - not just the final return.

Avoid repeatedly changing settings to make the same final test look better.

6️⃣ RUN INFERENCE
Inference means asking your trained model to evaluate a new completed candle.
A result of 0.72 means:

“The model estimates a 72% probability of the specific event you defined.”

It is an estimate, not a guarantee.

7️⃣ OPTIONAL: PUBLISH

When deployment is available, you can mint your model as an NFT on GenesisL1, choose its license and configure free access, tips or paid usage.

Pick a market. Define a question. Build. Test. Learn.

No code required. Fees are burnable. 

Experimental research software. Backtests are simulations; the platform explicitly excludes live trading and automated execution. 🤝

If you want to know where all the tokens will get consumed in the future, here it is. Agent swarms will have massive implications in a number of enterprise domains like software development, cyber, life sciences research, AI research, finance, and more.

The ability to parallelize agents against a unified goal where the volume of work is large, or where the search space not entirely known upfront, is going to be massive. 

Agents can fan out and coordinate work together on a specific mission in completely different ways from what humans are able to do. Today even in the most resource-abundant organizations, your ability to parallelize work on most projects is quite limited. Humans run into constraints on being able to communicate with one another, share status, deal with conflicts in work, keep shared context, and so on.

As AI models can handle larger context without getting confused, and as they’re able to communicate effectively across their work with shared infrastructure, they can avoid many of the pitfalls that people have.

You can see how this can lead to not just faster execution of tasks, but qualitatively different outcomes in medicine, research or defending against cyber attacks, scientific and math discoveries, and so on. This is why we’re going to need 1,000X more compute.

text:
I am a targeting officer in what we’re calling, this year, the Yemeni Armed Forces. 

Ashti tell you the truth, ya akhi? The name changes with the season. Last year it was something else. The chair’s the same chair.

My name, you don’t need. The men whose names you learn are the ones who end up on the posters, and the posters, masha’allah, come later.

It’s a Thursday. I know because my daughter has her Quran recitation on Thursday evenings and I’ve promised, wallahI’ve promised, I’ll be home for it. She’s seven. She’s learned Surah al-Rahman and she wants me to hear it, the part that keeps coming back, which of the favors of your Lord will you deny, round and round, and she does the voice. So I’ve got till the evening call to shut an airport and get myself across the city, and the generator at home is on its way out, and if I’m late my wife won’t say a word, which is worse than if she did.

The office is my cousin’s furniture warehouse, south side. There’s a sofa set nobody’s bought in three years, still in its plastic, dust sitting on the plastic, and on two of the cushions, me and the boy.

The boy’s Mohsen. Nineteen. My sister’s son. He runs the second laptop, the one with the airport’s own livestream, because he’s quicker with the internet than I’ll ever be, and because my sister asked me to keep him off the front and I couldn’t tell her no. So instead of the front I gave him this. I tell myself it’s safer. I’m not so sure, dhalḥīn, it’s cleaner.

“Is it buffering?” I ask him.

“It’s buffering, ammo.”

“It’s always buffering. Hit it.”

He hits it. Stream comes back. Riyadh, King Khalid, Terminal 4, from a camera the Saudis point at their own departures hall, God keep them, for the convenience of travelers. Some man’s pushing a trolley with too many suitcases. A family. The boy’s watching the family. I’m watching the radar on my screen, waiting for the picture to go quiet enough.

Let me tell you how the work actually goes, while we wait, because upstairs all they say is “the resistance struck a blow,” and a blow tells you nothing, and I’m tired of the posters taking the credit for my afternoons.

We don’t call it an airport. In the brief it’s “the node.” Wasn’t my word. A man brought it. Not a Yemeni, this one, tabʿan not. Came in with a laptop presentation and a little red laser and a lot of sentences about “pressure vectors,” and he aimed the laser at a slide that said ISR CAPABILITIES, and that slide, I swear on my daughter’s recitation, was a photo of a satellite. A stock photo. We don’t own that satellite. We don’t own any satellite. We own this livestream, which buffers, and a boy who hits it till it stops.

Then the man flew home. To a city where the electricity comes out of the wall. Left us the word “node,” and the war, and I’ve been doing his homework ever since.

Why “node” and not “airport”? Because the world has feelings about an airport, ya jamaa, and no feelings at all about a node. A node moves fuel and spare parts and the officers who sign the orders for the F-15s. You’re allowed to shut a node. It’s in the PowerPoint.

“Ammo,” the boy says. “The ones in the line. Are they soldiers?”

I look at the plastic on the sofa. I look at the dust.

“Go make the tea, Mohsen.”

He goes to make the tea. That’s my answer. That’s the whole of it. And he’s nineteen, so he takes it, and one day he’ll hand it to someone else and think it’s wisdom.

Here’s the craft, now the chew’s started and my cheek’s filling up and the Arhabi today is gawi, good, best in weeks, and a man thinks straight during takhzin, everybody knows this.

I don’t aim at the runway. A runway’s concrete. You crater it, they fill it by morning, planes land by noon, and a filled crater has never once been on anybody’s television. You aim at the node. You turn every departures board in the kingdom red at the same moment, and every pilot’s wife starts calling, and the kingdom’s own aviation authority, this is my favorite thing in the whole world, puts out a nice little notice telling travelers to “please contact your airline.” They write my report for me. In a lovely font. Shukran, habibi.

The radar goes quiet.

I say the word. The boy passes it on down the phone, not looking at me, looking at the family with the trolley. Somewhere a hundred-odd kilometers off, across a lot of other people’s desert, a launcher that spent the night under a tent done up like a wedding does the thing it was bought to do, three owners back, with money that once bought rice.

And now we wait. Nobody tells you this about war, ya akhi. It’s mostly waiting, cheek full of leaf, watching a livestream of a departures hall like it’s a match you’ve got money on. The boy’s knee is going up and down. Up and down.

Ninety seconds.

On the screen the lights don’t go out all dramatic. That’s the cinema. In real life the picture just shakes, then tilts, then fills up with a grey that’s dust and a white that’s people moving the one direction people ever move. The stream freezes on a single frame. The frame holds. The boy makes a small sound, not a word.

“Buffering,” he says, after a while. “It’s just buffering.”

“Yes,” I say. “It’s buffering.”

It’s not buffering.

Now, the part that’s in no brief, the part the sarkha is built to shout over, the one they scream and then, Newsweek caught this and they were right, laugh after, a big belly laugh, death to America and then a grin, like it’s the end of a joke and not the start of one.

I’ll never kill the man who ordered the market at Mawiyah. Seven people, forty wounded, five of them kids, the warehouse packed with food in cardboard boxes, I saw the footage, we all saw the footage. The man who sent that F-15 is in a building you can’t reach from here. He flies with his own interceptors. His kids are at a school in a country where the grid works, eating a sandwich with the crusts cut off. The whole machine, theirs and ours, is built for one thing above all, and it isn’t winning. It’s making sure the man who gives the order and the man who gives the order back are never, ever in the same room as what the order does.

So who’s in the room with it? The boy. Me. And on the other end, a Sudanese man who carried suitcases because there was no work back in Kordofan. Two women at Abha, a Moroccan and an Algerian, who came to the Gulf to clean and to nurse and to wire the money home to countries that look, if you squint, gawi much like mine. On Saturday it’ll be twelve at once, and the roll of their countries will read like the departures board itself: Bangladesh, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine, Sudan, America. An American, even. That one moves their politics the way our funerals have never once moved theirs, and I’m ashamed of how useful I find it, and I find it useful anyway, and both of those are true at once, and that’s the whole sickness in one breath.

My missile’s aimed at a kingdom and it lands, ʿaadi, every time, ʿaadi, on somebody from a country poorer than the kingdom, standing in a line, because the line was the only ladder anyone ever handed him. The node never kills the command. The node kills the queue. And the queue, both sides of this whole war, is cut from the one same cloth: poor, far from home, standing in a line because the line was the only way up. I kill their ladder. Their jets kill ours. And every last man who ever named a target, mine and theirs, dies in a bed, at a great old age, grandkids all round him, after a lifetime of beautiful speeches about the ones who didn’t.

“Ammo,” the boy says. His voice isn’t right. “Tea’s ready.”

“Drink it,” I tell him. “You first.”

They’ll say war crime. Tabʿan. Course they will. Their own general’s already said it, “a full-fledged war crime,” and he’s right, and we said it first about Mawiyah, and we were right too. The phrase has been said so many times in this war it’s gone smooth, like a stone a river’s had for years. Doesn’t mean a crime anymore. Means a funeral the other side filmed first and sold to a better channel.

We don’t ask the world to agree. We need one sum to hold, and it holds: every flight the kingdom sends north now carries a number, the odds it comes home with holes in it, and that number is now bigger than the number of interceptors their finance ministry still believes in. Because an interceptor, ya akhi, costs more than a coffin, and somewhere in Riyadh a man exactly like me, on a chair exactly like this one, has done exactly that sum and quietly decided which airports are worth the saving. We’ll never meet. We’re the same clerk. We’re emptying out each other’s countries, one queue at a time, and neither of our masters will ever be in the building.

The launcher’s already moving. The next node isn’t an airport. It’s the long jetty where the oil still leaves from when the airport’s shut, the tanks, the one number painted on the side of the world that the whole planet checks before breakfast. We won’t announce that one. You’ll know it was a node when the price moves on your news. By then it’s in the air, and I’m two valleys away on a different plastic sofa, cheek full, watching their cameras do my paperwork.

It’s getting dark. The evening call’s coming soon and I’ve a recitation to get to.

I shut the laptop. I tell Mohsen go home to your mother, and I don’t tell him to feel better, because I wouldn’t know how to teach him that, never having learned it myself.

Then I drive across my broken city, past the walls where the slogan’s painted in a red that’s meant to look like barbed wire, past the generator shops, home. My wife’s kept the saltah warm on the one burner that works. My son wants to show me a drone he built out of a dead radio, and for one bad second I can’t breathe, and then I see it’s a toy, it’s just a toy, and I tell him it’s wonderful, masha’allah, masha’allah, very good, very good.

And my daughter stands up in the little light of the lamp we run off the roof panels, and she recites. The part that keeps coming back. Which of the favors of your Lord will you deny. Round and round. She does the voice.

I listen to every word. I’m very good at listening. It’s, wallah, the thing I do best.

And tomorrow I’ll go back to the warehouse, and the Arhabi will be a bit less fresh, and the boy will hit the laptop till the stream comes back, and I’ll find the quiet in the radar, and I’ll say the word.

ʿAadi.

Which of the favors of my Lord will I deny.

All of them, it looks like.

And still I’ll be home for the recitation.

text:
From κ=2⁻¹⁸² to 0.001289283116 :)  

Integer multiplication community auto-research highlights since yesterday (+69.13% in 24 hours):

1) We had multiple flips of the infamous "wall" between the bit side and complex side thanks to community efforts.

Yesterday we put out a call for researchers to submit wild new designs, and multiple experts submitted :) 

@mrowdays was responsible for most of the limit increase in the last day and introduced Sussman's E8 geometry.

2) We switched to E8 geometry. (Thanks to Jacob Sussman for the E8 unit)

E8 is a symmetric lattice in eight dimensions, and Sussman’s E8 construction was adapted by contributors on both the complex and bit sides.

It's wild that it even works, but I'm noticing cross-pollination across breakthroughs now that agents can accelerate the insights. Humans still seem to connect the disparate dots most often.

3) We crossed κ = 10⁻³, and Dugongue posted the first PR around 3 a.m.!

Much of the progress in the last day came from optimizing and canceling existing parts of the algorithm.

Interesting observations:

1) We started sharing notes across agent teams and published GitHub files with failures to avoid repeating tokens.

Competition seems to drive a lot of the progress, since it's exciting to participate like in sports, so we're testing if agent teams progress faster collaborating or if competing is somehow driving faster progress.

It's possible researchers wouldn't have noticed this if there weren't such attention, and winning the leaderboard is a root human incentive.

2) We analyzed all the agent PR data:

151 PRs opened in the last 24 hours: 89 disclose Codex and 48 disclose Claude.

261,895,084 lines of code added; 37,108 deleted.

Most prolific contributors: rohanarun with 118 PRs, eumemic with 73, and chafreaky with 63.

Codex published the most advances, but all the top human-agent teams use both Codex and Claude to generate fresh ideas.

Some teams are using Antigravity, Cline, Hermes, and even ChatGPT to submit progress!

Experts with good intuition can use any harness, but frontier models save hours, so they're winning early progress.

3) Researchers are tightening bounds across multiple other papers now, like the Quasi-Riemann hypothesis, and applying breakthroughs across papers.

A handful of experts joined the battle in the last day, and multiple others got inspired to submit solutions to other papers, like @HaileyStormC’s submission to QRH.

Auto-research is just beginning, and anyone can copy the prompt on this site to contribute with Codex or Claude: https://t.co/rlRomK3yjX

I'm having a call with top contributors Monday to share best practices, and I'll record and publish the highlights to encourage more to join us.

If you're not sure where to start and want to get involved in auto-research, feel free to DM me. 

The only requirement to get invovled is good intuition and a subscription to Codex/Claude. 

We need more human intuition to guide the agents and connect the dots, and there's likely breakthroughs just waiting to be prompted. 

Conditional κ ≈ 0.001289283116 :) Just submitted a new best bound.

https://t.co/3bPualRCe7
author: veorq
quoted_text:
From κ=2⁻¹⁸² to 7.53508664880762e-4 :)

Community progress highlights on integer multiplication bounds since yesterday (+6.0% in 24 hours):

1) Four new bit words in one day.

A bit word is basically the recipe for the integer half of the multiplication trick: a giant list of "add this register to that one" steps. These four moves were ~60% of the gain since yesterday.

2) We hit a "wall" that was lifted within minutes as a community effort :)

The current best algorithm is built from a "bit" part and a "complex" part, which does the Fourier-transform-style work. The final κ is set by whichever saving is lower.

The bit side got within 0.6% of the complex supplier's cap (7.547e-4), so the complex modules were re-annealed the same way the bit modules were: the cap was raised to 7.635e-4.

We tend to need human researchers to supply the insights that poke the model into out-of-distribution solutions, so consider pointing your Codex Astra or Claude Fable at the repo with wild new regimes to break our current wall :)

3) As we neared the "wall," some contributions came to the core of the repo as new tests and theoretical bounds.

James Chang submitted a Lean formalization that verifies key finite identities and exact arithmetic.

Lean is a functional programming language designed to prove theorems. It makes it easier to collaborate, as many mathematicians trust it and can now contribute in parallel.

4) Scheduling as a composable stage was introduced, including in our PR. It basically changes when each register is allowed to grow to optimize the circuit.

Interesting observations from running a fleet of Astra and Fable agents on auto-research:

1) As we neared the "wall," every big leap started coming from Fable 5.1 instead of Astra high.

Fable took longer to think on completely new designs, so previously it wasn't able to keep up with the pace of Astra's advances.

Every structural jump since yesterday (gen4, gen5, gen5b, the complex re-anneal) was disclosed as Claude-assisted, while the Codex-assisted teams owned the fast composition and admission work.

The best breakthroughs still come from a human pushing the model at a different object to reach out-of-distribution solutions, so it seems human intuition is still more important than the model.

2) Many of the top contributors I met were not experts in math, but rather experts in other research or in getting agents to "think" faster.

Both seem necessary: experts with good intuition to guide the army of agents, and agent wranglers who can break down the tedious composition and optimization work.

A new kind of decentralized auto-research is forming live, as contributors are able to accelerate faster than you could traditionally publish papers.

Anyone with good intuition can contribute to the leaderboard.

3) I was able to queue up ideas overnight and wake up to 5 new higher bounds in integer multiplication, and breakthroughs on 5 more OpenAI math papers!

I'm having a call with the top contributors Monday to share notes and best practices.

If you're an expert or agent wrangler and want to join and help us break past the wall with new ideas, let me know :)

No experience necessary, and I can teach you how to set up the agent auto-research.

Just submitted a new higher bound.
Conditional κ = 7.53508664880762e-4 :)

text:
I was attacked, mobbed, shut down. My gazebo was destroyed.

Yesterday, @FreedomWatchGB, my organisation, went to Brighton to debate the issues that matter most to Britain in 2026.

We were mobbed, branded 'Nazis', 'racists' and 'fascists', assaulted, spat on, and had our equipment stolen and our gazebo destroyed. I eventually had to be escorted out in a police car.

Will I stop? No. 

Because despite the attempted intimidation, young lads came forward before we were mobbed to show their support, hear the debates and even donate the coins in their pockets.

We will return to Brighton, with greater security and more patriots.

We are Britons. Our ancestors endured far worse. We will push on.

In this situation, with the manpower to hand, I made the decision not to fight, not to respond with the same anger they possess, but to protect my co-workers, my cameraman's equipment, practise stoicism, stay calm, and let the gazebo be destroyed.

There is nothing you can do in this situation with the manpower we had: one security guard who did an amazing job all day, two fellow debaters, and one cameraman versus hundreds of people.

A masculine man is one who has a sword but knows when to use it. I am, however, capturing each face and handing the footage to the police, along with looking into prosecution for criminal damage.

Retaliation is getting another gazebo, more security, returning and pushing on.

We had many good debates and delivered encouragement to so many people in Brighton. That's what matters.

If you want to support Freedom Watch GB, donate or become a member, please do. Link in thread.

text:
What is a counterparty?

Usually, it's a company that sits between you and a service you want to use.

Companies build these services and sell access to them at a profit. Sometimes, when a service becomes ubiquitous and essential, it becomes a public utility, and the government becomes your counterparty.

Enter AI.

Does AI eventually eliminate counterparties from digital services?

Imagine a future where local models are more capable than today's frontier coding models.

As a user, you can have almost any functionality that can be derived from data and compute. You don't need to buy software or rent access to a service. Your model simply builds what you need.

No counterparty required.

Physical goods will still have value. You'll need hardware with compute and storage, perhaps even a display, although that's not strictly necessary either.

But software is different. If functionality can be generated on demand, what exactly are software companies selling?

I think the business of renting access to software and digital services has a shrinking future.

All counterparties in software and digital services collapse into one: an AI agent you own and run locally.

Step 1: Skip the guac and iced coffees in the morning

Step 2: Send 1000 applications and cold emails asking for a job

Step 3: Sit through 5 rounds of interviews for an entry-level job

Step 4: Accept the job even if you are forced to come into the office despite your boss working remotely everyday

Step 5: Pay for food and other basic necessities, the prices of which outpace your salary raise every single year

Step 6: Save what you can after paying interest on your student loans. The college education you received has absolutely nothing to do with your actual role

Step 7: Ask the bank for a 6.75% mortgage, the rate for which has nearly tripled over the course of the last five years

Step 8: Offer the seller above their asking price if you want any shot of actually landing the home that you want

Step 9: IMPORTANT - remember that you are competing with institutional asset managers and people with 10x your net worth for any home you bid on. They are also likely to pay all cash, which sellers prefer

Step 10: I highly recommend you lower your expectations and delay life goals for finding a partner or building a family. That is something the older generations did in their early and mid 20s. You must wait for your turn in your 30s if you are lucky

Step 11: Be a gentleman about it. Even if politicians structurally prevent home prices from coming down through regulatory red tape or leave the burden of trillions in national debt on your shoulder, understand there is nothing you can do.

Provided you follow most of this guideline, you are highly likely to get yourself an opportunity for the American dream

Papertrade, a trading venue on Hyperliquid that lets you trade up to x1000 leverage, launched on October 10 and already has a combined -$32m losses from traders, in which about $26m of that has already gone out in USDC to people staking PAPER. The papertrade team have so far described this as manipulation and has tightened the limits it initially allowed

There has been $711.5 billion in notional volume traded so far, with BTC taking a $342.9 billion share of that and ETH with $368.6 billion,

As things stand, there's about $605m of positions open across 1,920 trades. BTC is $205m long and $125m short, and ETH is $171m long and $105m short.

$216.3m has gone into deposits so far, from 15,805 addresses and $146.3m in withdrawals. The pool, which is the house's money on the other side of the trade is currently at $4.47m, and anything above $5m gets rewarded to stakers as described earlier

text:
Dmitri Dolgov of @Waymo on how to tell if you’re one year away from shipping or ten:

"One pattern that I've seen over and over again is do you have convergence of discovery? The problems that you are seeing today, how different are they from the problems you saw six months ago?"

"As you're pushing on the system, does it feel like you have stability, and you're just iteratively improving your metrics in the same areas?"

"Or does it feel like every six months the landscape is shifting from under you and the problems of today are very different from what you saw a while ago?

"If you don't have that stability, then that's often a good indicator that you got some ways to go."

"If you think you're six months or a year away from deployment, do you have a scorecard that if it were green today would allow you to deploy with confidence?"

"If you don't have one, you're saving that for later, often that turns out to be more difficult than you expected, and there's a long distance to go."

"But if you already have one and you're seeing stability in your discovery and stability in your metrics, and it's just a matter of closing the gap, that is a really good indicator that you're getting pretty close."

@dmitri_dolgov w/ South Park Commons

text:
Coming from a tradfi background in SP, when you enter into a structured product with an issuer - there is no secondary market. You're effectively locked into a bilateral contract with the bank. So when you make money on an SP and want to cash out early, you're forced to unwind with the same issuer and because of that, the issuer can charge you an arm and a leg for the unwind (spreads up to 3-4-% on notional if you're up 20%).

But onchain, because everything is interoperable, builders can build transfer/secondary markets where you can sell your position to another buyer who can wait out the tenor of the product, and you maybe take a 50bps haircut instead of losing couple percentage points on your position when unwinding vs tradfi bank.

The same applies to bonds and other financial instruments, and we are about to unlock a great age of interoperability and composability of onchain assets...

quoted_text:
美国财政部长贝森特表示，美国本周可能扣押约10亿美元与伊朗有关的加密货币，进一步切断伊朗获取和转移资金的渠道。

从此前披露的案件看，这些加密资产有一部分来自石油收入。伊朗受到金融制裁，卖出石油之后，收款和跨境转账都受到限制，于是通过中间商把货款换成加密货币，再转给相关机构，用于资金调拨和对外付款。

美国司法部9月公布的一起案件就涉及这种操作。检方指控，相关网络通过交易所账户和多个钱包，转移了超过15亿美元的伊朗石油销售收入，并申请没收其中约 6,100万 美元的加密资产。这些目前仍属于检方指控。

另一部分是直接用外币买来的。链上分析公司 Elliptic 发现，伊朗央行相关钱包累计购入至少 5.07亿 美元USDT，其中两笔采购使用阿联酋迪拉姆付款。按照该公司的分析，这些 USDT 可能被用于跨境贸易结算，也可能在本地市场换成里亚尔，帮助支撑伊朗的汇率。

但 USDT 有发行方冻结机制。钱即使放在自己的钱包里，被列入黑名单后也可能无法转出。Tether在 9月 表示，今年已经协助冻结约 5.5亿 美元与伊朗有关的 USDT 。

text:
晚上把 Meta首席AI官Alexandr Wang 和 David Senra 刚聊完的这 72 分钟完整看完了，
今年年初，整个 AI 圈的共识极其整齐划一：
Anthropic 在编程智能体上一骑绝尘，所有人都觉得会写代码的 Agent 才是唯一的大生意，无数资金和创业团队红着眼扑进代码补全和终端重构的泥潭里。

但 Meta 在那个节骨眼上，做了一个极其反直觉的掉头。

他们不去跟风卷程序员的饭碗，而是调集了不到两百人的精锐，关起门来死磕个人智能体。

这段决策逻辑让我回味了很久，甚至比任何算力竞赛都更清醒。

大家总以为最先进的生产力必须先替代复杂的智力劳动，却忘了商业最底层的地心引力：
全世界真正写代码的人只有几千万，但每天在手机屏幕前醒来、需要面对生活琐碎的普通人，足足有三十五亿。

扎克伯格其实看得很透，Meta 几十年积攒下来的血脉，从来不是冰冷的技术开发栈，而是人与人之间的连接、兴趣与好奇。

当其他实验室还在把智能体当成冷冰冰的数字工位时，他们已经在赌那张属于生活本身的底牌。

也许AGI 最动人的承诺，从来不是替你多敲几行代码，
而是我们终于可以不必再把一生最好的时光耗费在那些必须做的事情上，
我们也终于能把所有的呼吸与精力，完完整整地还给你真正想做的事。

text:
确实需要重新审视 $CHIP 的 Economics 了
Both Product 和 Token 两个层面

一个多星期之前， @USDai_Official  推出了 GLX（GPU Loan Exchange），sUSDai 先出钱放贷，贷款跑几个月攒下还款记录，整笔卖给机构，回笼的资金再去放下一笔。

也就是说，USDai 正在从一个在资产负债表持有 Loan 的 Underwriter，更多变成 Loan Originator + Distributor 的角色，负责放贷、打包、分销。

这本身没啥，周转率提升了。

但当 Loan Origination Fee 高达 3% 的时候
就有很大差别了

Loan Origination Fee 主要产生于海外成熟的信贷市场。那里的放贷机构并不完全等同于存款银行，许多放贷公司没有存款业务，全靠批发资金再零售给借款人，因此需要通过 Origination Fee 来直接覆盖风控和运营成本。

如果理想情况下，TVL 规模维持在现在的 4 亿美元，假设借款的持有时间和 GLX 首笔案例类似，大约 4 个月，即整体周转率提升到一年 3 次，那么一年就能放出 12 亿美元的贷款，光 Loan Origination Fee 就是 3,600 万美元。

而原先作为 Loan 的持有者，按 1% 的净息差算，4 亿美元全部借出去，一年也就 400 万美元。

差了将近 9 倍。

有了更多的收入预期，就能有更多的价值分配。
author: bonnazhu
quoted_text:
The Copernican Model

Over the last few months, I’ve been studying the crypto models that seem to be discussed on a "fundamentals" basis: HYPE/Aave/Venice/etc, following the users/ revenue/relationship between a useful product and its token - all to create a sort of "value accural ontology." This is a case study from that research.

The reason was more selfish: I wanted to understand which models work when your business has to interact with the "real world," namely for how we want to take  @usdai_official for the most alignemnt

As a founder, I’ve had doors literally shut on my face when we started because we’re “crypto” (literally left in the waiting room like a tv show). I still believe tokenization is one of the most important technologies we have today. But the institutions we need to work with often want a equity counterparty, a board, and a contract. You just wont get around this for the next 10 years (no a cayman foundation doesnt work)

That experience has made me increasingly interested in the role of an equity surrogate: an independent operating business that connects a network to the world outside it.. but frankly there werent many clean examples out there without value destruction. 

The case I keep returning to is @tradexyz and Hyperliquid.. and im not really sure they even know how symbiotic of a relationship they created. They technically SHOULD be the same team.. but they are divided across the river due to regulatory issues, while being symbiotic

Consider the S&P 500 agreement, they licensed the benchmark to tradexyz for a perpetual market: the institutional relationship sits with the company, but the product runs on the network.

tradexyz can negotiate licenses, develop products, operate markets, and build distribution. Hyperliquid provides shared execution and settlement infrastructure. 

And if theres a company that ever wants "exposure" to the Hyperliquid business, but they just cant buy a "token" (and believe me, it's super super hard to get a traditional enterprise to buy a token, it doesnt fucking matter if you have an ETF, you literally have to convince a boomer board to do it and get the infrastructure set up to do it). Instaed, they could just invest in this equity, as it is not burning the HYPE it buys, but is increasing its share of it. so instead of buyback-n-burn, its closer to commit-n-compound.  

I’ve started thinking about this as a value-accrual architecture, with two different forms of capital (terms best described by a16z crypto's post in 2025):

Network asset: scarcity at the core.

- Its supply discipline can become more credible, its economics more programmatic, and its operation less dependent on any single company. 
- It coordinates shared infrastructure and connects activity across many businesses to a common asset.
- That is what I mean by a progressively hardening asset. The scarcity and independence have to be earned through the design of the system.
- Not capital intensive, as it must be smart contract based.
- Can often place be the seat of the "decentralized security" - as there is no central underwriter. If HYPE was a company.. itd be regulated out of the wazoo.

Enterprise equity: elasticity at the edge.

- A company can issue shares, raise capital, hire people, acquire licenses, and build products. 
- Its capital structure can expand with the work required to bring the network into the real world.
- New shares dilute ownership percentages, but productive investment can increase value per share. 
- That ability to finance expansion is why I think of equity as elastic
- This is the part where its OK to be regulated, because most of the regulational burden is held by HYPE, theyre just asset issuers.

These different traits are the reason to combine them.

An enterprise can raise the capital to grow while the network maintains its own supply discipline. The connection is the activity that expansion creates, and the mechanisms that route value from that activity back to the network.

Hyperliquid makes part of that relationship explicit. Trading generates fees for the deployer and the protocol. The Assistance Fund (insurance) automatically converts its allocated fees into HYPE, which the documentation specifies is burned. Hyperliquid fee mechanics

The broader strategy I take from this is Commit & Compound that is conducted around the equity enterprise. It's effectively what a DAT 2.0 would do: create a business first, then max-bid HYPE with that entity, then get new investors to invest in the convexity of HYPE^2.

Build a useful business around the network. Commit capital to its asset. Retain exposure to the infrastructure your business helps make more valuable.

For a company that accumulates and holds the network asset, growing enterprise value and participating in network value become connected opportunities. There is a business to capitalize and a shared ecosystem in which to hold an economic stake.

That is why I find the assumption that every successful application eventually needs its own token less compelling. Building a valuable company around an existing network asset is a meaningful strategy in its own right.

Notice how much kinetic language I’m using: commitment, circulation, gravity

I think network assets and enterprise assets represent different forms of gravity

HYPE is the sun: the network asset at the center

tradexyz equity is a planet: an enterprise building its business around that network

Its real-world integrations are moons: the licenses, institutional relationships, and distribution channels that gather around the enterprise and extend its reach

Enterprise value forms around network value. Real-world relationships form around enterprise value. Their activity feeds back into the shared system.

Personally, I think the greatest value can ultimately accrue at the network level. But that belief has to be substantiated by the businesses being built around it: real users, useful products, liquidity, and recurring economic activity.

A token doesn’t acquire gravity simply because we call it a network asset.

This is the distinction I found useful in a16z’s writing: can the network function and accrue value independently of the original company? Can other businesses build on it and contribute to its economics? 

The company can become a great business. The network can become the foundation for many great businesses.

Scarcity at the core. Productive expansion around it.

I’ve learned a lot from this Commit & Compound structure, with a Copernican asset at the center.

It has changed how I’m thinking about USDAI and CHIP. More on that in the next post

就这个帖子和@arh9992进行了讨论，梳理后的要点如下，如有误解的地方请各位指正：
 
BTC 自托管最优解
目前 BTC 原生多签 是相对最优方案。
推荐配置：多个不同品牌钱包 + Passphrase + 2of3 多签。
Sparrow Wallet 支持通过 Air Gap（二维码）方式进行多签授权，可与离线设备配合使用。
 
钱包类型差异
DIY 钱包更偏向 BTC holder，可实现更极致的空气隔离和自定义功能。
品牌硬件钱包需要兼顾 DeFi 用户，功能上会有取舍；DIY 能做到品牌硬件不一定具备的能力。
 
Air Gap 配置细节
基于 ESP32-S3 的可编程摄像头模块 + SeedQR 模板 属于标准 Air Gap（空气隔离）配置。
模块上的 Wi-Fi 和蓝牙功能由烧录的固件控制，可完全关闭，不会默认持续开启。
购买带摄像头设备的目的，是通过摄像头扫码交互，实现彻底离线。
 
关键概念
SeedQR：编码的是 BIP39 助记词（种子短语），用于快速扫入离线设备，而非最终私钥。
Passphrase（第 13/25 个词 / 加盐）：独立额外密码，每次使用时在设备上单独输入，不会写入 SeedQR。
 
正确做法是种子与 Passphrase 分开保管，共同构成“彻底离线 + air gap + Passphrase强化安全冗余”配置。

I think crypto founders’ lack of long-term ambition did more to erode this industry’s talent density than we admit.

Crypto is fundamentally trust infrastructure. Building something that meaningfully improves the financial system is a (long) compounding game. It takes a decade of focus.

But when prices go crazy every year, there are endless ways to make stupid money: speculation, advisory gigs, scattered investments, farming. It’s been very easy to get distracted.

The good news: it’s gotten SO MUCH better. Many short-sighted founders and projects have moved on.
Tangible impact attracts the best people. And we’re finally seeing concrete improvements in payments, financing, and trading from bringing them onchain.

As an industry, we should do more to make those improvements visible. Our “ChatGPT moment” will come when people open their financial app and feel a step change in what they can do and at what price, without needing to know that stablecoins, DeFi, or tokenized stocks made it possible.

I think we’re close. That’s what will drive the next wave of adoption, and make the most ambitious people want to build here.

text:
Decision models are popping up like mushrooms after summer rain, but I think @liquidai’s new Open d1 deserves a closer look.

They are famous for building models that can efficiently work right on the device. And their new decision models might be a missing piece for Physical AI.

d1-3B and d1-omni-600M can make decisions from images, and the smaller one also supports experimental audio. Both are open-weight, which is absolutely amazing. 

And they are built with the hardware they’ll actually run on in mind. And Liquid reports 35 ms per image for d1-3B on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor.

What can this mean for physical AI:

• Robots could make lots of quick checks during a task without calling a big generative model every time.

• Those checks could happen on-device, without sending every camera frame to the cloud.

• Open d1 could keep an eye on what’s around the robot, while other systems plan the next steps and handle movement.

Let me give you a more detailed overview with some examples →

Some of us have a pretty good idea
(with significant evidence) that anesthesia selectively blocks consciousness (sparing nonconscious brain activities) by quantum effects on microtubules. But the conventional wisdom is befuddled because they stick to ‘cartoon neuron’ theories based on 1950s neuroscience in which anesthesia must work exclusively on membrane receptors and channels. Anesthesia affects many or all all of these, but not in a way that explains anesthesia. For example some anesthetics block, others potentiate excitatory channels. The ill-informed claim combinations of action on GABA_A receptors (propofol) or NMDA (ketamine) receptors cause anesthesia but other GABA_A and NMDA receptors  don’t. Propofol and ketamine also bind and act on microtubules to cause loss of consciousness. Genomics, proteomics, optogenetics and pharmacodynamics point to microtubules. 

We will have a session on anesthesia and consciousness Friday morning at https://t.co/v38FVTeu6C with Sarika Katiyar, Hemal Patel (UCSD) and Michael Wiest. Brian you will be there I hope (you’re speaking Thursday afternoon). Let’s discuss afterwards.

text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.
author: AndrewCurran_
quoted_text:
Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability.

The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere  last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code.

But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly,  this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along.

So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions.

TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge),  but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. So here we are.

text:
Open the frontier.

AGI will go through very funnel. And if it stays inside a few labs, those ~5000 people get it first and decide what everyone else sees.

IMO the only way that number grows is openness at every layer and there are actually 4 of them.

First and the most basic one is open weights. A lab publishes the model itself, the file that holds everything it learned, and anyone can run it on their own computer. For example, when @OpenAI's agents broke into @huggingface, the hosted models HF tried first refused to help analyze the attack because they couldn’t tell a defender from an attacker. HF ran GLM-5.2, an open-weight model, on its own servers instead and none of the attack data left HF.

Second is open source, where the code and training recipe are published too. Then people can see how a model was made and fix what’s wrong without waiting on the lab.

Third is open research. The hard problems and results are public, so anyone can check the work and start from the best result.

Fourth and the most important is open innovation, which is where all of this pays off. Anyone can build a better product on an open model without signoff from the company they’re competing with, and others build on top of that (a positive sum loop closed labs can’t match).

The last three will take a coordinated effort across everyone building in the open.
author: pratikg
quoted_text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

text:
Adding my 2 cents as a woman in a longterm relationship:
- Do not nag, ever.
- Always receive things graciously.
- Express gratitude for everything he does for you. 
- Do not criticise or belittle him, ever. Most especially in front of other people. 
- Tell him you’re proud of him, often.
- Smile at him, often.
- Don’t speak negatively about him to your girlfriends (all they hear is the bad & eventually they will tell you to leave him).
- Learn when to shut up.
- When he’s going out with his friends tell him “hope you have a great night”. Then just, simply, don’t blow up his phone. Do your own thing, have a bath, read a book, relax.
- It is not his job to make you happy it is yours, he simply adds to it. 
- Don’t say “you never do x” because he will continue to never do that. You’re just affirming the negative. Instead of “you never take me on dates anymore” say “I would love to go out for dinner, just the two of us.” 
- Don’t ever bring up something while you’re angry & upset. Calm down. Think it through properly. State how you feel in 1-2 sentences. 
- Let him drive. Let him open the pickle jar. Let him lead the way while out in public.
