text:
I built a really cool personal project to automate dealing specifically with refunds and customer service, got me and my friends about $22,000 back in the last 6 weeks from Delta, Uber. Verizon, Chase, and a landlord. Initially was thinking about opening it up to everyone but it’s expensive to run.

Started thinking about monetization and the same questions as @mignano’s post came up. A monthly sub? Pay per task? How much? Fixed or percentage? How do you charge after success since refunds go back to original payment method? First task free then pre-pay for the next task? Escrow an expected % and difference is returned? 

Then I realized maybe the user isn’t the customer at all. As compute costs go to 0, and they will eventually, charging customers for tokens will seem archaic. Agentic use case is also transforming the relationship between user and company rapidly. Companies built ai chat bots and service reps to deal with humans, now humans are also using personal assistants to talk back, which means customer service is becoming agent v agent. 

So for products like mine, at a certain adoption scale, it makes sense for the company to directly pay me to resolve the customer’s issues with their authorization and flatten the loop. Increasingly I believe this is where the internet will see its redesign and power structures transform.
author: sxtvik
quoted_text:
It’s pretty clear to me that the internet is headed toward a new business model that we may not have figured out yet. 

Consumers will increasingly outsource tasks to agents, and agents will work around the clock to execute them on their behalf. These tasks require inference spend.

The most obvious way to cover these costs is by passing them through to the user. Users pay a monthly subscription or simply pay for credits that get deducted as inference gets spent. 

But with the cost of inference dropping over time, this will ultimately be a race to the bottom. Pass-through pricing will get commoditized and won’t be able to sustain margins. So startups and incumbents will have no choice but to offer a different business model.

Paying for task-based outcomes is an obvious iteration. You can imagine customers paying agents when they achieve certain goals, such as successfully booking an appointment or executing a refund the user wouldn’t have taken care of on their own.

But most tasks aren't worth paying for one at a time. The most scaled business models on the internet let everyone participate, even when they can't pay directly. This is why advertising dominated as the primary business model of the past 30 years. 

Incumbents will subsidize usage dramatically over the next few years to onboard as many customers as possible. We’re already seeing this with Muse. 

But the question is, how will this work get paid for long-term? Can agents adopt a form of advertising that covers the cost? Or do we need a completely new model where the few big paid outcomes subsidize everyone else's usage?

We may be headed toward a new world of haves and have nots. Or a world of abundance where everyone can get anything done at any time for free.

text:
There has been a lot of talk about the recent XRP Ledger overflow bug. It was a serious vulnerability, but it’s also an example of responsible disclosure working. Researchers reported it privately, developers built a fix, and validators upgraded before any known exploitation on a public network.

The XRP Ledger’s account-based model lets you inspect every account’s XRP balance. Include XRP held in escrows and payment channels, which are also public, and you can audit holdings across the entire ledger. There isn’t some hidden place where newly created XRP could sit outside that accounting.

The XRP Ledger isn’t the only blockchain to have had this sort of vulnerability. Bitcoin had the same class of bug, an integer overflow, in 2010. Unlike the recent XRP Ledger vulnerability, Bitcoin’s bug *was* exploited, creating more than 184 billion BTC out of thin air.

Its developers, miners and node operators then had to coordinate a fix and reorganise the chain to remove the exploit.

Half a bitcoin in, 184 billion out
On 15 August 2010, Bitcoin block 74,638 included a transaction that spent just 0.5 BTC and produced two outputs of roughly 92.2 billion BTC each. Quite a lot for a system intended to have a maximum supply of 21 million.

Jeff Garzik flagged it on the Bitcoin forum in a thread titled “Strange block 74638”. The discussion is still available, and you can read people working through the incident as it unfolded.

The problem was in the arithmetic used to validate transactions.

Bitcoin stores amounts as whole numbers of satoshis, with 100 million satoshis to one BTC. The software checked that individual outputs weren’t negative, but it didn’t adequately check their upper limits or prevent overflow when adding them together.

A computer integer has a fixed amount of space. If a calculation exceeds what it can hold, it can overflow. In this case, adding two enormous positive values produced a negative total, which slipped through the checks intended to prevent a transaction spending more than its inputs.

Nobody had broken the cryptography or defeated proof of work. The software checking whether the money added up had got the answer wrong.

The recent XRP Ledger bug involved the same class of failure. A deliberately constructed payment could credit hundreds of offer owners their full XRP amounts, while the total charged to the buyer overflowed to a much smaller number. The difference would be newly created, spendable XRP.

Its “no XRP created” safety check also used arithmetic that could overflow in the same way. The fix added overflow checks and changed that safety check to use a wider counter.

Fixing Bitcoin meant *replacing accepted history*
Gavin Andresen posted an initial patch, and Satoshi Nakamoto followed with additional checks. A patch was committed within hours of the public discovery, with the fix released in Bitcoin version 0.3.10.

But the exploit transaction was already in a block, and miners were building on top of it. Fixing the software wouldn’t, by itself, remove the billions of BTC already accepted by the network.

Satoshi asked people to stop mining temporarily so there would be less affected history to replace. Upgraded participants rejected the bad block and built an alternative branch from before it, excluding the exploit.

For a while, two branches competed. Unpatched miners continued extending the affected branch, while upgraded miners extended the corrected one.

The corrected branch overtook the other at height 74,691 and became the accepted Bitcoin chain. The exploit transaction was excluded from that history, so the BTC it had created no longer existed on the accepted chain.

I think this is useful context for the current discussion. A supply limit written into a protocol still depends on software correctly checking every transaction.

Both networks had integer overflow vulnerabilities in the calculations intended to enforce their monetary rules. Bitcoin’s was exploited and required an emergency recovery and rewriting Bitcoin's history. The XRP Ledger’s was responsibly disclosed and fixed before any known public-network exploitation.

That doesn’t make the XRP Ledger bug less serious. It does mean the researchers who reported it and the operators who acted quickly deserve credit. Finding and fixing a critical vulnerability before it causes damage is exactly what we want a security programme to achieve.

I am absolutely crushed to learn of the passing of my old friend and trusted journalist confidant, Mark Stephens, known to the world as the legendary @RobertXCringely.

Throughout my career, I had the distinct privilege of serving as a trusted insider source for Mark. For decades, I provided him with the inside intelligence on companies and executives that fueled his iconic, must-read columns  at @InfoWorld.

His incisive writing shaped the industry narrative across Forbes, Newsweek, Success, The New York Times, Upside, and Worth. He also brought his unique perspective to the screen as Cringely in the landmark documentaries Triumph  of the Nerds (1996) and Nerds 2.0.1 (1998), as well as the PBS series Plane Crazy.

It feels profoundly fitting, yet bittersweet, that his "Spy vs. Spy" counterpart, the brilliant John C. Dvorak—my ride-or-die and godfather to my daughter—passed away only a few months earlier.

The history between them is the stuff of tech legend: Robert X. Cringely was listed as a field editor on the InfoWorld masthead just nine months before John left for PC Magazine. Three months later, the first Cringely column  appeared. Perhaps InfoWorld knew a legendary voice couldn't truly be replaced, and so a new icon was born.

The tech industry has lost two of its most brilliant, fiercely independent storytellers. They will be deeply missed. 🕊️💻

text:
I am a Director for Energy and Sanctions at the National Security Council.

On loan from Treasury, technically, which matters at performance-review time and at no other time. My desk is in the Eisenhower building, the wedding cake next to the White House, room with a radiator that has two settings: off, and Riyadh in August. I keep a fan going in October. This is the nerve center of the free world. The fan is from CVS.

You picture the Situation Room. The long table, the screens, the generals. I’ve been in it twice. Mostly I work from a cubicle with a government laptop that takes nine minutes to boot and a second monitor I had to fill out a form to get. Foreign policy, at my level, is a man refreshing Truth Social to find out what he’s about to have drafted.

Let me walk you through a Friday. Columbus Day weekend, so half the building’s already mentally in Rehoboth.

I’m at my desk eating the sad desk salad, the kind in the plastic clamshell from the place in the basement, $11.40, croutons optional, and I’m only half-watching the markets, when the President posts.

He’s just had a call with Putin. Hour and a half, I’ll learn later from the Kremlin readout, which I read to find out what my own President said, which is normal now, I don’t even flinch. He wished Putin a happy birthday. Belated. The birthday was Tuesday. Passed along regards from Melania. This is in the readout. This is in my reading, of my government, from theirs.

And the post says Russia will “immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace.” Then 500,000 more in November. Then a million “immediately thereafter.” Then, and I want you to feel the rhythm of a man who has never once been edited, “based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries,” another 3,000,000. All caps for the finish: “Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!”

My phone goes off before I’ve swallowed the crouton. Not from my boss. From a trader I went to grad school with, who makes four times what I make and texts me “lol is this real” at the exact moment I am learning it is my job to make it real.

Because here’s the thing nobody tells you about this building. The President doesn’t send me an instruction. The President sends a post. And the post becomes the instruction by the simple fact that it exists and 200 million people have seen it and crude just twitched. My job, from 1:40 to roughly 4, is to build the legal floor under a sentence that was already falling.

So I open the template. We have a template. Of course we have a template. It’s a Word doc with the formatting locked, and you fill in the CFR parts, and you write paragraph (a), the authorization, and paragraph (b), the carve-out, and the OFAC Director signs it, and that’s a sanctions regime being lifted, a thing people imagine happens in a vault and actually happens in Calibri 11 with the track changes off so nobody can see who softened “prohibited” into “authorized.”

General License 135. That’s the real number, by the way. The one hundred and thirty-fifth time we’ve carved a hole in our own wall. It authorizes Russian diesel transactions “through 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time, April 7, 2027.” I chose 12:01. You always choose 12:01. One minute past midnight, so that technically it’s a new day and nobody can say you did it in the dead of the old one.

Let me tell you about paragraph (b), because paragraph (b) is the only honest line in the whole document and I’m a little proud of it. Everything the deal gives away, it gives away in paragraph (a). Paragraph (b) is the one thing we kept: it says the license does not authorize any payment into the accounts of the Russian central bank, the National Wealth Fund, or their finance ministry. Read that again. The single asset the United States refused to hand over, in a document handing over the rest, was a line protecting the Kremlin’s own bank accounts from an accounting technicality. We didn’t protect the Ukrainians. We protected the plumbing. It’s beautiful. It’s in the file.

Now. The number I did not put anywhere near the President’s post.

The first two tranches, the 300 and the 500 thousand tons, come to about 6 million barrels. America burns through diesel at roughly 3.6 million barrels a day. So the great announcement, the COMING DOWN IN RECORD NUMBERS AND FAST, is about a day and a half of American trucks. A day and a half. Our own analysts flagged it. One of them, not ours, a commodities guy, told a reporter, “I cannot overstate how much of a nothing burger this is.” Another said it was “shuffling deck chairs on the Titanic.” I read both. I printed neither. The diesel was never going to move the price. The post moved the price, three cents, overnight, before a single barrel existed. That’s the most honest three cents in the American economy. We printed it. I printed it, in a locked Word template, between a salad and a 3pm sync.

Here’s the part I’m actually good at, and I want credit for it even though my name will never be on anything, which is the whole design of the job.

For months the price had been climbing, and it was climbing because the Ukrainians were doing exactly what we spent three years and a mountain of money begging them to do. They were hitting Russian refineries. A refinery every three days, this summer. Russia’s diesel exports fell off a cliff. Moscow had to ban its own diesel exports in July because there wasn’t enough to go around at home. It was working. It was the single most effective thing in the entire war against Putin’s budget.

And every burning refinery was a cent on a sign at a Shell station in Evergreen, Colorado, and every cent on that sign was a question the President did not want shouted at him in Syracuse, where he was flying that very night to campaign. Diesel is in everything. It hauls the lettuce, it runs the combine, it moves the Amazon box. Diesel at six-twenty-eight a gallon isn’t an energy story, it’s a grocery story, and a grocery story four weeks before the midterms is a loaded gun with the President’s own numbers on it.

So we told them to stop. Not in writing, yallah, never in writing, you think I was born yesterday. You tell them in a resort in Miami, where Witkoff keeps a club, while their delegation is sitting across the table believing they’ve come to talk about a sixty-day ceasefire. You have the envoy and the son-in-law explain, gently, over whatever Miami serves, that the President wants the refinery strikes stopped and is, as it happens, “preparing to allow Russia to sell its diesel.” You don’t say “or else.” Saying “or else” is for amateurs and movies. You let them do the subtraction. They’re clever people. They did it while the coffee was still warm.

And watch what that sentence actually does, because this is the craft, this is the whole job in one move. The Ukrainians’ best card, the one weapon genuinely bleeding Russia, their ability to make Russian diesel expensive, we don’t defeat it. We can’t defeat it; it’s working too well. So instead we reclassify it. We price it into our midterms, and then we take it out of their hands, and then we call the removal a peace process. Their leverage doesn’t die on a battlefield. It gets moved onto our balance sheet and labeled “market stabilization.” One sentence, three channels, no fingerprints. The President got his three cents. Putin, a week after saying out loud he wouldn’t ship a drop until sanctions came off, got his sanctions off. Eight days. I looked it up. Eight days between “no diesel until you lift them” and me lifting them, in Calibri, at 12:01.

The timing was the part I’ll take to my grave, quietly, the way you do. The license dropped the same afternoon the Ukrainians were in the room. They flew to Florida to trade their last chip and found out, from their phones, from a Truth Social post, same as me, same as the trader, that the chip had already been cashed. That morning. By us. For the other side. Their president called it “a weak decision of strong partners.” I thought that was generous. It wasn’t weak. It was the strongest thing we did all quarter. It just wasn’t aimed where he was looking.

The President, for his part, suggested the Ukrainians “get a new leader.” Then he got on the plane to Syracuse.

And here’s the engineering that lets me sleep, in my apartment in Pentagon City, next to a woman who has stopped asking what I did today because the honest answer frightens us both. The arrangement does not require anyone to agree. It requires only that one side needs the price more than the other side needs the story to stay the same. If Russia hits the Ukrainian grid tonight, and they will, it’s winter, that’s their whole plan, we have a sentence: the Ukrainians provoked it. If Ukraine hits a refinery tonight, we have a sentence: they chose higher prices for American families. Both sentences are drafted. Both are in the folder, in a subfolder, named something boring on purpose. The ceasefire the President announced on Sunday, “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE,” which the Ukrainian president learned about, his words, as “news for me,” and which the Kremlin has not confirmed and which Russian drones were violating before the ink dried, that’s not an agreement. It’s a word with two pre-written exits, and I hold both doors.

Does it help Putin? Habibi, of course it helps Putin. His September oil revenue was down twenty-two percent. He was in a real fiscal hole, the kind that ends wars. And we reached in and handed him back the ladder, a high-margin export channel, right as the squeeze was finally closing. “Helps Putin” is a phrase for the Sunday shows. In my building it’s “market stabilization measure,” and the measure moves a swing county in Pennsylvania, and a swing county in Pennsylvania is a national security interest the way a day and a half of diesel is a peace plan.

The license can be closed in an afternoon. I know, because I can close it in an afternoon. One document, track changes off, paragraph (a) swings shut, and the price climbs again, and we find someone convenient to blame that week. That’s the quiet power of the thing, the real power, not the kind in the Situation Room. The war is almost impossible to end. The sentence about the war is extremely easy to rewrite. We have decided, as a government, to keep rewriting the sentence.

It’s getting dark over the EEOB. The cleaning crew comes through, a woman named Rosa who I only know is named Rosa because it’s on the lanyard, and she empties my bin with the sad salad clamshell in it and the printout of the “nothing burger” quote that I did, in the end, print and then throw away, and she says have a good night, hon, and I say you too, and she has no idea she just emptied the trash on a Russian sanctions regime. Neither did I, at 1:40. You learn these things from a phone, same as everyone.

I’ve already started the next draft. The contingency for when the price starts climbing again, because it will, because a day and a half of diesel was never going to hold it against a war with Iran and the Strait of Hormuz. The draft narrows the license, reassigns the blame, protects the post. Two pages. The war it’s about is in its fourth winter.

The President will read it, when the time comes, as if he thought of it. He always does. That’s the job. I draft the sentence; he becomes the author; the price moves; Rosa empties the bin.

And somewhere a Ukrainian grid operator is about to have a very long night, and somewhere a trucker in Evergreen is looking at a sign, and neither of them will ever know my name, which is the point, which was always the point.

I get the metro home. The diesel buses idle out front. I don’t think about it. You can’t do this job and think about it. You do the needful and you catch the Blue Line and you let the President be the author.

That’s the job.

quoted_text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

text:
In a normal functioning ecosystem, when the price of tokens drops below the cost of production, the quantity of tokens declines to normalize with pricing. In this case, nothing in AI has any unit economics and you don’t see normalization because everyone is still going full-speed ahead with external funding. (Sort of like shale oil in 2016-2019). Meanwhile, compute prices are based on LT contracts that were signed at above market prices, and are now capital destructive. They’ll eventually catch down to token prices in free-fall.

What we’re seeing here is spot price negatively diverging from term pricing. Usually, when this happens in a cyclical industry, it’s INCREDIBLY BEARISH. Especially when there are take-or-pay contracts that make it difficult to ration supply at prices below cost. What we’re witnessing is a world where losses will accelerate, just as more supply comes online….

text:
Andrej Karpathy 说，人们对 AI 能力的理解差距在扩大，这种认知差距正在变成一个漏斗。

约 60 亿人几乎没接触过大模型；10 亿到 20 亿人偶尔用免费版 ChatGPT 查东西、写东西，觉得用处不大，很多数学和编程以外的专业人士也在这一层，对 AI 的进步只是道理上懂。

约 2000 万人（Karpathy 按 0.2% 估算的，我觉得偏高，至少除以 10）在编程和数学里重度使用最前沿的模型，亲眼看着要做几周、几个月的项目，一段提示词发给 Agent 几天就能做完；还有约 5000 人能在公司内部用上更强的系统。

差距主要有三个原因：

一是问题够不够大，一段话就能答完的问题用不到 AI 的真本事。

二是能力只在部分领域冒尖：编程和数学的结果能自动验证，比如代码测试通没通过，模型很适合用强化学习（做对了就给奖励）来练，这类能力卖给企业又最赚钱，厂商投入最多；文章写得好不好很难判定，进步就慢。

三是能用到哪一档，免费版、付费版、内部版看到的东西差别很大。

所以，如果你只偶尔问问免费的聊天机器人，看到的离最前沿差了好几层；如果你主要拿 AI 写东西、查资料，觉得这一年没怎么进步，这个感觉也没错。

text:
Andrej Karpathy’s point: Many people only use AI occasionally for search or writing and see little value in their daily lives. Even many professionals understand its progress mainly in theory. 

People using advanced models extensively for coding and math experience huge capability gains, widening the gap in how people perceive AI.

And this impression has been confirmed here in Paris during my trip. When I talk to people, I realize they're completely unaware of how capable AI already is. They're unaware of the possibilities it offers. They haven't heard that OpenAI solved a Millennium Prize problem, or recently solved 372 math problems, some of which had remained unsolved for decades.

Currently, we're living in an ivory tower.

text:
He will not cast you out.

If you are not trusting Jesus Christ for your salvation - hear what He has already said.

“All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out”. 

The invitation is not for the cleaned-up. It is for the one who comes. He does not say he will review your record and decide. He says he will never cast out the one who comes to him. Your past is not the obstacle you think it is. Refusing to come is.

The world will not make this easy. Jesus told his own, “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16). Trouble is promised. So is his victory. 

You do not have to defeat sin, death, and judgment before you can come. He already has. You come to the one who overcame, not to a life you must first fix.

And the victory is not a slogan. It is a finished work. He bore the sin. He broke the grave. He disarmed the powers. Death no longer has the last word over those who are his, and neither does the accuser. 

“Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ”

In him you are not fighting for a win that is still in doubt. You are joining a King who has already won. Tribulation remains. The outcome does not. 

Take heart: He has overcome the world, and everyone who comes to Him shares that victory.

He is not in a hurry to slam the door. “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance” (2 Peter 3). The delay you feel is patience, not indifference. He wants repentance, not destruction. That patience will not last forever. It is open now.

So come. Not when you feel worthy. Not after you have improved. Come to Christ as you are, and trust him - his death for your sins, his life for your righteousness, his promise never to cast you out. He overcame the world. 

The victory is His, and He gives it to all who are His. He is patient today. Whoever comes, He will never cast out.

author: emollick
quoted_text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

author: chintanturakhia
quoted_text:
We started running "pirate and architect" pods at Coinbase back in May of this year and I used this slide to talk the team through it. It works.

1 pirate, 1 architect, and a part-time designer.

It lets each archetype lean in to their superpower and get more shit done without all the coordination overhead and "what if-isms". 

The pirate ships like mad, is product-minded and customer-obsessed. Always willing to throw-away code for a better version. The pirate is usually the DRI at the beginning too, working with customers, driving requirements, and a ship plan.

The architect makes sure stuff is built for scale, takes the pirate's prototype, and drives its scale-out through spec for agents.

The designer is building with both to constantly shape the experience and hill-climb to delight. 

There's a helpful mental model that I like:
-Make it possible. 
-Make it reliable. 
-Make it delightful (or efficient).

Previously, those 3 were done in a waterfall approach and was slow. Most people were just stuck on "make it possible." 

With agents and a new way of working, you have every opportunity to parallelize them and go 100x faster.

text:
We were able to fine tune an open weight model (Qwen3.5-9B) on proprietary internal data at @coinbase, and it out performed frontier models, at much lower cost and speed, for a specialized task (fraud prevention in this case).

I think we'll see more of this pattern inside companies. The frontier models are amazing generalists. But increasingly you'll see specialist models out perform on more narrow tasks, either working on teams, or by themselves.

We're making it easy to fine tune models internally for our employees. We even have a skill for it in our internal harness that makes it easy to spin these up and start training them:

"/fine-tune-and-serve-llm I want to fine-tune Qwen for payments risk review. help me get started"

I imagine we'll have some backend services that could be replaced entirely by this new architecture.

author: elonmusk
quoted_text:
Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability.

The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere  last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code.

But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly,  this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along.

So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions.

TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge),  but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. So here we are.

author: garrytan
quoted_text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

An update on what we have been working on in the last few days. 

The compliance and operations team has been replying to affected users. PDPC and relevant authorities has been informed, and a police report has been made. We are working closely with law enforcement on the card data breach incident. 

Card operations continue working as per normal. 

Our trading wallet and app is not affected by this. The wallet is self-custodial and we do not host the keys. 
Social logins are managed by Privy. You can continue to trade with Based. 

We've seen questions about an admin dashboard said to have leaked five months ago. That said “admin dashboard” is separate from our card operations and is not related to the card incident. It held no customer data. It was part of an early developer build of a managed OpenClaw product we prototyped in March 2026. We tested it with a small internal group, decided not to release it, and discontinued it shortly after.

Based has grown to where we are through various growth strategies. Hyperliquid lists a few example of frontends, but it’s ultimately the team’a responsibility to grow market share via their own means. We will continue to accelerate our growth via marketing in different channels.

For now our priority is to:

1. Continue to address and provide support for affected customers in data breach;
2. Further tightening security controls within team and enhancing monitoring;
3. Continue to build the best trading experience for our traders

author: dotey
quoted_text:
REA：让 AI 智能体帮你逆向没有源码的软件

开源项目 REA（Reverse Engineer Anything）把逆向分析工具接到了 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor 这类 AI 编程智能体上。看到别人 App 里有个好功能，可以让智能体去拆这个程序，讲清楚功能是怎么实现的，附上证据，再在你自己的项目里写一个类似的。逆向分析指的是手里没有源代码，从编译好的程序反推它是怎么写的。

REA 本身是一个 MCP 服务。MCP 是 AI 智能体调用外部工具的通用接口，接上以后，智能体在对话里就能直接调用 REA 的分析功能。安装只需一行命令 npx rea-agents setup，它会注册到 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor、Gemini CLI、Grok Build 等智能体里，改配置前会先备份并让你确认。不用智能体的话，也可以在终端里直接跑命令。

能分析的东西很多。原生程序（直接编译成机器码的软件）要借助 Hopper、Ghidra 或 IDA 这几款反汇编工具，把机器码还原成汇编和近似 C 语言的伪代码。Electron 应用（用网页技术做的桌面软件，比如 Notion）可以直接拆开安装包里的 ASAR 归档文件，理清模块和进程间通信，不需要额外工具。此外还支持 .NET 程序、安卓 APK、固件、网站、抓包记录、以太坊合约字节码，以及在 Linux 和 macOS 上记录程序运行时的行为。

分析在本机进行，REA 不上传目标程序，但分析结果会交给智能体背后的模型服务商，数据怎么处理看各家政策。

项目给了三个案例。一是经典打砖块游戏 DX-Ball：从一次播放音效的调用，追到根据球的位置计算左右声道的函数，把不完整的伪代码还原成 C 代码，3205 组测试结果和原版一致，编译出的 63 个字节也和原版完全相同。二是 Notion 桌面版：追踪复制粘贴从界面一路经过预加载脚本、进程间通信到主进程的完整链路。三是日本老电脑 PC-98 上的游戏《东方幻想乡》（TH04）：从 16 位指令里还原出弹幕子弹环的角度算法。

对安全研究员、做老游戏复刻和软件保存的人来说，以前要自己对着反汇编工具一行行读、一层层追调用，现在可以让智能体先追，人来核对它给出的证据。普通开发者想研究竞品某个功能的做法，也多了一条路。

README 显示项目在 GitHub 上已有 5 万星。npm 包今年 7 月首次发布，最新的 6.3.0 版今天刚发。

使用前注意两点。项目声明只支持合法的逆向研究，授权和合规由使用者自己负责，逆向别人的软件可能违反用户协议或版权法规。项目还说明从未发行或背书任何加密货币，借用 REA 名字的代币都与它无关。

🇺🇸 Seven senators, including four Republicans, say Trump's Russian diesel deal breaks the law

Sens. Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal, Ron Wyden, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis said Sunday that Trump's decision to allow Russian diesel imports "runs directly counter" to a 2022 law banning Russian energy imports until Moscow ends its war on Ukraine. They said the administration never consulted Congress or explained its decision, as the law requires.

Trump announced the deal Friday after a call with Putin, saying Russia would release more than 35 million barrels of diesel to the US and global markets to bring down fuel prices, which have soared since the US-Israeli war on Iran. Energy experts say the amount is too small to have a meaningful impact on record diesel prices. "The Administration must immediately reverse course," the senators said.

text:
医疗行业的英伟达可能已经出现了！ $LLY  礼来，这家拥有150年历史的制药公司，正在创造过去传统医药行业很少见的增长速度。最新季度营收暴增48%，毛利率达到85.8%，而真正推动这一切的，竟然主要是两款药！

2026年第二季度，礼来营收达到229.74亿美元，同比增长48%，净利润约71亿美元。公司甚至将全年营收预期提高到了850亿—870亿美元。

最恐怖的是旗下两款核心产品。

Mounjaro：单季度营收99.43亿美元，同比增长91%，主要用于治疗2型糖尿病。

Zepbound：单季度营收49.28亿美元，同比增长46%，主要用于体重管理及相关获批适应症。

两款产品合计贡献将近149亿美元，占礼来季度营收约65%！

为什么我认为礼来值得长期研究？因为减肥药正在从一个细分医疗市场，发展成全球大型制药企业最重要的增长领域之一。糖尿病、肥胖及其相关并发症涉及庞大的潜在患者群体，随着治疗方案改善和支付覆盖扩大，市场空间可能继续增长。

更重要的是，礼来并没有停留在现有产品上。

2026年，公司已经在美国推出口服减肥药Foundayo，同时下一代三靶点药物Retatrutide在多项三期临床试验中取得积极结果，计划于2027年第一季度向FDA提交上市申请。

这意味着礼来正在形成从现有注射药物、口服产品到下一代创新药的完整产品梯队。

但它也并非没有风险。诺和诺德等竞争对手正在加速研发，医保支付和药品降价可能影响利润率，研发失败与产能扩张也存在成本压力。

尤其值得注意的是，礼来最新季度产品销量增长60%，但实际销售价格下降13%。这说明需求强劲，不代表未来药价可以无限上涨。

我认为礼来最值得关注的地方，与$NVDA有某种相似之处：两家公司都站在高速增长的产业需求中心，同时拥有技术、规模和产品生态优势。

但优秀公司未必对应便宜的股价。未来礼来真正需要证明的，是现有产品增长和下一代药物能否持续创造超过市场预期的利润。

text:
Google 面试开始允许用 AI 了

Google 正在试点一种新的软件工程师面试：候选人拿到一段现成的代码，可以开着 Gemini 一起读代码、找 bug、做优化。面试官要看的是你会不会用 AI，以及能不能看出 AI 哪里答错了。

最早是 Business Insider 在今年 5 月披露的，依据是一份 Google 内部文件。Google 发言人向 Business Insider 确认，试点期间的 AI 助手就是 Gemini。负责招聘的副总裁 Brian Ong 说，Google 一直在调整面试流程，这次试点是为了让面试更贴近团队在 AI 时代的实际工作方式。

这一轮叫“代码理解”（Code Comprehension）。以往的编码面试，是在在线编辑器里从零写一道算法题，也就是程序员常说的“刷 LeetCode”。新的这一轮反过来，给你一段别人写的代码，让你读懂、调试、优化。内部文件写明，面试官会评估候选人的“AI 熟练度”，包括怎么写提示词、怎么检验 AI 的输出、怎么调试。

试点范围不大：只针对初级到中级岗位，只在美国的部分团队，最先参与的是 Google Cloud 和平台与设备部门，计划从今年下半年开始，效果好再推广到更多团队和地区。同一批改动里，原本以行为问题为主的“Googleyness 与领导力”轮会加一段技术设计讨论，聊候选人做过的项目；初级候选人还会多一轮开放式的工程问题。

网上流传的不少细节目前没有可靠出处，比如：
- “200 到 500 行的陌生代码库”
- “在 CoderPad 里做题”
- “限时 60 分钟”
- “替代了一轮传统编码题”
- “要求先独立调试再用 AI”。

这些说法来自社交媒体和面试培训网站的文章，Google 没有公开确认，Business Insider 的报道里也没有。截图里说“5 月试点”也不准确，5 月是消息曝光的时间，试点安排在下半年。报道也没说算法题会被取消，“告别 LeetCode”言过其实。

去年已有报道称 Meta 在试点类似的允许用 AI 的编码面试，大厂面试在往同一个方向调整。

对准备 Google 面试的人来说，算法题照样要练，但得多补一项能力：拿到一段陌生代码，能很快理清它在干什么、哪里有问题；让 AI 帮忙时，能判断它给的答案对不对。这也是很多程序员现在每天在做的事，读懂并修改别人写的代码，其中越来越多出自 AI。

WE’RE BACK TO BUILDING

For some time now, we have taken a step back from shipping publicly. That was intentional. After completing all our KPIs for the @0xIntuition Cohort 1 Grant 4 months ago, we spent time reflecting on how we could be better and where we wanted to take things next. We wanted a powerful product that would solve a real problem.

We had a direction, but we knew it needed to deliver a stronger and more sustainable value. Being a gateway into an ecosystem isn’t enough. You need the systems that turn discovery into long-term, meaningful interaction between projects and the people who discover them.

So, we took a step back to rethink how far Nexura could go beyond its original vision. We wanted a long-term vision that takes Nexura beyond engagement and builds lasting relationships between projects and their communities.

After taking the time to rethink our direction and work through what comes next, we’re happy to say that we now have a clear long-term vision, and we’re ready to start building towards it. And we’re coming back with a lot to build toward.

WHAT'S CHANGING?

Our new long term vision comes with a new direction, as well as a lot of changes to the current in-app design. Some of the colors you’re already accustomed to will also change.

We are making changes across Nexura to bring the product closer to the bigger vision we have been working on behind the scenes. We’ve been redesigning the app, starting with the Nexura Studio. We've completely resigned and upgraded the Studio. The other parts will start soon.

Over the coming weeks, you’ll start seeing these changes roll out across the Nexura app. We will be shipping consistently again and, this time, we’ll be keeping the community much more involved along the way.

Expect more updates, changes, and more communication from the team as we continue turning this vision into reality. 
We also ask for more patience, as we will be redesigning and redeveloping the entire product, including the underlying infrastructure.

We know the community has been waiting patiently, and we really appreciate everyone who continued to stick with Nexura during this period.

We appreciate your patience and your belief in us. Not just from using the app on a daily basis, but also from contributing to our different community events. Thank you for your patience. It tells us that we have a community that is focused on our goals with us. Thank you for continuing to contribute, and thank you for believing in what we’re building.

author: Altimor
quoted_text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

text:
Acyclical Shocks, Not Wages, Are Keeping US Inflation Above 2% Target

The San Francisco Fed's decomposition of core PCE shows that acyclical components, those driven by industry-specific or structural factors rather than the broader business cycle, are primarily responsible for keeping inflation elevated. 

Natixis economists Hodge and Aker cite this framework directly: cyclical components, which respond to monetary policy, are trending down, while acyclical components, sensitive to tariffs and energy shocks, are doing most of the lifting.

Hiking rates compresses cyclical price pressures. It does not address acyclical ones. If the SF Fed decomposition is right, additional tightening has limited marginal impact on the components currently holding inflation above target.

We're making it easy to fine tune models internally for our employees. We even have a skill for it in our internal harness that makes it easy to spin these up and start training them:

I imagine we'll have some backend services that could be replaced entirely by this new architecture.

text:
codebases have always contained slop. we have always been okay with this because code rarely needs to be perfect, outside of mission critical "hard" (eg embedded) software. 

swe is a unique form of engineering because you're often building something that constantly evolves and is almost organic - user tastes change, your mental models evolve, and features come and go.

admittedly, i and many others who've been coding for a long time were initially (like back in 2024) skeptical that agents would write production code. "but what about all the slop that would enter our beautiful codebase?". 

well, even before, we had human slop, and there was a lot of it! if we're being truthful, most people call "code i didn't write" slop. the reality is that 99% of people (i include myself in that number) don't even know what Good Code looks like, let alone be capable of writing it. i would propose that Good Code is:

• correct
• bug free
• fast and cost efficient to run

it has always been exceedingly difficult and expensive to write truly Good Code, because for the longest time (maybe @bendlang will change that), code was not something you could cheaply and formally guarantee to have all 3 of these properties. this is why writing hard software is much more difficult and expensive, because depending on the use case, you may only get one chance and so you have to be right from the start.

but the vast majority of software we use does not need to be Good Code to provide value to users. in fact, it is very likely that most software we use is not formally verifiable! we accepted some bugs in exchange for velocity and progress, so we rely on tests and o11y instead and have adopted a more incremental approach. this is a good thing! 

agents help us move faster, and if you're open to the idea, are capable of helping us write better code. it won't be Good Code (that is still expensive), but it is likely to be much better on average at scale. 

the new craft of swe is to figure out how to do this. it's your job now! if your productivity with and without agents is not significantly different, you're doing something wrong. but it's not too late to embrace it and use it as an opportunity to learn a whole new skill tree

author: HarryStebbings
quoted_text:
Podcasts frustrate me because they are fluffy and high-level.

This is the most in-depth discussion on the framework that @tryramp have used to hire, monitor, and scale their sales team.

- Why you should overpay reps

- Why you should cancel forecasting calls

- Why bankers make the best reps

- Why comp plans are BS and you should not have one to start

@max11free, SVP of Sales is truly epic here and my notes from the discussion below.

-- 

1. Why You Should Overpay Your Sales Reps

The early bet was to pay SDRs well above market rate and expect output well above market in return. Reps earn 2X a standard SDR but book 40, 50 or 60 meetings, four to six times the usual target, so the unit economics still work.

2. You Have to Treat Hiring a Sales Team Like Moneyball: How to Find Hidden Talent

Go-to-market recruiting should follow Billy Beane, targeting top sellers at companies that grew revenue past nine figures despite a low NPS score. Those reps had to create their own demand, work complex cycles with weak third-party reviews and sell at a premium to cheaper rivals. The number one or two seller there can thrive in a system like Ramp.

Single biggest advice on finding hidden gem talent @rabois?

3. Why Bankers Make Great Sales Reps

Bankers are programmed to work, and a nine-to-five is foreign to them. Before the company had brand recognition, a cold call to a CFO from someone who had just left Goldman TMT IB carried weight. Early sales teams lack time to teach cold call and email basics, so bankers kept the team in pure execution mode.

Find this also @PeetsChad

4. Why I Advise Not to Have a Comp Plan

Founders are advised to pay 100% OTE for at least the first two quarters instead of setting a comp plan. A quota set too low can be blown out in six months, leaving the company owing a seller multiple six figures. A target picked arbitrarily can also prove unattainable and stall momentum.

Haha, interested to hear your thoughts on this one @Carles_Reina 

5. Never Hire Sales Reps One at a Time

Hiring one seller or SDR at a time leaves no way to benchmark performance, and comparing them against the founder is not reasonable. Onboarding is laborious and expensive, so hiring in pairs is better, bringing competition and collaboration and keeping reps from being lonely.

6. Why the Most Annoying Sales Reps Tend to Be the Most Successful

Sellers who constantly ask about account strategy, pipeline and product during onboarding show a direct correlation with being incredible. Quiet reps, or those asking questions an AI or Notion bot could answer, usually give a weak signal, though the inverse is not always true.

7. What Should Sales Talent Focus on When Deciding Which Company to Join?

Sellers joining an early-stage company should not index on equity, cash and comp, but on the market, the talent density of the business and the founders. Taking a VP title and lots of equity at a mediocre business growing 20 to 30% a year is the wrong trade.

Biggest advice to talent on choosing which company to join @breeves08

再過幾個小時，就是 1011 一週年了。

我永遠忘不了那一天。

兩個很好的朋友，在那天之後永久退圈了。

一個回去接家業，一個重新回去上班。

兩個人都曾經在這個市場拿過大結果，照理說早就該上岸了，最後卻以這樣的方式離開了市場。

我自己其實沒有受到太大的損失。

因為當時 CK 數據已經顯示市場過熱，我原本沒有持有任何槓桿倉位。

唯一的例外，是睡前看了一下比特幣的支撐位，手動在下方掛了一筆小額逐倉槓桿多單。

這筆單成交後，短短一個小時內就被清算，損失了 4 萬多美元。

公司的量化策略當時也空手，完全沒有受到影響。

但我永遠記得，那天打開山寨幣線圖時的震撼。

很多幣的走勢，已經完全超出我對市場的認知。

論整體市值跌幅的慘烈程度，1011 可能還比不上當年的 312。

但論市場混亂程度、流動性枯竭，以及離岸交易所與法幣交易所之間誇張的價格偏離，絕對是 Crypto 歷史上最極端的一次。

做了這麼多年交易，我一直以為自己已經見識過 Crypto 市場各種荒謬的行情。但 1011 還是讓我開了眼界。

更讓我難以接受的是，即便一年過去了，我們能拼湊出的資訊依然非常片面。

究竟發生了什麼事？為什麼不同交易所之間會出現如此誇張的價格偏離？又是哪些環節出了問題？

直到今天，仍然沒有一個足以讓人信服的完整解釋。

Crypto 這個產業聚集了無數優秀的人才，走到今天，我認為我們值得一個更透明、更成熟的市場。

在這種極端事件發生之後，市場參與者有權知道自己究竟經歷了什麼。

我們不應該永遠只能面對一個黑盒子，然後被要求接受所有結果。

或許多年之後，事情的真相會在某個人的回憶錄中，被輕描淡寫地提起。

但對那些在那一夜付出慘痛代價的人來說，答案不該來得那麼晚。

那些荒謬的 K 線，如今回頭看都已經成了歷史資料。

但對某些人來說，那一天真的永久改變了他們的人生。

text:
This 2024 paper I coauthored with @skominers and other friends on the next phase of the data economy anticipated much of the shift we’re seeing:
https://t.co/ZBJdBAkVJ4

Individual agency + data liquidity - enabled by personal agents.

Muse and Instinct are delivering on the agency side: acting on people’s behalf and removing friction. But portable, user-controlled personal context is still early. For now, it’s mostly permissioned access across services

The value capture models are taking shape too: free tiers, subscriptions and proposed transaction take rates…
author: skominers
quoted_text:
It’s pretty clear to me that the internet is headed toward a new business model that we may not have figured out yet. 

Consumers will increasingly outsource tasks to agents, and agents will work around the clock to execute them on their behalf. These tasks require inference spend.

The most obvious way to cover these costs is by passing them through to the user. Users pay a monthly subscription or simply pay for credits that get deducted as inference gets spent. 

But with the cost of inference dropping over time, this will ultimately be a race to the bottom. Pass-through pricing will get commoditized and won’t be able to sustain margins. So startups and incumbents will have no choice but to offer a different business model.

Paying for task-based outcomes is an obvious iteration. You can imagine customers paying agents when they achieve certain goals, such as successfully booking an appointment or executing a refund the user wouldn’t have taken care of on their own.

But most tasks aren't worth paying for one at a time. The most scaled business models on the internet let everyone participate, even when they can't pay directly. This is why advertising dominated as the primary business model of the past 30 years. 

Incumbents will subsidize usage dramatically over the next few years to onboard as many customers as possible. We’re already seeing this with Muse. 

But the question is, how will this work get paid for long-term? Can agents adopt a form of advertising that covers the cost? Or do we need a completely new model where the few big paid outcomes subsidize everyone else's usage?

We may be headed toward a new world of haves and have nots. Or a world of abundance where everyone can get anything done at any time for free.

text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.
author: Altimor
quoted_text:
Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability.

The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere  last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code.

But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly,  this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along.

So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions.

TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge),  but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. So here we are.

今晚币圈最疯狂的赌场开业了：MIT量化+链上巨鲸操刀，1000倍杠杆、亏钱挖矿，1小时交易量突破1000亿美元！

Papertrade上线约1小时，成交量突破1020亿美元，未平仓合约93.5亿美元，TVL约1.2亿美元。

平台根本就不需要任何初始做市资金，所有用户都跟协议对赌，用户亏得越多，协议的流动性池反而越大，亏损者还能拿到 PAPER，分享未来交易平台的收益。

创始人 Jez（@izebel_eth），2015年毕业于 MIT，学的是计算机与管理科学，后来在摩根士丹利工作了4年，还曾担任加密风投 Standard Crypto 的 Venture Partner，个人投资项目包括 FOMO、neutrl 等。

他还是一名扑克高手，2024年参加世界扑克巡回赛 WPT Prime Championship，最终拿到第7名，奖金18.6万美元。量化交易、VC投资、职业级扑克竞技经验，基本把金融市场、风险定价和博弈论凑齐了。

另一位创始人 Blurr（@blurr）更偏链上原生玩家，2017年前后进入 Crypto，经历过 CryptoKitties、Compound、Curve 等早期链上机会，还曾部署过 Refund（$RFD）。

Papertrade 的交易设计非常激进。它部署在 HyperEVM，利用预编译合约直接读取 Hyperliquid 订单簿买一卖一的中间价，以此合成 BTC、ETH 永续仓位，实际不会去 Hyperliquid 开对冲仓，所以没有传统资金费率、盘口滑点和点差。

听起来像免费交易，但盈利平仓会受到非对称收益折减，尤其针对极小价格波动的套利收益抽得更重。这套逻辑明显吸收了 Rollbit 的高杠杆赌场模型，只不过把定价、仓位和盈亏结算搬到了链上。

最有创造性的地方是 Martingaler 流动性自举机制。传统赌场必须先准备一大笔本金，才能赔付赢家。Papertrade 的 LP 从0美元启动，输家的亏损直接补充资金池。

如果庄家只有500万美元，而赢家需要领取600万美元盈利，协议可以先支付500万美元，剩余100万美元进入 FIFO 债务队列，等待未来交易者亏损后逐步偿还。

它用未来的亏损现金流解决初始资金不足的问题，但这笔债务不会凭空消失，极端情况下赢家可能长期拿不到全部利润。

再看 $PAPER，代币经济学才是这套设计的核心。没有预挖、没有团队和 VC 分配、没有空投，只有真实发生交易亏损或清算，才能铸造代币。

LP 追踪余额低于200万美元时，每亏损1美元最多按基础规则铸造100枚 PAPER，超过门槛后按照衰减曲线降低发行速度。

PAPER 质押者可以领取协议分配的 USDC 收益，当 LP 超过500万美元的目标余额后，超出部分的新增收益按机制分配给质押者。

PAPER 已发行约14.9亿枚，其中13.7亿枚被质押，累计质押奖励约24.8万美元。

Papertrade 可能是今年 Hyperliquid 生态最激进的一次交易所经济模型实验。它把做市商的收益、赌场的庄家优势和 DeFi 的代币激励揉进了同一个系统，甚至把普通交易者的亏损变成了协议融资手段。

author: socrates1024
quoted_text:
The sovereign AI stack for the future:

Compute - an always-on box you control. At home (something like @voravault) or a confidential VM in the cloud. Reachable over your own overlay network (e.g. @Tailscale).
Data + memory - everything personal lives on that box. A memory layer like Hindsight (@Vectorizeio) makes it better over time. If you use external AI services, have them continually update your memory.
Inference - local for small/sensitive work, open-weight models in attested TEEs (e.g. @near_ai) for heavy lifting. Nobody reads your prompts.
Agent - an always-on runtime that acts for you (e.g. Hermes by @NousResearch).
Software - apps generated for you by AI, hosted on your server, thrown away when done. No subscriptions. Seamless interoperability, since they can all talk to each other.
Money - stablecoins to pay for inference and services.
Exit - open formats and open source. Encrypted backups. Restore anywhere, leave any time.

author: businessbarista
quoted_text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

quoted_text:
Honestly, I sold most of my spot crypto and offboarded today. It's just not worth the headache.

I don't want to check every single headline about AI math and cryptography research wondering if I'm about to get rugged. I don't want to wonder if every ancient BTC address making a transfer is ECDSA being cracked.

I had already refocused most of my time and energy on equities at this point, and Justin Drake's post just killed the rest of my desire to hold crypto. This isn't impulsive, I read hours of counterarguments. 

1. People say this is incredibly unlikely. I just don't trust any human to predict the capability ceiling of superhuman mathematical AI. Have seen people be wrong about AI capability ceiling over and over. 

2. What if I miss the next great bull cycle? Honestly, that's fine, there's plenty of other assets to trade with less stress of existential left tail risk.

3. People say that we would have bigger problems. Yes, I know that banks etc would also be at risk and society would be a clusterfuck, but the government should step in to save my money (and society) at that point. I don't know that they will for crypto. Plus, why would a malicious practitioner rather burn the whole world down over just stealing infinite crypto?

4. People say this is just like Quantum FUD. Nah, this is much more concrete and near term. This doesn't require a new scientific breakthrough, only the continued march of AI progress that we've been scaling on for years.

I got into crypto as a techno optimist but there's other investment expressions of that now. The development of AI (and recently the intersection of bio x AI) is more intellectually interesting to me. Being in crypto feels like being short AI progress, and I do not want to be short AI progress.

This is not investment advice, everyone should decide for themselves how they feel about the topic. I am just one random human being on the internet, expressing my thoughts.

text:
okay now that we're past that tired discussion, let's talk about how we get agents to write more correct code (note: this won't mean the code will be Good, but it should at least work)

this is the entrypoint into your most basic agentic loop: verification. it means giving your agent the ability to verify its own work, most commonly by actually running and interacting with it like a real user would. whether your interface is a cli/api/ui/whatever, you want to start here so that your agents can close the loop. if you want you can even have your agents model the problem in TLA+ and attempt to verify if you have things like state machine bugs.

the point is to give yourself confidence in the agents' work by them producing some kind of artifact that proves that 1) that the work is correct, 2) that it matches what you intended, and 3) is easier to review than reading the whole PR. most commonly this would be a video and/or screenshots for UI work.

everything else like skill packs are really bonus and optional, all you need is a way for your agents to verify their own work to start using them more autonomously. some caveats are that not all domains can be verified easily yet, and that verification is just approximation and can still be wrong. it's no different than trusting that a human actually ran the code they wrote and trusting it

so start here!

text:
I've been thinking about this a lot. I think the problem is that modern/contemporary art has divorced "good" from "obviously good."

A lot of classic poetry is both "good" AND "obviously good." Take "Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night" by Dylan Thomas, or "Ozymandias" by Percy Bysshe Shelley. Both are celebrated by the literary elite, but even the common man can appreciate their craftsmanship.

On the other hand, consider Rothko: maybe his work is "good," but it's certainly not "obviously good." Many laypeople are completely baffled by it. "What's so great about THAT? I could have painted that!"

(And for "obviously good" but not "good," perhaps Thomas Kinkade, Bob Ross, or Marcello Barenghi.)

And this Carson poem is the most extreme case. She was awarded the Nobel--maximally good--and yet it reads like complete hokum--maximally not obvious. Even the least sophisticated person could concede that at least Rothko uses pleasing colors, but with this it feels like there's nothing. We're just taking the literati at their word: "trust us bro, this is fire."

The outcome of this constraint is many more small clusters. To turn non-IG credit into IG, you need diversification. That’s the alchemy that unlocks large swaths of capital. Not 1bn to one borrower, 1bn to 100 borrowers. Then you can forget the Nvidia backstops and ig wrappers, and turn GPUs into a standalone financable asset class. Standardization is what makes ai legible to Wall Street. 

The parallel constraint in the power market is already pushing us towards 2-5mw deployments instead of 250mw. Both of these forces will be positive for the sustainability of the industry, as small deployments with a couple of month lead time can better match supply to actual, current demand, reducing the risk of overbuilding. 

Ironically, over time we might even see these smaller deals pricing similarly to larger ig deployments, despite worse credit, as the project complexity becomes a major tradeoff if there is an abs market to sell into.

现在 AI 可能把类似的数学突破再来一遍，甚至连被寄予厚望的抗量子格密码，也可能因为新算法而降低实际安全性。

前几天，以太坊研究员 Justin Drake 就警告，AI 可能抢在量子计算机之前，找到破解 ECDSA 的方法，甚至呼吁行业提前准备防御模式。

V 神甚至表示，没有 AI，以太坊现在规划的 Lean 路线图可能要到 2040 年甚至 2050 年才能实现。

过去币圈担心量子计算机破解私钥，现在 AI 数学家可能更早带来冲击。

quoted_text:

卧槽，OpenAI 这次公开的数学仓库，影响可能远远超出 AI 圈。

以太坊基金会核心研究员 Justin Drake 直接向整个加密行业发出警告：

保护比特币、以太坊等加密资产的椭圆曲线密码学，可能在量子计算机成熟之前，就被 AI 找到破解方法。

他甚至提出了一种极端情况：最快几个月内，攻击者可能只需要大型 GPU 集群运行一周，就能从公钥反推出私钥。

我们一直以为，只要助记词不泄露、硬件钱包不被攻破，资产就安全了。

但如果 AI 找到了破解底层密码算法的数学捷径，黑客可能根本不需要碰你的设备，只要拿到已经暴露的公钥，就有机会算出私钥。

交易所冷钱包、巨鲸地址、机构托管，以及大量依赖椭圆曲线签名的链上基础设施，都可能面临风险。

所以 Drake 呼吁整个行业开始准备进入钱包防御模式，说白了，就是大户和机构先把大部分资产有序转移到公钥尚未暴露的新地址，尽量减少旧公钥暴露带来的风险。

以后每次签名，也考虑更换地址。

他还点名 Binance、Robinhood、Bitfinex、Tether 等机构，呼吁提前加强防护。

不过，不同链和地址类型的保护机制并不相同，这套办法也无法替代真正的抗攻击密码学升级。

这一切的导火索，就是 OpenAI 公开的 722 篇数学手稿。

它让 Drake 开始认真考虑一个过去看起来很遥远的风险：

AI 可能突然发现人类几十年都没有找到的数学捷径，让原本需要天文数字计算量的密码学难题，变得可以被普通计算集群攻破。

不过目前没有证据证明 ECDSA 已被攻破，Drake 所说的几个月也只是极端风险推演，大家千万不要恐慌性转账。

但我觉得，所有加密圈的人都应该认真看待这次警告。

以前大家担心量子计算机会不会攻破比特币，现在连 AI 都成了必须考虑的潜在威胁。

加密行业可能需要提前为一场尚未发生的密码学危机做准备了。

那些说 AI 对自己没什么用的人，很多时候并没有说错，他们的生活里确实没有一个需要动用这种能力的问题。这不是他们的问题，而是这个时代悄悄换了一道考题：从你能做什么，变成了你想做什么。
