author: indigox
quoted_text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

author: DanielMiessler
quoted_text:
# on shortification of "learning"

There are a lot of videos on YouTube/TikTok etc. that give the appearance of education, but if you look closely they are really just entertainment. This is very convenient for everyone involved : the people watching enjoy thinking they are learning (but actually they are just having fun). The people creating this content also enjoy it because fun has a much larger audience, fame and revenue. But as far as learning goes, this is a trap. This content is an epsilon away from watching the Bachelorette. It's like snacking on those "Garden Veggie Straws", which feel like you're eating healthy vegetables until you look at the ingredients.

Learning is not supposed to be fun. It doesn't have to be actively not fun either, but the primary feeling should be that of effort. It should look a lot less like that "10 minute full body" workout from your local digital media creator and a lot more like a serious session at the gym. You want the mental equivalent of sweating. It's not that the quickie doesn't do anything, it's just that it is wildly suboptimal if you actually care to learn.

I find it helpful to explicitly declare your intent up front as a sharp, binary variable in your mind. If you are consuming content: are you trying to be entertained or are you trying to learn? And if you are creating content: are you trying to entertain or are you trying to teach? You'll go down a different path in each case. Attempts to seek the stuff in between actually clamp to zero.

So for those who actually want to learn. Unless you are trying to learn something narrow and specific, close those tabs with quick blog posts. Close those tabs of "Learn XYZ in 10 minutes". Consider the opportunity cost of snacking and seek the meal - the textbooks, docs, papers, manuals, longform. Allocate a 4 hour window. Don't just read, take notes, re-read, re-phrase, process, manipulate, learn.

And for those actually trying to educate, please consider writing/recording longform, designed for someone to get "sweaty", especially in today's era of quantity over quality. Give someone a real workout. This is what I aspire to in my own educational work too. My audience will decrease. The ones that remain might not even like it. But at least we'll learn something.

quoted_text:
The recent XRP Ledger security fix raised a lot of questions and some misconceptions. Let's clear them up.

1. Was any XRP created?

No. XRP's supply was fixed at 100 billion when the XRP Ledger launched, and no transaction is allowed to create more. This bug was a way around that rule, and 3.4.1 fixed it 2 weeks ago.

You don't need to trust us on this. All ledger data is public, and explorers and data sites read it every day. New XRP would show up in account balances for everyone to see. There is no hidden place for XRP on the XRP Ledger, every balance is public.

We monitor the XRP Ledger 24/7 and have verified the supply throughout the history of the ledger. Others in the community verified this too, and anyone can do the same.

Transaction fees are destroyed, so the supply is deflationary. About 99.986 billion XRP exist today.

2. How did this go unnoticed, and what's next?

No normal payment comes anywhere near triggering it. It took hundreds of deliberately constructed operations.

AI makes bugs like this faster to find, for the bad guys and the good guys. 

Together with RippleX and the community, we will ensure the XRP Ledger is protected against such vulnerabilities. This means radically applying Formal Verification and AI adversarial testing, collaborating closely with security researchers, and strengthening the bug bounty program.

You'll hear a lot more about this as we progress.

3. XRP Ledger decentralization at the core of this.

A public fix shows attackers where the bug is, and AI makes that fast. With a normal amendment vote, the fix would have been public for weeks before it took effect, risking network security.

As a reaction to this, the XRPL community came together, and among them the XRP Ledger Foundation, RippleX, core devs and validators formed a social consensus and agreed on a path forward that involves shipping the fix directly. Patching a live network is never trivial, so the plan was also designed to minimize disruption for everyone running on it.

We shared the build with the default UNL validators, using the contact details each one publishes in its xrp-ledger.toml file. Public binaries followed the same day, September 25.

No single party could make that call alone. Every validator and node operator chooses what software to run, and 3.4.1 only became required through a normal amendment vote with more than 80% validator support for two weeks. Protocol changes still go through amendments.

Big thanks to Cayden Liao and Veria AI for finding and reporting this responsibly, to the XRPL core developers for building and testing the fix, and to every node operator who upgraded so quickly, especially the validators.

author: DanielMiessler
quoted_text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

text:
Be the 60% spouse.

The person you marry is one of the most important decisions in your life. You will spend more time with this person than anyone else. You will make decisions together, grow together, and raise children together. If you choose the right person to marry, your life will be filled with happiness and prosperity, but if you choose the wrong person, you will be condemned to a life of unhappiness, drama, and financial problems.

But choosing the right spouse is only half the battle.

A good marriage is not created on your wedding day. It comes from the constant work that you and your spouse do to be a good partner to each other over time. Because the word “partner” gets used often when speaking about marriage, most people think a husband and wife should each bring 50% of the value to the relationship.

A happy marriage isn’t 50/50 though. It is 60/40 with both partners trying to be the 60%.

When you and your spouse are trying to bring the extra effort to the relationship, it is nearly impossible for the marriage to get off course. This is especially important on the hard days when one of you is tired, annoyed, or angry.

My wife and I have seen the benefits of this principle over the years. She constantly looks out for me, tries to predict things I may need in the future, is always ready with a few words of encouragement at the right moment, and does whatever is necessary for our marriage and our family to be successful.

I do my absolute best to return the favor. Sometimes this extra effort can be small things like buying her flowers unexpectedly, surprising her with a date night, or doing a few extra chores around the house. Other times I may help with her professional work or spend time talking with her about the important things going on in her world. Whenever I see an opportunity to do something that will make me the 60% of the relationship, I try to seize it.

And the beauty of our marriage is that she does the same thing.

So my wish for each of you is that you find a spouse that has a similar approach to marriage. But here is the secret: you will only find this person if you first become the type of person who aspires to be the 60% in a relationship. It is this lack of selfishness that will attract the person who is a good partner you can build an amazing life with.

The 60% approach applies to any relationship you are a part of, including business, investing, or your personal life. Those who give the most tend to get the most. It is a powerful law of the universe. But nowhere is it more important than in your marriage.

As you get older, and you have been married for longer, life starts to happen. There is the complexity of managing chaotic schedules, children become more needy, and it is easy to be less intentional about your marriage as you focus on other things.

But don’t fall into this trap.

Be the 60% spouse. Go the extra mile, and you will pick your head up in 50 years and be proud of the incredible relationship you built with the person you love most.

This is an excerpt from my new book, How To Live An Extraordinary Life Volume 2. You can buy a copy of the book here: https://t.co/KW3fShJkON

quoted_text:
Bending Spoons is worth $24 billion.

It trades at 8x ARR and buys B2B companies at 2.3x to 2.7x ARR.

5 learnings from its first 102 days as a public company:

#1. Revenue grew 126%. Organic growth was 3%.

Nearly all of the $393M of added revenue in Q2 came from six acquisitions. The CEO says he doesn't optimize for organic growth. He optimizes for EPS, which grew 167%.

#2. R&D is 8% of revenue. Sales and marketing is 10%.

HubSpot and Datadog each spend about 70% of revenue on those two lines. Bending Spoons spends 18.6%. About 60 people run Vimeo. The core team is under 700 people, at $4M+ of revenue each.

#3. Miro sold at 2.3x ARR, five weeks after Airtable at 2.7x.

$1.08B of ARR for $2.64B, signed 37 days apart. Miro was valued at $17.5B in 2022. Bending Spoons underwrites to a 25% unlevered return. At its 54% margin, that supports about 2.2x ARR.

#4. 1,830 people came with AOL, Eventbrite and Vimeo. Only a few hundred were kept.

Airtable arrived with 935 employees, more than Bending Spoons’ entire core team. Reorganization costs were $51M in Q2 alone.

#5. AI writes 90%+ of the code. Customers pay about 10% more for the AI features.

The CEO says a customer who paid 100 will now pay about 110. The AI gain shows up as capacity: the same 60 people on a business four times the size.

If you're at $300M to $800M in ARR growing under 25%, this is the buyer most likely to at least call.  But ... the only do a handful of deals a year.

Its own stock trades at roughly 7x to 8x revenue. Your revenue is worth about 3x more inside Bending Spoons than it is in your hands.

author: sinavaziri
quoted_text:
Brothers Karamazov was Einstein’s favorite novel, a verdict he shared with Freud, Hillary Clinton, and Murakami. Dostoyevsky was Pope Francis’s favorite author. Indeed, he approvingly quoted Elder Zosima; perhaps an interesting case of art molding life. At the risk of betraying my relative shallowness and inferiority, I confess that I did not love it.

Written in the shadow of the death of Dostoyevsky’s son (also Alyosha), and, more broadly, after a life of repeated tragedy, Karamazov attempts most of all to address the problem of evil in Christianity. Ivan presents a trenchant argument, asking how the suffering of children may possibly be explained given the existence of a supposedly benevolent God (Dostoyevsky collected real court cases for Ivan), culminating in Ivan’s famous return of the ticket.

The book gives some sense for how dislocating the nineteenth century must have been. The ascendant authority of science, the spread of materialist philosophy, the doctrine of evolution, the aftermath of the French revolution and its supposedly enlightened empiricism: in Karamazov, we get the feeling that finding some kind of consilience wasn’t just an abstract philosophical challenge, but a source of intense spiritual torment. If inherited tradition is no longer an adequate basis for faith, why would we rationally cleave to an apparently irrational theology? All of this was in the air: it was only two years later that Nietzsche declared God to be dead.

Perhaps demonstrating the utility of the novel as a medium, Dostoyevsky does not even attempt to solve the problem, but merely to illustrate a response, showing how individuals (Alyosha, Elder Zosima) may in the face of the inherent injustice present in the world nonetheless pursue lives of benevolence and charity: theodicy-by-example. In so doing, Dostoyevsky tacitly concedes that none of the teetering justifications expounded over the centuries can actually survive critical pressure and be defended through pure logic.

Ultimately, though, I don’t find myself being fully compelled by Dostoyevsky’s characterization of the problem or his proposed solution. As another sprawling confrontation with and attempt to reconcile the problem of evil, Grossman’s Life and Fate is maybe a useful counterpoint. Unlike Karamazov, Life and Fate shows actual people confronting great wickedness. Ikonnikov, a small but important figure, is ordered to help in the construction of a gas chamber. He refuses, with full awareness of the consequences that will ensue. The Karamazovs, by contrast, live middle class lives unvisited by greater events. Ivan has money, education, and leisure; his torment is the invention of his own mind and thus a kind of self-indulgence. Even Alyosha, the novel’s most sympathetic character, is never tested. His crisis is spiritual: there is a slightly comic kerfuffle about Zosima’s noisome corpse, which challenges his faith, but no circumstance requires him to stake his life or even his comfort.

Thus, a fundamental issue with Karamazov is that the problems of the book are on some level fake: they’re the self-inflicted derangements of febrile and dysregulated men. How much can or should we learn from the insane?

To be charitable to Dostoyevsky, we might say that he understood the spiritual dislocation of the era that later gives rise to the larger evils of totalitarianism in the twentieth, even prefiguring them in the Grand Inquisitor. (Dostoyevsky explored this theme in greater detail a few years earlier in Demons.) Camus in 1959: “The real nineteenth century prophet was Dostoevsky, not Karl Marx.” In this interpretation, the problems in Karamazov set the stage for those in Life and Fate.

Maybe. At least as a work of art, I’m not sure that this anticipation is enough to make the book stand on its own. In Karamazov, one continually wonders why the brothers don’t just pull it together. Dostoyevsky seems to transpose his own inner depths and spiritual torment onto his characters, but most people are not tortured writers, and it does not feel that the unhingedness of the characters is ever fully earned.

In attempting to address evil, Grossman’s conclusion is ostensibly similar to Dostoyevsky’s: the only resolution lies in senseless kindness. For Dostoyevsky, this message is embodied in Alyosha, who represents a kind of fervent innocence. For me, however, it’s not clear that Alyosha ever fathoms the realities and extremities of evil, and hence he’s not fully persuasive: does he even reckon with the misdeeds of his brothers?

Grossman is willing to engage head on. Far beyond gruesome newspaper anecdotes or neurotic and volatile siblings, Ikonnikov directly experiences the Holodomor in Ukraine and then the murders of the Jews. He has no patience for the kind of revolutionary ideas that animated Ivan’s contemporaries: “whenever we see [the dawn of an eternal good], the blood of old people and children is always shed.”

Alyosha believes in the Church and is willing to set aside its failures to address suffering. The book closes on his declaration that all shall rise again. That is, Alyosha does not accept the tragedy of Ilyusha, an innocent boy’s death, but rather seeks to deny and escape it. “We shall see each other and shall tell each other with joy and gladness all that has happened.”

Life and Fate flatly rejects providential resolution. The heavens may be empty, and there is no greater meaning in evil. We can simply choose (freedom the other great theme of Life and Fate) to pursue acts of charity, generosity, and comfort:

“Yes, as well as this terrible Good with a capital ‘G’, there is everyday human kindness. The kindness of an old woman carrying a piece of bread to a prisoner, the kindness of a soldier allowing a wounded enemy to drink from his water-flask, the kindness of youth towards age, the kindness of a peasant hiding an old Jew in his loft. The kindness of a prison guard who risks his own liberty to pass on letters written by a prisoner not to his ideological comrades, but to his wife and mother.”

These acts don’t ennoble the suffering but are instead justified on their own terms. Such altruism cannot become a catechism, as clearly lies in Alyosha’s destiny (and Karamazov was planned before Dostoyevsky's death as the first of two works); instead, our kindness must be senseless. And we should presume no salvation in adherence: Alyosha imagines a kind of sacred tutelage, but Ikonnikov is unceremoniously shot.

Karamazov doesn’t show true evil, and Dostoyevsky’s solution, such as it is, involves a kind of denial, or at least evasion through metaphysics. Grossman saw it directly, and instead argues, humanistically, that we should be kind just because.

—

If Dostoyevsky came to his works by trying to understand and depict Russian society, they in turn became tapestries for others to understand national souls.

In the aftermath of WWI, Russia was the great power defined in opposition to the West. As Germany tried to rediscover its own soul in the wreckage of defeat, it looked east to Russia, and frequently to Dostoyevsky himself.

Carl Jung thought that the German people had a kind of Karamazovian quality. In particular, he believed that Christianity had disciplined them without fully transforming the impulses beneath their ostensibly civilized conduct: the “Germanic barbarian” was divided into upper and lower halves. Religion had domesticated the former while leaving the latter untamed. Waning faith consequently threatened to release forces that its authority had long restrained: “As the Christian view of the world loses its authority, the more menacingly will the ‘blond beast’ be heard prowling about in its underground prison, ready at any moment to burst out with devastating consequences. When this happens in the individual it brings about a psychological revolution, but it can also take a social form.”

Dostoyevsky was reputedly invoked on a weekly basis at Max Weber’s Sunday gatherings. At the beginning of Reflections of a Nonpolitical Man, Thomas Mann’s later-repudiated 1918 nationalist polemic, he quotes approvingly Dostoyevsky’s characterization of Germany as the “protesting Western empire”, never quite adopting or feeling at home with the inheritance of Rome. In the same year, Spengler wrote Decline of the West, and explicitly perceived in Russia a youthful vigor, primitiveness, and irrationality that contrasted with the senile high culture of the German and Western worlds. In Magic Mountain, Mann later used Clavdia Chauchat to personify the seductive dangers of Eastern (i.e. Russian) illogic.

Hermann Hesse declared that, for all their differences, Fyodor, Dmitri, Ivan, and Alyosha are actually all of one type; the Russian man. In them, he perceived that “the ideal of the Karamazov, primeval, Asiatic, and occult, is already beginning to consume the European soul”, which was leading to the downfall of Europe. In Hesse’s conception, the Russian man rejects inherited ethics and morals, and even beneficent Alyosha represents an “amoral impartiality.” Man is, Hesse says, halfway between animals and higher consciousness; the former restrained through the process of civilization and domestication. The Karamazovs represent the fraying of the ties.

Hesse proceeds, ominously, to notice that the Germans in particular are more vulnerable than any European people to the temptations of “all those evils which one may regard in different ways, but which collectively signify the Karamazov.” While he was prescient in anticipating some of what would follow, he was in the end too sanguine in his hope that the spiritual dislocation could remain limited to that. “It is possible that the whole Downfall of Europe will play itself out only inwardly, only in the souls of a generation, only in changing the meaning of worn-out symbols, in the dis-valuation of spiritual values.” Alas!

In general, it is interesting to trace the mutual obsession between Russia and Germany: how preoccupied each was with the respective supposedly corrupting influences; how urgent the question of the national soul was felt to be. Many of the analyses seem a bit contradictory—Hesse actually inverts Dostoyevsky, for whom “everything is permitted” nihilism is a Western import for which Russian Orthodoxy is the cure—but there’s a striking intensity in the attempts to apprehend.

Most of all, I’m struck by how anachronistic it all feels today: a country’s writers investigating the national soul and the nation’s fate through the lens of foreign literature.

Which novels or works of art do we use to understand our contemporary issues? Should we be using such works? Do they inform or do they mislead? Today, the US worries a lot about China, but this mostly manifests at the level of trade balances, AI policy, and military prowess. We don’t seem to worry much about the spiritual force of Chinese ideals, and for all of the policy fractiousness, China continues to import and absorb American culture with enthusiasm that is mostly undimmed. There is a genre of jeremiad and cultural analysis in the US that rhymes a little with early twentieth century German criticism, but it today tends to be much more clinical, hinging around PISA scores, smartphones, lower fertility, and not around higher aspirations and ideals as such. So, to what extent should there be analyses of the national soul? And to what extent should they connect with major novels and works of art?

text:
换句话说，如果能用上 Claude Code 和 ChatGPT 付费版，你可能就属于全球最顶尖的 0.2 % 人群。

但 Karpathy 的 0.2% 不止要会员，前沿模型 + 代码/数学 + 当饭碗用，三样都占才算数。

他今天把 4 月那条推文翻出来，说 AI 导致人与人差距的鸿沟在变宽，已经成了一个漏斗：

60 亿人几乎没碰过大模型
10–20 亿人偶尔用免费版，看到的是个有点傻的聊天机器人
2000 万人，0.2%，在代码和数学里职业化地用前沿模型，几周几个月的项目，一个 prompt 交给 agent 做完
5000 人，在实验室内部用着还没放出来的系统

漏斗为什么这么陡峭，他给了三个原因：

1. 影响随野心放大，一段话就能答完的问题，压根测不出它的上限，你得手里攥着一堆真正在乎的大难题

author: wquguru
quoted_text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

text:
Almost a year ago, UBS demonstrated its in-production tokenized fund workflow using @chainlink's Digital Transfer Agent standard.

Consider how many separate processes a fund transaction involves:

> An investor submits an order.
> Eligibility needs to be checked.
> The fund's NAV needs to be available.
> Cash and fund shares need to settle.
> Records across the relevant systems need to stay synchronized.

UBS's implementation combines DTA with CRE, CCIP, ACE and NAVLink to coordinate those processes, and shows that automating more of the fund's operations can reduce manual processing, improve settlement efficiency and allow asset managers to expand distribution without proportionally increasing operational complexity.

As tokenized funds scale, the infrastructure required to operate them becomes an increasingly important part of the opportunity. That infrastructure is Chainlink.

It was sold to 3 pre-named, linked wallets at $50–$100, while backing was up to ~$177. Their public desk's discount is capped at 7.5% by contract; these sales were ~90% below market.

Their Superstore docs say pTEAM NET pays a backing-neutrality fee so holders aren't diluted. Their RWA desks paid it. This desk paid it on 0 of 31 orders, about $331k of backing holders never got.
Those 3 wallets turned $137.5k into ~$1.37M, largely by selling into buys from the Sleeve, a Safe owned by the same single key that minted the NET.

VC rounds and OTC deals get announced, with a price and usually a lockup. This had no announcement, no lockup, and the protocol's own Safe was on the buy side within minutes.

text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.
author: zerohedge
quoted_text:
Judging by my tl there is a growing gap in understanding of AI capability.

The first issue I think is around recency and tier of use. I think a lot of people tried the free tier of ChatGPT somewhere  last year and allowed it to inform their views on AI a little too much. This is a group of reactions laughing at various quirks of the models, hallucinations, etc. Yes I also saw the viral videos of OpenAI's Advanced Voice mode fumbling simple queries like "should I drive or walk to the carwash". The thing is that these free and old/deprecated models don't reflect the capability in the latest round of state of the art agentic models of this year, especially OpenAI Codex and Claude Code.

But that brings me to the second issue. Even if people paid $200/month to use the state of the art models, a lot of the capabilities are relatively "peaky" in highly technical areas. Typical queries around search, writing, advice, etc. are *not* the domain that has made the most noticeable and dramatic strides in capability. Partly,  this is due to the technical details of reinforcement learning and its use of verifiable rewards. But partly, it's also because these use cases are not sufficiently prioritized by the companies in their hillclimbing because they don't lead to as much $$$ value. The goldmines are elsewhere, and the focus comes along.

So that brings me to the second group of people, who *both* 1) pay for and use the state of the art frontier agentic models (OpenAI Codex / Claude Code) and 2) do so professionally in technical domains like programming, math and research. This group of people is subject to the highest amount of "AI Psychosis" because the recent improvements in these domains as of this year have been nothing short of staggering. When you hand a computer terminal to one of these models, you can now watch them melt programming problems that you'd normally expect to take days/weeks of work. It's this second group of people that assigns a much greater gravity to the capabilities, their slope, and various cyber-related repercussions.

TLDR the people in these two groups are speaking past each other. It really is simultaneously the case that OpenAI's free and I think slightly orphaned (?) "Advanced Voice Mode" will fumble the dumbest questions in your Instagram's reels and *at the same time*, OpenAI's highest-tier and paid Codex model will go off for 1 hour to coherently restructure an entire code base, or find and exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems. This part really works and has made dramatic strides because 2 properties: 1) these domains offer explicit reward functions that are verifiable meaning they are easily amenable to reinforcement learning training (e.g. unit tests passed yes or no, in contrast to writing, which is much harder to explicitly judge),  but also 2) they are a lot more valuable in b2b settings, meaning that the biggest fraction of the team is focused on improving them. So here we are.

text: Informative discussion by very knowledgeable experts about the threat to modern cryptography posed by AI models. The good news is that the models can vet cryptosystems much faster than the human mathematicians we've relied on in the past, building trust and allowing more rapid deployment.
author: rhackett
quoted_text:
AI is getting better at solving hard math problems, especially given recent drops. But what does that mean for the cryptography that protects everything from private messages to healthcare to banking and crypto wallets?

Stanford cryptographer Dan Boneh, with @eddylazzarin, @SuccinctJT, @liz_harkavy, and @smc90, makes sense of the warnings sounded recently. They cover:

- what’s fact vs. assumption
- what’s new and what risks cryptographers have long prepared for
- where quantum computing doesn't (and does) fit
- opportunities for builders

Highlights:
00:37 – What sparked the most recent debate about AI and cryptography
01:35 – Signal vs. noise: What the math does and doesn’t tell us
05:29 – Why cryptography depends on open problems
09:25 – Why the stakes go beyond blockchains
10:43 – How AI could strengthen confidence in cryptography
13:50 – Considerations for users and institutions
20:10 – Where AI and quantum threats overlap
22:32 – Building systems that can change cryptographic methods
23:59 – Hash-based versus lattice-based cryptography
33:07 – Opportunities for builders, and better security tools
38:14 – What comes next if there were a cryptographic break?

这是一个高度集中、激进的AI主题2千万美金的投资组合（0杠，分配大概率维持到2028年底），围绕当前AI基础设施与变现链条构建，向“马斯克生态倾斜”和带“镐与铲”偏向，对SpaceX进行了刻意的大幅超配 。

1. SpaceX主导仓位（31%）
将SpaceX视为核心高上行仓位，而非卫星仓。它结合了发射基础设施、Starlink连接能力，以及AI相关敞口（通过xAI/Grok整合及更广泛的马斯克生态）。该仓位规模反映了对SpaceX具备超越纯AI硬件的多年增长期权的强烈看法。

2. 硬件为主的核心（约44%）
最大板块集中在半导体与光模块：
存储（美光 + SK海力士）——定位于HBM持续紧张及AI加速器需求。

定制硅与网络（博通、迈威尔、英特尔）——暴露于超大规模厂商定制ASIC及数据中心互联。

光模块（Coherent、Lumentum）——AI集群规模扩张推动高速光互联需求。

英伟达与AMD保持较小但存在的仓位，提供直接加速器敞口而不主导组合。

3. 选择性云/平台敞口（约20%）
Meta与谷歌为最大云端持仓，同时反映AI基础设施支出与应用层变现。亚马逊与微软经过前期减仓后仓位较小。其如加上SpaceX等，其实51% 都是云。

4. 特斯拉作为战术性AI/机器人袖套（5%）
特斯拉仓位有意义但非主导，捕捉自动驾驶、Optimus及Dojo相关AI敞口，而不使组合过度依赖。

5. 5% 现金 / 国债
永久性流动性缓冲，用于波动管理、机会性再平衡或新想法。这是有意设置，而非剩余现金。

整体方法
激进且集中：头部持仓按设计较大；组合接受较高的特异风险（尤其是SpaceX）以换取上行空间。

“镐与铲”偏向：硬件、存储与光模块获得的资本多于纯软件/应用名称。
马斯克生态倾斜：SpaceX（31%）+ 特斯拉（5%）= 合计36%敞口。

迭代优化：当前权重反映了多轮调整（移除台积电、降低英伟达、提升博通与美光、加入光模块名称、锁定现金）。

该结构适合优先考虑基础设施瓶颈与高信念个股的激进AI主题委托，而非广泛多元化。它具有较高波动性与单名风险，需根据AI资本开支趋势、存储定价及SpaceX特定发展进行主动监控。

text:
路透社今天早上发了一篇独家调查，披露杨植麟等月之暗面高管正在与杨植麟上一家创业公司循环智能及其部分投资人展开和解谈判。

这件事得从 2016 年说起。

当年杨植麟和张宇韬共同创办了循环智能，2023 年又创办了月之暗面。循环智能及部分投资人认为，当年的新公司在成立过程中，涉嫌未经授权使用原公司的技术和数据，甚至涉及服务器转移、关键数据删除和不实陈述。

这些目前都只是循环智能一方的指控，杨植麟此前否认过相关不当行为，代理律师也认为案件缺乏事实和法律依据。

当年月之暗面成立时，循环智能其实已经拿到了 9.5% 的初始股份。如今争议方又提出了相当于初始股本 10.5% 的补偿要求。按照知情人士的估算，考虑后续股权变化，这笔潜在赔偿仍可能超过 7 亿美元。

我觉得这件事有两个特别值得关注的地方。

首先，IPO 正在改变这场纠纷的谈判筹码。

2024 年双方开始打仲裁的时候，月之暗面还是一家快速成长的创业公司，大家有的是时间慢慢耗。现在上市窗口摆在面前，历史股权安排、技术资产权属、创始人的利益冲突，每一个都可能成为尽调和信息披露中必须解释的问题。

老股东显然也清楚这一点。公司估值越来越高，上市前解决纠纷的时间压力也越来越大。一场持续两年的仲裁，如今有了重新谈判的条件。

当然，即使最后双方达成和解，也不能据此认定相关指控成立。企业为了消除上市的不确定性而支付和解成本，本身就是一个商业决策。

其次，我觉得中国这一代 AI 创业公司，可能还有不少类似的历史问题尚未浮出水面。

过去几年大模型创业太热了，大量研究人员从高校、实验室和原有公司出来创业。团队拆分、技术迁移、股权重新分配，很多事情都发生在融资和产品快速推进的过程中。

但创始人脑子里的研究经验、原公司的训练代码、服务器里的实验数据，以及最终形成的模型能力，彼此之间的界限很难完全划清。

公司小时候，几个人坐下来谈一谈，拿几个点的股份，事情似乎就解决了。等公司估值涨到几百亿美元，当初每一个百分点的分配、每一份授权协议，都可能重新成为争议焦点。

中国大模型公司的 IPO 潮，值得关注的远不止收入、亏损和模型跑分。它也会是一次对过去几年中国 AI 创业史的集中清算。

那些在融资狂热时期被暂时搁置的股权、知识产权和公司治理问题，迟早要在公开市场面前给出交代。

月之暗面可能只是第一个被如此详细地摆到台面上的案例。

至于这场和解最后要花多少钱，我反而觉得是次要的。更值得追踪的是，一家 AI 公司的技术价值，到底应该如何在创始人、原公司和老股东之间划分。

这可能会成为下一轮中国 AI 创业分拆时，所有人都绕不开的问题。

The compliance and operations team has been replying to affected users. PDPC and relevant authorities has been informed, and a police report has been made. We are working closely with law enforcement on the card data breach incident. 

Card operations continue working as per normal. 

Our trading wallet and app is not affected by this. The wallet is self-custodial and we do not host the keys. 
Social logins are managed by Privy. You can continue to trade with Based. 

We've seen questions about an admin dashboard said to have leaked five months ago. That said “admin dashboard” is separate from our card operations and is not related to the card incident. It held no customer data. It was part of an early developer build of a managed OpenClaw product we prototyped in March 2026. We tested it with a small internal group, decided not to release it, and discontinued it shortly after.

Based has grown to where we are through various growth strategies. Hyperliquid lists a few example of frontends, but it’s ultimately the team’a responsibility to grow market share via their own means. We will continue to accelerate our growth via marketing in different channels.

For now our priority is to:

1. Continue to address and provide support for affected customers in data breach;
2. Further tightening security controls within team and enhancing monitoring;
3. Continue to build the best trading experience for our traders

text:
AI 强到让一小部分人彻底改变工作方式，同时又蠢到让绝大多数人觉得它不过如此。

Karpathy 今天重新翻出了今年 4 月的一条帖子，他发现，人类对 AI 的认知差距正在以一种非常夸张的速度扩大。

他粗略估算了一下全球人口：

60 亿人几乎没怎么接触过 LLM。

10 亿到 20 亿人偶尔使用免费版 ChatGPT，拿它搜索、写邮件，觉得还挺方便，但也就那么回事。

大约 2000 万专业人士，已经开始用前沿模型完成过去需要几周甚至几个月的编程和数学工作。

而最顶端，可能只有 5000 人能够接触到 AI 实验室内部的前沿系统。他们看到的是数千个 Agent 连续协作数周，挖掘零日漏洞、推进前沿数学研究，甚至开始出现人类理解和审查速度跟不上 AI 产出的情况。

今天我们讨论 AI 到底有多强，很大程度上取决于你站在这个漏斗的哪一层。

我以前总觉得，随着模型越来越便宜、越来越普及，这种认知差距迟早会缩小。但现在看来，情况可能恰恰相反。

因为 AI 的能力释放有一个很容易被忽略的前提，你得有足够复杂、足够有价值，而且能够验证结果的问题交给它。

你让 ChatGPT 帮忙写一封邮件，模型再强十倍，你也未必能感受到多大的变化。但如果你手里有一个原本需要十几个工程师干半年的项目，情况就完全不同了。

我们过去一直在讲 AI 会带来生产力平权，每个人都能拥有自己的超级助手。但至少在现阶段，最先享受到能力跃迁的人，往往已经拥有最好的技术背景、最贵的模型访问权限，以及最复杂的问题。

他们有能力把任务拆解成 AI 能执行和验证的工作，也有足够的预算让成百上千个 Agent 持续运行。AI 越强，这些人能够完成的项目就越大，积累的经验也越多。

这很可能形成一个正反馈。AI 一边降低了完成某件事的技术门槛，一边又在放大那些原本就拥有资源、判断力和复杂任务的人的优势。

当然，代码和数学领域的进展还不能直接外推到所有职业。现实世界有太多无法靠自动测试判断对错的事情。

但我现在越来越担心，等大多数人终于意识到前沿 AI 已经能做什么的时候，一部分人可能已经利用这段认知差，完成了好几轮生产力升级。

所以眼下围绕 AI 的很多争论才会显得特别割裂。

有人觉得 AI 泡沫快破了，因为他昨天让 Agent 做个 PPT，还是一塌糊涂。

有人觉得 AGI 已经近在眼前，因为他上周刚让 Agent 独立完成了过去需要整个团队才能做的工程。

两个人都在根据自己的真实经验做判断。

但他们看到的，已经快不是同一种技术了。
author: sleepy0x13
quoted_text:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

We were able to fine tune an open weight model (Qwen3.5-9B) on proprietary internal data at @coinbase, and it out performed frontier models, at much lower cost and speed, for a specialized task (fraud prevention in this case).

I think we'll see more of this pattern inside companies. The frontier models are amazing generalists. But increasingly you'll see specialist models out perform on more narrow tasks, either working on teams, or by themselves.

We're making it easy to fine tune models internally for our employees. We even have a skill for it in our internal harness that makes it easy to spin these up and start training them:

"/fine-tune-and-serve-llm I want to fine-tune Qwen for payments risk review. help me get started"

I imagine we'll have some backend services that could be replaced entirely by this new architecture.

我又又又发现了一个更好玩的地方，OneKey 今天更新最新用户协议，里面的签约主体，是香港 ONEKEY LIMITED。我顺藤摸瓜去查了查。

我查到这家公司的周年申报表显示，截至 2025 年 12 月 9 日，这家公司的已发行及已缴股本只有 1 港元。

中文用户跨境维权本来就难，如果签约主体没钱赔，又没有其他可追偿方，即使赢了官司，也可能拿不到钱。

还想问个问题，开曼母公司有没有法律上必须兜底的义务？有，请公布担保文件；没有，也请明确说明。

再看最新更新的赔偿条款：

第 15.4 条：在法律允许的最大范围内，对数字资产损失免责，无论损失由何种原因造成。

第 15.5 条：如果仍被认定要赔，一般累计上限是以下三项取最高值：涉案设备或备份产品的实付价格、事发前 12 个月支付给 OneKey 的相关服务费、100 美元。三项不相加，也不是保证赔付。

有些 KOL 收钱推广硬件钱包，安全性吹得天花乱坠，连最基本的用户协议都没看过。

厂家自身的安全缺陷导致用户丢币，赔不赔？赔多少？谁来赔？这些直接关系到用户利益的条款，好歹看一遍，提醒一下粉丝。

推广时只讲好处，出了问题就悄悄隐身，再用一句“我也不知情”推得干干净净。钱你收了，风险全让粉丝承担。

连这些最基本的功课都不做，还谈什么对粉丝负责？你不过是把粉丝当成赚钱的工具，用完就丢。

注：本推文引用 OneKey《用户协议》2026.10 版，最后更新于 2026 年 10 月 11 日。目前协议正文仅提供英文，点击中文版也会跳转到英文版。原文链接放在下方，大家可以自行查阅核对。

text:
英伟达投资了一家能让客户更容易换掉英伟达芯片的公司。现在，亚马逊想花 70 亿美元把它买走。

《华尔街日报》最新报道，亚马逊正在谈判收购 AI 创业公司 Decart。这个价格比它今年 5 月近 40 亿美元的估值高了 75%。

Decart 最早靠 AI 实时生成游戏世界的 Oasis 出圈，后来又做了视频模型 Lucy。但我觉得，真正让巨头们盯上它的，是底层一套叫 DOS（Decart Optimization Stack）的软件系统。

这套系统能帮开发者在英伟达 GPU、亚马逊 Trainium、Google TPU 等不同芯片上运行和优化 AI 模型，降低迁移成本。

亚马逊、Google 这些年都在拼命造自己的 AI 芯片，理论性能和成本已经很有竞争力，但英伟达真正难以撼动的地方，一直是 CUDA 积累起来的软件生态。

客户的模型、代码、工程团队都围着这套生态转，光靠一颗更便宜的芯片，很难让人愿意搬家。

所以 Decart 的收购故事特别有意思。

英伟达自己投过它，还曾经谈过收购。后来 Anthropic 加入竞争，一度推进到尽调阶段，却在 9 月放弃。现在亚马逊又报出了 70 亿美元。

实际上，双方早就有合作。2025 年亚马逊给了 Decart 提前接触 Trainium3 的机会，AWS 后来披露，Decart 的实时视频生成推理在 Trainium3 上实现了相较 GPU 约 4 倍的速度、约一半的成本。

过去几年巨头们花了几千亿美元建设 AI 算力，大家都想摆脱对英伟达的依赖，但硬件投入只是第一步。谁能降低模型在不同芯片之间迁移的成本，谁才有机会真正改变算力市场的竞争格局。

当然，我还有个疑问。

Decart 之所以值钱，恰恰因为它能在不同厂商的芯片上工作。如果它最后被亚马逊买走，Google、英伟达以及其他云厂商还愿不愿意使用这套软件？

一家靠跨芯片兼容性建立价值的公司，被一家拼命推广自家芯片的巨头收购，这里面的利益冲突其实很值得观察。

70 亿美元能买下一套技术，但未必能买到整个行业对它的信任。

base:0x940181a94a35a4569e4529a3cdfb74e38fd98631 looks primed to rip higher over the next 10 days before the Aero upgrade

I had previously weighted base:0x940181a94a35a4569e4529a3cdfb74e38fd98631 slightly lower in my core positions because I worried that the tokenomics were too complicated for institutions and whales to understand and feel comfortable bidding. 

@citrini not only included base:0x940181a94a35a4569e4529a3cdfb74e38fd98631 in their token basket, they had it at the same weight as $HYPE and nearly twice the weight of ethereum:0x1f9840a85d5af5bf1d1762f925bdaddc4201f984. Don't think the market has fully digested how much that stamp of approval means.

I also worried that there could be some last minute delay, as the previous Aero launch date delay led to a considerable nuke.

With the greenlight for launch on 10/21 and the recognition from Citrini, both of those risks are removed, and I now feel considerably higher conviction on base:0x940181a94a35a4569e4529a3cdfb74e38fd98631. 

Previously to the Citrini piece, I expected most people to stay sidelined and wait for the flywheel to fundamentally prove itself post Aero upgrade. @wagmiAlexander expects spot volumes to roughly double by EOY, so that was my timeline where a rerating would organically occur without speculative fervor. 

I'm now of the opinion that this recent bit of attention will cause price to lead fundamentals, and we might actually get a real pre-upgrade breakout. 

The early August 2025 price action where base:0x940181a94a35a4569e4529a3cdfb74e38fd98631 doubled from $0.75 to $1.50 in just 10 days is a good example of what I think could happen in the pre-upgrade window. Due to how much supply is locked in LPs and veAERO, base:0x940181a94a35a4569e4529a3cdfb74e38fd98631 is naturally extremely reflexive.

It's very difficult to justify why ethereum:0x1f9840a85d5af5bf1d1762f925bdaddc4201f984 is trading at 5x the market cap of base:0x940181a94a35a4569e4529a3cdfb74e38fd98631. I don't expect parity until after the upgrade, but I do think there's a world where base:0x940181a94a35a4569e4529a3cdfb74e38fd98631 rerates to 50% of ethereum:0x1f9840a85d5af5bf1d1762f925bdaddc4201f984 market cap as the sidelined scramble to get exposure prior to the 10/21 upgrade. This coincides nicely with a run at the previous base:0x940181a94a35a4569e4529a3cdfb74e38fd98631 ATH of ~$2.30.

再转发这场李录哥大对谈，有三点分享：

第一点："Wealth, in the end, is really the percentage ownership of global purchasing power."（财富归根到底，是你在全球购买力中所占的百分比。）

用我自己的话解读：定投指数，本质上就是在买世界经济增长的一小部分份额。这么做的目的不是追求最大收益，只要分母涨的时候你也在船上。

第二点我最喜欢，最认同："If you can compound your knowledge sustainably, eventually your capital will compound as well."（如果你能让知识持续复利，资本的复利早晚会来。）

复利大家都听过，但因果顺序别搞反：先有知识的复利，才有资本的复利。知识复利是最慢的，也是唯一不会被市场先生没收的。

这一场对谈里还有一句：“复利最基本的前提，就是不要失去你已经拥有的东西”。不只指本金，还包括你的知识、信任和健康。

第三点，我去查了李录过去的持仓：2019年底建仓美光，一度占13F组合100%，成本50多块。2022年存储寒冬，美光从90多跌到50，腰斩——他拿住了，没卖。2023年二季度，60多块清仓，持有3.5年。然后HBM大行情启动。

连李录都会卖飞，“拿得住”个字，含金量比想象中还高。
author: KelseyDingMD
quoted_text:
但斌分享，李录哥大对谈44分钟

假期回来花时间回顾了一下李录的访谈，先把这场会的"底细"交代清楚。

2026年10月5日，纽约时间中午12点到1点半，整整90分钟，地点是第五大道的大都会俱乐部，不是商学院教室。

哥大海尔布伦中心有个坚持多年的传统：这个以《证券分析》两位作者命名的午餐会，35届以来从不发布官方录像和文字稿——1991年第一届如此，这一届也如此。

所以我们现在能看到的一切，源头是同一个人：但斌。他在现场用手机拍了8段视频，北京时间10月6日凌晨5点半发上微博，聪明投资者随后用whisper转写英文原声、人工校对排序，拼出了约44分钟的有效内容——刚好覆盖全场一半。

换句话说，你看到的所有"全文实录"，一半是现场原话，一半是整理者依据李录过去两三年的公开框架补全的，读的时候心里得有这根弦。

李录，1966年生于唐山，喜马拉雅资本创始人及董事长；哥伦比亚大学经济学学士、MBA、法学博士（三学位）；查理·芒格家族资产管理人，管理资产规模约$150亿；哥伦比亚大学董事会成员，加州理工学院董事。

01｜开场先讲六条原则

前三条是格雷厄姆的：股票是公司所有权、市场先生为你服务而非指导你、未来不可预测所以要安全边际。

第四条巴菲特加了能力圈，第五条芒格加了"去有鱼的地方钓鱼"，重点在第六条——李录自己的贡献，以下是现场英文原话：

"Wealth, in the end, is really the percentage ownership of global purchasing power. It isn't really expressed, especially in the modern economy, in the amount of gold and diamonds or currencies of any kind." （财富归根到底，是你在全球购买力中所占的百分比，而不是黄金、钻石或任何货币的数量。）

02｜经典问答一：那个"半神的IPO"

主持人Tano Santos问他怎么看当下市场的极端集中，李录先抛数据：标普2010年以来年化14%-15%，但2000到2010年几乎为零，26年拉平就是高个位数——这才是锚。

然后他讲了自己刚读过的一份募资文件（懂得都懂，我就不写公司名字了），收尾时全场大笑，英文原话是：

"In my view, you don't have to participate in the prospectus that calls itself an IPO of a demigod." （在我看来，你不必参与那份自称"半神IPO"的募资文件。）

03｜经典问答二：AI是工具还是造物

这是全场最长的一段，18分58秒。

李录的判断是：AI永远有随用量增长的增量成本，和互联网"一次投入长期摊销"完全两样，所以财务纪律永远在场，"我们很可能会经历不止一轮巨大的繁荣和巨大的崩溃"。

红线只有一条，他的英文原话：

"It cannot be without a human in the loop. In other words, firmly establish it on the tool side rather than the creature side." （绝不能没有人参与其中。换句话说，要把它牢牢钉在"工具"这一侧，而不是"造物"那一侧。）

04｜经典问答三：教堂旁边，永远连着赌场

有学生问该怎么选职业路径，李录回了巴菲特那个著名比喻，然后加了自己的一层：

"This is the basic setup, a church with a casino attached to it, as part of the permitting process because of the human condition." （基本格局就是这样：一座教堂，旁边连着一个赌场，这是人性决定了的、拿施工许可时必须附带的一部分。）

教堂这一侧是双赢、给社会创造净收益；赌场那一侧是零和、是社会成本。

两边永远共存，因为这就是人性。

选哪边，是你的事。

05｜经典问答四：加密货币（此段视频未拍到，以下为中文整理版）

有学生问怎么看加密货币，李录答得毫不客气："我的回答非常简单，我根本不去想它。从根本上说，我认为它就是个虚假的东西……一种真正能被兑现、被接受的货币，背后必须存在可以强制执行的制度和力量。

李录：如果让我说，干脆禁止掉可能大家都会过得更好。

06｜经典问答五：收尾的人生复利

最后一个问题问他过去十年学到了什么。他说每过十年都发现自己学到了太多东西，以至于某种程度上变成了另一个人。然后落在那句被疯传的话上：

"而复利最基本的一个前提其实就是：不要失去你已经拥有的东西。这不仅仅包括资本，也包括你的知识、信任关系、智慧，甚至健康。" （If you can compound your knowledge sustainably, eventually your capital will compound as well.）

07｜李录重申的六条投资原则

哥大演讲中，李录再次强调了几条价值投资的基本原则：

股票代表公司所有权。 买股票，本质上是买下一门生意，而不是买一张可以随时转手的交易凭证。

市场先生为你服务，不是指导你。 市场价格是机会来源，不是判断企业价值的唯一标准。

未来不可预测，所以需要安全边际。 预测越不确定，买入价格越重要。

理解能力圈的边界。 知道自己懂什么很重要，知道自己不懂什么同样重要。

去有鱼的地方钓鱼。 注意力会带来竞争，竞争会侵蚀回报；被忽略的市场有时更容易找到好价格。

在有活力的经济体，以合理价格买入优秀企业并长期持有。 财富的本质不是账户里有多少货币，而是这些资产最终能换取多少真实商品与服务。

08｜他说的，和他的13F对得上

8月14日披露的Q2 13F：喜马拉雅美股持仓37亿美元，压进8只票。谷歌A+C合计约48%纹丝不动；拼多多加仓133.5%至1076万股、占比22.2%，伯克希尔加仓23%至15%，华美银行、Crocs、腾讯音乐、苹果未动。同时一季度刚建仓的穆迪、标普全球、MSCI、H&R Block，加上美国银行、西方石油，六只一个季度内全部清掉。

有数据机构回算，他加拼多多的平均成本约92美元，6月底浮亏约8%——下跌途中一路买，这很李录。

另外还有个细节值得玩味：这场饭局的"菜单"上，开场主持人还介绍了哥大学生组合今年的新买入——Equifax、Humana，还有日本自行车零件巨头禧玛诺。

大师在台上讲道，学生在台下管钱，这也是哥大这个中心35年一直在做的事。

教堂旁边永远连着赌场，李录36年前在那间教室选了教堂。最近这两年，赌场门口排队买"半神"的队伍很长，而那个从唐山到哥大的人，还在用老办法钓鱼。

另：访谈中还有关于ZG经济的看法，谈的很委婉这里就不再赘述。

text:
You carry the fractures inside,
the hidden cracks left behind when the world was ruthless,
and people who should have been careful
handled your heart with reckless, dirty hands.
You learned to pull the coat tight, to look at the horizon,
and tell yourself it can’t rain every day.

Hurt tries to tell you that you are nothing,
that the darkness is your permanent address.
It wants to slow your pulse until you stop fighting the current.

But you are a shark in the deep water.
You do not have the luxury of standing still, you only know how to move forward.

The healing doesn’t come from a soft, easy promise.
It comes from the grit in your teeth,
the raw, unyielding instinct that refuses to let the shadows win.
Every single blow that was meant to break you
only made the shell thicker, the spine straighter, the resolve absolute.

You are still here, breathing the cool air,
standing tall in a world that tried to flatten you.

So let the music hit your chest like a physical force.
Let the internal fire burn out the old static.
You have survived every midnight stretch they threw at you,
and you are walking out of the dark, completely unbroken,
because the light inside you is a fire they can never put out.

text:
I am getting lots of incoming questions about the public execution of Nidal Hasan, mostly because I have been outspoken on wanting public executions for over a decade.

My position is simple:  Executions should be public and brutal, not private and medicalized.  They are the ultimate example of the state's monopoly on violence, and the only way to keep that from running out of control is to confront voters with the trade they have made every single time, that they might have appropiate confidence or revulsion in the institution.

This is not new thinking.  George Washington thought the same.  The way we have shifted from hanging to firing squads to doctors quietly injecting chemicals that send our worst gently off to sleep is awful and dystopian, a total short-circuiting of important feedback mechanisms.  It makes needless executions more likely, not less so.  People who demean this as barbaric or yucky miss the whole point.  It doesn't somehow become torture or inhumane (as the UN is suddenly claiming) just because we decline to hide the act behind a curtain.

And then there are those who suggest any revel in the death of those who truly deserve it is an indicator of a broken or diseased mind.  To the contrary.  It is normal, good, and aligned with our natural and national order.  That it has not been done here in 60 years is an indictment in and of itself.

And that is without even getting into the fact that men were not hung for stealing horse, but that horses may not be stolen.

"I would to God that one of the most attrocious in each State was hung in Gibbets, up on a gallows five times as high as the one prepared by Haman. No punishment, in my opinion, is too great for the Man, who can build his greatness upon his Country’s ruin." 
- George Washington, 1778

quoted_text:
In 1975, Steve Jobs told Steve Wozniak that Atari had paid them $700 for a game they built together. He handed Woz a check for $350.

Atari had actually paid Jobs about $5,000.

In the video below, Woz says: "Who cares about money? Well, you do care about friendship and honesty."

Jobs was working the night shift at Atari. The company wanted a new arcade game called Breakout, built with as few chips as possible.

Jobs couldn't build it. Woz could. He already had a full-time job at Hewlett-Packard, and Jobs said they had four days. Woz went four days with no sleep. Both of them came down with mono.

Woz did it in 45 chips. Atari's own engineers were using 150 or more.

He took his $350 and was happy with it. Jobs took the rest and went up to Oregon to buy into a farm.

About ten years later, Woz read the real number in a book about Atari. By then the two of them had built Apple, and Woz was a multimillionaire.

If Jobs had just told him he needed the money, Woz says, "I would say take it all."

It wasn't the last time. Before Apple went public in 1980, Jobs refused to give stock options to Daniel Kottke, his friend since college, who had helped build the first Apple computers.

Woz did the opposite. He sold his own shares cheaply to Kottke and other early employees who had been left out.

One friend kept almost all of a $5,000 bonus. The other gave away millions.

Was Jobs a genius who knew what business takes, or just a bad friend?

you wanna know why crypto is just speculation and gambling now? 

put yourself in the shoes of an actual dev who showed up to the space relatively early, say 2018-2020. 

consider what it feels like to be someone with an elite background putting in 60-100h weeks every week, while watching people who trade full-time out earn you on a weekly basis 

consider watching the other builders who take the predatory deals from VCs get rich by dumping on their community and then retiring with no consequences 

consider how it feels to have your treasury get destroyed by FTX or Anchor and to be left with nothing while half the people involved just walk away 

how many would still be left? 10%, 20%? 

then go through the pumpfun era. watch people who launch bundled scams calling themselves "devs" and once again, out-earning you 

march through multiple bear markets, do it all without rugging, and watch the protocols who fuck people over win over and over and over again 

deal with the fact that everyone outside of tech assumes you are the same sort of person as the people who retired off rugs, think about how it feels to be labelled a "crypto scammer" by default if you talk about your job as one of the only people trying to actually build things 

then, after all that, consider that a new, uber-fast moving industry full of new frontier tech shows up next door and sucks up all the VC funding 

would you still be in "Web3"? would you still be committed To The Vision? 

no, you would not. you'd either rug, or move on. and that's what everybody did.

quoted_text:
大概理解了，說一說我的看法：

1.  @yetone 暴怒/回懟是有正當理由的： @Seefs_ 這句「一開始也沒打算把控住」屬於未審先判，只用想當然爾的方式提出結論，沒有任何佐證自己說法的資料（哪怕指出產品的任何缺陷也好），這看在開發者眼裡和走在路上被人抹屎差不多

2.  @ThirteenYizuka 的評論字面意義上合理，但放在這個語境下屬於「正確的廢話」。同樣的照樣造句，我可以拿來質疑別人的產品、評論者的利益歸屬、甚至是各位翻牆的正當性！  

3. 承上，什麼樣的評論才不是廢話呢？就是可「證偽」或「方向明確」的文字

@ThirteenYizuka 最後那一句「究竟經過了怎樣的審查和驗證」乍聽一下合理，但細想一下，就算 @yetone 回覆自證了又怎樣呢？  他又沒提出什麼標準或告訴大家「怎樣才是好的方式」，因此往後的討論只會淪為無意義的浪費精力， @yetone 直接回懟的作法才是幫我們省了時間

4. 承上，那怎麼樣的批評才不會變成上述的廢話呢？我的話會用「可比較的對象」或「具體的細節」來展開討論

例如：「那個類似 magpie 的產品用了 XXX 方法來做測試，出來的 feature 達成 OOO 的效果，你要不要考慮看看？」

或者：「我發現 magpie 在 XXX 有問題，在 vibe coding 時是否可以加入更多 harness，這些我寫的測試先放在 PR 裡面了」  

用我的方式提出批評，我不相信 @yetone 反應會這麼大  

5. 總結來說，我認為上面提到的兩個帳號其評論實在沒建設性，屬於不說比說出來好的情況。有些開發者可能會用友好的方式回應，但 @yetone 直接回懟我認為是沒問題的（甚至還省了大家時間呢） 

有些人覺得 @yetone 說話態度有問題，但要知道浪費公眾/開發者的時間與精力這檔子事，可比前者嚴重的多啊！

6. 回到 @iseki_zero  你最開始主題：「開源能不能批評」

當然是可以的！社交平台上想發什麼內容都是個人的自由意志，只要沒有違反 user term 說的多難聽都可以。但相對地，別人也可以對批評的內容做出自己的評論，同樣說的多難聽都可以

真正的「不能批評」不是積極回擊，而是從根本上否定你你說話的權利，這個區別是很重要的

author: HarryStebbings
quoted_text:
Podcasts frustrate me because they are fluffy and high-level.

This is the most in-depth discussion on the framework that @tryramp have used to hire, monitor, and scale their sales team.

- Why you should overpay reps

- Why you should cancel forecasting calls

- Why bankers make the best reps

- Why comp plans are BS and you should not have one to start

@max11free, SVP of Sales is truly epic here and my notes from the discussion below.

-- 

1. Why You Should Overpay Your Sales Reps

The early bet was to pay SDRs well above market rate and expect output well above market in return. Reps earn 2X a standard SDR but book 40, 50 or 60 meetings, four to six times the usual target, so the unit economics still work.

2. You Have to Treat Hiring a Sales Team Like Moneyball: How to Find Hidden Talent

Go-to-market recruiting should follow Billy Beane, targeting top sellers at companies that grew revenue past nine figures despite a low NPS score. Those reps had to create their own demand, work complex cycles with weak third-party reviews and sell at a premium to cheaper rivals. The number one or two seller there can thrive in a system like Ramp.

Single biggest advice on finding hidden gem talent @rabois?

3. Why Bankers Make Great Sales Reps

Bankers are programmed to work, and a nine-to-five is foreign to them. Before the company had brand recognition, a cold call to a CFO from someone who had just left Goldman TMT IB carried weight. Early sales teams lack time to teach cold call and email basics, so bankers kept the team in pure execution mode.

Find this also @PeetsChad

4. Why I Advise Not to Have a Comp Plan

Founders are advised to pay 100% OTE for at least the first two quarters instead of setting a comp plan. A quota set too low can be blown out in six months, leaving the company owing a seller multiple six figures. A target picked arbitrarily can also prove unattainable and stall momentum.

Haha, interested to hear your thoughts on this one @Carles_Reina 

5. Never Hire Sales Reps One at a Time

Hiring one seller or SDR at a time leaves no way to benchmark performance, and comparing them against the founder is not reasonable. Onboarding is laborious and expensive, so hiring in pairs is better, bringing competition and collaboration and keeping reps from being lonely.

6. Why the Most Annoying Sales Reps Tend to Be the Most Successful

Sellers who constantly ask about account strategy, pipeline and product during onboarding show a direct correlation with being incredible. Quiet reps, or those asking questions an AI or Notion bot could answer, usually give a weak signal, though the inverse is not always true.

7. What Should Sales Talent Focus on When Deciding Which Company to Join?

Sellers joining an early-stage company should not index on equity, cash and comp, but on the market, the talent density of the business and the founders. Taking a VP title and lots of equity at a mediocre business growing 20 to 30% a year is the wrong trade.

text:
这才是真正的派发！但，也没那么可怕。

数据显示：10月7日至8日长期持有者（LTH）累计向交易所转入约3.2w枚BTC。这是自今年2月5日大跌后，第2大LTH单日转入规模（图1）。

如果这些筹码不是用于币本位合约保证金（事实上OI也没有增加这么多），那么大概率是潜在的卖出意图。

不过，这3.2w枚BTC并不能全部视为LTH的主动派发。

因为就在同一时期，美国政府相关钱包向Coinbase Prime转入了约1.72万枚BTC（币龄1-2年）。

考虑到Coinbase Prime是美国法警署指定的官方托管和交易服务商，因此，这笔转账并不必然意味着卖出，也可能与资产托管整合或案件处置有关（图2）。

剔除这部分特殊转账后，剩余约1.48w枚才是我们更需要关注的潜在抛压，主要来自币龄6-12个月及3-5年的长期筹码。

在熊牛过渡期，LTH日均向交易所转入2000-3000枚BTC，通常属于正常范围。一旦转入量突然大幅超过均值，往往伴随着特殊事件或行预期偏空。

但问题是，“行情下跌+LTH筹码派发”，就一定是坏事吗？我认为：未必如此！尤其是在熊牛过渡阶段。

从实体调整后的CDD（币天销毁量）数据来看，每当行情回调且CDD大幅上升（图3），往往意味着部分沉寂已久的筹码开始活跃，甚至选择离场。

（CDD的计算方法是将BTC的花费数量乘以持有天数，所以CDD暴涨，即代表有“老币”被大量花费）

但事后看，下跌虽然带来了短期抛压，却也促使部分不坚定的筹码完成换手。潜在的卖盘提前释放，反而为后续行情减轻阻力。

如果把观察周期拉长，这种现象就更容易理解。

在完整的牛市进程中，随着价格不断上涨，越来越多持有时间更长的筹码，也会逐渐加入派发行列。

这种变化通常会推动LTH-ASOL（长期持有者已花费输出平均币龄）曲线逐步抬升（图4）。因为当被花费的老筹码占比提高时，整体平均币龄也会随之增加。

例如，10月8日当天被花费的LTH筹码，平均币龄达到712天，而7月14日只有651天。

这意味着，参与链上转移的长期筹码正在呈现更明显的老龄化特征。

从另一个角度来看，这也是牛市进程中，长期沉淀的筹码逐渐被激活、换手活跃度不断提升的一种表现。

所以，我们不必对每一次LTH派发都过度担忧。真正值得关注的，是这些筹码能否被市场有效承接。

毕竟，一轮牛市不可能只有买入而没有卖出。老筹码持续释放，新资金不断承接，本身就是市场完成价值再发现的过程。

只要需求能够有效消化供给，阶段性的派发不能成为趋势的阻碍。充分的筹码换手，反而是一轮行情能够走得更远的重要基础。

5.5万枚BTC去哪了？$83K-$84K筹码峰正在透露一个重要信号

在9/21 BTC首次冲高至$87K后至今，交易所余额从高点回落约5.5w枚BTC（图1）。

同期持有>100k和10k-100k的地址合计减少约5.5w枚，而持有1k-10k的地址增加了5万（图2-4），数量几乎一一对应。

对长期趋势来说，这是积极的信号。说明之前堆积到交易所的筹码开始被接走了。

1000 倍杠杆、亏损挖矿，Papertrade 上线就遇操纵争议

玩合约亏了钱，平台给你发币；质押这些币，还能分走平台之后的部分收入。Papertrade 想用“亏损挖矿”吸引交易者，但 10 月 10 日刚上线，就遇到了价格操纵争议。

这个永续合约平台建在 HyperEVM 上，支持用 USDC 做多或做空 BTC、ETH，最高杠杆达 1000 倍。交易的对手方由协议自己的 USDC 资金池承担：你赚了，池子付钱；你亏了，损失流入池子，协议再按规则给你铸造 PAPER。

PAPER 可以质押，按份额分享部分协议收入，以及资金池超过规定门槛后的额外收益，分配用 USDC 支付。早期奖励较高，同样亏一笔钱，可以换到更多 PAPER。

quoted_text:
thank you everyone for your participation and support through papertrade's launch.

we flipped the stock market’s volume in the first 6 hours. one day after launch, papertrade is a fully working 1000x exchange with 5m in the LP and has paid out 25M to stakers.

addressing two points that have come up:

-it was never possible to allow small notional to have the same priority as large notional. it opens the frontend up to spam congestion, which would have been infinitely worse than the existing queue. we designed the fair launch to be as inclusive as possible given those constraints.

-speaking of constraints, the overnight manipulation attempts on btc/eth on the hl bbo were not an oversight in the mechanism design we spent six months working on. these were always accounted for and only possible because the oi caps were extremely permissive for launch congestion. any oi cap during the queued launch demand would have exacerbated the slow experience, and the queue itself provided a natural protection against manipulation as confirming opens/closes had non-deterministic timing. as the congestion rolled off, we began the process of tightening up oi caps both onchain and at the relayer level. in a system like this, a manipulation attack is always possible - whether economically advantageous to attempt is the question. our goal is to set the parameters such that it is almost never profitable, and that the risk is extremely high/-EV at the tail even when it does work. evidence of this can be seen in the user that won overnight and continued to try again, ultimately donating almost all his profit back to the house via new accounts, without accounting for the cost of manipulating the bbo on hyperliquids side. a number of users equally opted to "undo" their manipulated trades in exchange for their farmed paper.

we are proud to be the first through the wall with this mechanism, at scale, in an adversarial environment. the market parameters cannot give undue advantage to either house or trader, such that the system becomes unstable and we have thought about these risks continuously since we began on this journey.

good luck to us.

most people trying to get hired right now are doing it backwards

they send 300 applications, tweak the same résumé, get ghosted, and blame the market

but a résumé only says what you could do

here's what the people getting hired rn are doing instead: they pick one company they actually want, find something broken or missing in their product, and build the fix in a weekend with Claude Code, Codex, or Grok Bot

then they send it straight to someone who can say yes. no cover letter, just a link and two sentences on what it does

a hiring manager skims a hundred résumés a week. almost nobody sends them a working fix for their own product

it works outside of tech too. a marketing plan for their next launch, a cleaned-up onboarding flow, a better version of their worst landing page

try it this week: open the product of the company you want to work at most and write down the first three things that annoy you

if you can't find one, you don't know the company well enough to work there

the job market hasn’t disappeared

it just stopped rewarding people who only apply instead of build

text:
New paper from the team at Sakana AI:
Recursive Self-Improvement through Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS)

How do we keep improving AI when the tasks become too complex for humans to reliably evaluate?

For open-ended research, we eventually hit a "supervision bottleneck." If we use the model itself as the solver, optimizer, and evaluator, it gets trapped in a homogeneous loop, reinforcing its own blind spots rather than correcting them.

To break this loop, we drew inspiration from Marvin Minsky’s Society of Mind. What if you prompt a single model to organize copies of itself into a structured team, then distill what the team learned back into the base model?

MASS alternates between two loops:

1/ Workflow Optimization: the model iteratively evolves its own multi-agent workflows, figuring out how subagents should communicate and route information to each other.

2/ Workflow Internalization: fine-tune the shared model on the successful multi-agent trajectories so the coordination behavior gets baked into the weights.

After two cycles with a 27B open-weights model, performance improved 1.2-1.6x per output token on tough research benchmarks (MLR-Bench, ScienceAgentBench, DSBench).

Multi-agent traces were also much better training data than single-agent ones. The model learns faster from jointly learning high-level orchestration and bounded subagent execution. The results showing that the model can bootstrap its own coordination skills by organizing copies of itself into teams feels promising as a mechanism towards self-improvement.

Blog: https://t.co/rTEQ5mJxS8
Paper: https://t.co/kRvqLHxpOM

Incredible work by Hyunin Lee, Jinglue Xu, Jeffrey Seely, Yujin Tang, and our collaborators from UC Berkeley (Somayeh Sojoudi, Matei Zaharia, Donghyun Lee)!
author: hardmaru
quoted_text:
Introducing Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS): Recursive self-improvement through collective intelligence

Blog: https://t.co/LkQe5k7jOW

As AI systems tackle increasingly open-ended research problems, human experts may struggle to assess results and guide further progress. The model itself may be the best available optimizer and evaluator. The challenge is obtaining useful self-supervision within that homogeneous loop, where a model risks reinforcing its own blind spots rather than correcting them.

We ask whether a model can learn from the collective intelligence of its own team.

We introduce Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS). One shared model solves tasks through a team of virtual subagents, searches for better multi-agent workflows, then uses its own judgments to select the best ones.

Training on the best team’s executions provides self-supervision by distilling the team’s collective experience into the shared model.

We ran two cycles using a 27B open-weights model on synthetic open-ended research tasks. After the second cycle, score per output token reached 1.2-1.6x the base model's level across four research benchmarks.

Three key results:

First, MASS enables role generalization within an RSI loop: training only on task-solving data from the optimizee naturally improves the capabilities of both the optimizer and the evaluator.

Second, multi-agent trajectories are more efficient training data than single-agent trajectories for RSI.

Third, optimizer capacity, rather than evaluator capacity, can be the bottleneck in the speed of improvement.

We believe the community needs to investigate homogeneous RSI carefully to support AI safety. When a model is also its own evaluator, shared blind spots could allow mistakes to be accepted as progress and reinforced through training. For AI to improve beyond human expertise safely, we need to understand these failures and preserve effective ways to detect them and intervene.

Paper: https://t.co/SzXDlAzrUO
Code: https://t.co/xc870ZHRgh

This work was a collaboration with researchers at UC Berkeley.

✅ 团队代币 TGE 零解锁
✅ 私募投资者 TGE 零解锁
✅ 团队和私募均有 12 个月锁定期，随后 24 个月逐月释放
这意味着初期不会直接面临团队和私募的大规模解锁抛压。
当然，初始流通量低不代表一定上涨，后续生态及社区代币释放仍然值得关注。

💎 四、这次空投到底值多少钱？
我们可以简单算笔账。
假设 $AXIS 上线 FDV 分别达到：
▪️ $100M FDV：全部社区空投价值 $10M
▪️ $200M FDV：全部社区空投价值 $20M
▪️ $300M FDV：全部社区空投价值 $30M
▪️ $500M FDV：全部社区空投价值 $50M

如果按照 $300M FDV 来计算：
第一季 4% 空投总价值就是 1,200 万美元，其中 TGE 解锁部分价值约 600 万美元。
注意，这只是不同估值下的理论计算，不是价格预测，也不代表每个参与者都能拿到空投。

👀 五、我的看法
我觉得 Axis 这次代币经济学最值得关注的，不是 10 亿枚的总供应量，而是它明确拿出 10% 给社区贡献者。
之前大家在平台上操控机器人、完成训练任务、积累 Axis Points，最担心的就是最后空投比例太小。

现在至少知道整个社区空投池有 1 亿枚，而且第一季就有 4,000 万枚。
再加上团队和私募 TGE 零解锁，整体分配结构对早期贡献者相对友好。
当然，最终每个人能分到多少，还得看积分与空投的具体兑换和分配规则。

现在我最关心的只有两个问题：
1️⃣ TGE 到底什么时候来？
2️⃣ 大家手里的 Axis Points 最终能换到多少 $AXIS？
之前一直在刷 Axis 的朋友，你们现在都攒了多少积分？
